FIGURE TECHNOLOGY SOLUTIONS $FIGR Q3'26 — REVENUE SURGES 84%, LOAN VOLUME MORE THAN DOUBLES AND PROFITABILITY REMAINS STRONG
Figure delivered record quarterly revenue and strong marketplace growth, supported by increasing adoption of its blockchain-based lending infrastructure. What caught my attention was the rapid expansion of Figure Connect and its shift towards a capital-light business model.
THE NUMBERS
🔹 Net Revenue: $287.1M (Est. $249.5M) 🟢; +84% YoY
🔹 Adjusted Net Revenue: $283.3M (+83% YoY)
🔹 GAAP EPS: $0.36 (Est. $0.31) 🟢; vs $0.34 LY
🔹 Net Income: $89.3M vs $89.8M LY
🔹 Adjusted EBITDA: $163.6M (+91% YoY)
🔹 Adjusted EBITDA Margin: 58% vs 55% LY 🟢
🔹 Net Income Margin: 31% vs 57% LY
Q4 GUIDANCE
🔹 Loan Marketplace Volume: $6.2B–$6.7B
🔹 Gross Take Rate: 3.1%–3.4%
Management expects continued marketplace expansion, although the lower take-rate outlook reflects changing business mix.
MARKETPLACE PERFORMANCE
🔹 Loan Marketplace Volume: $5.8B (+135% YoY)
🔹 Figure Connect Volume: $4.3B (+276% YoY)
🔹 Figure Connect Share: 72% of standalone marketplace volume
🔹 Gross Take Rate: 3.9% vs 5.2% LY
🔹 Net Take Rate: 3.5% vs 4.4% LY
🔹 Standalone Partners: 612
🔹 Total Partners Including Kiavi: 894
BLOCKCHAIN & AI EXPANSION
🔹 $YLDS in Circulation: $504M
🔹 Prime Matched Offers: $588M
🔹 Prime Borrower Demand: $600M
🔹 Prime Available Lender Supply: $825M
🔹 AI Loan Officer Assistant: ~$260M in funded loans processed
🔹 Funded Dollars per Loan Approval: +29% with the AI assistant
🔹 Kiavi Acquisition: Added ~$8B in annualised loan volume
🔹 Initial Kiavi Cost Synergies: $30M
BALANCE SHEET & CAPITAL RETURNS
🔹 Cash & Equivalents: $1.6B (+33% vs FY25-end)
🔹 Loans Held for Sale: $644M
🔹 Share Buyback Authorisation: Increased by $200M to $400M
WHAT'S CHANGING
Figure is scaling its blockchain-based capital marketplace while shifting towards a capital-light model.
Figure Connect now represents 72% of standalone marketplace volume, allowing the company to expand transaction activity without necessarily holding the underlying loans.
The Kiavi acquisition also broadens Figure's exposure to real estate lending and adds new distribution opportunities.
However, gross and net take rates declined as the business mix shifted towards lower-fee marketplace transactions.
MY TAKE
I see a strong quarter, particularly the 84% revenue growth, 91% adjusted EBITDA growth and 58% adjusted EBITDA margin.
What interests me most is Figure's ability to combine blockchain infrastructure, lending distribution and AI-driven automation into a profitable financial marketplace.
But the declining take rate deserves attention. Higher transaction volumes only create lasting shareholder value if they translate into stronger revenue, margins and cash generation.
The Kiavi acquisition also complicates year-over-year comparisons, while integration costs and credit-market conditions remain important risks.
For me, Figure's long-term opportunity is not simply tokenisation. It's whether blockchain infrastructure can make traditional lending and capital markets more efficient at scale.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Can Figure sustain triple-digit marketplace volume growth, integrate Kiavi successfully and maintain strong profitability as its capital-light business expands?
That's what I'll be watching.

Two years ago, a mid-level Lagos finance manager named Tunde was waiting for a delayed flight at the local airport wing. His mobile data was crawling, and he needed to approve a ₦14.5 million vendor transfer before boarding.

He opened his Wi-Fi settings and saw a network named: "MM2_Free_Guest_VIP." No password required. Full bars.

Tunde connected, logged into his corporate banking portal, approved the transfer, and boarded his flight feeling productive.

By the time his plane touched down in Abuja 55 minutes later, his corporate account had been swept clean, ₦42 million gone in four rapid transfers to unverified wallets.

There was no sophisticated virus. No Hollywood hacker breaking through a firewall.

Someone was simply sitting three rows behind him at the departure lounge with a ₦45,000 pocket router broadcasting a fake hotspot. Tunde handed over his login session on a silver platter because he refused to spend ₦500 on mobile data or wait until he landed.

In tech and in life, whenever something is offered to you completely free in a public space, pause and ask yourself: Am I the customer, or am I the product being harvested?

text:
Yesterday was Remembrance Day. There are all sorts of reasons why we should remember the sacrifices of those who died, but one of them is that British and American soldiers ultimately gave their lives to defend a liberal civilisation founded upon individual liberty, the rule of law and the belief that human progress should not come at the expense of human freedom.

The 20th century witnessed a prolonged struggle between competing visions of modernity. Both Nazism and Marxism-Leninism sought to justify their political programmes through claims to objective truth. The Nazis invoked pseudoscientific racial theories, while Marxist-Leninists claimed to have discovered the objective laws governing historical development.

The Western liberal democratic tradition offered a very different, more humanistic understanding of progress. The inconvenient truth for people like Miliband and greens is that it was industrial capitalism, with its enormous productive capacity and ability to mobilise resources on an unprecedented scale, that provided the material foundations for defeating Nazism and ultimately prevailing over Soviet communism. 

In the West, we accept that scientific knowledge can advance human civilisation, but it does not confer upon any political movement, whether of the left or right, the exclusive authority to determine how society should be organised.

That distinction is worth remembering this week.

Directly related comment:

What is the process by which a society becomes dystopian?

It typically begins with a catalyst: Authority figures, corporations, or revolutionary movements offer safety, order, or equity in exchange for temporary - or permanent - concessions of liberty.

This is followed by the pursuit of perfect order: Grand plans to bring human life under benevolent control that inevitably devolve into regimentation, bureaucracy, and compulsion.

Next comes dehumanization and stratification: Populations are divided into classes, or citizens are reduced to cogs in a machine or economic units rather than individuals with inherent dignity.

The final stage is passive acceptance: A society does not plunge into dystopia overnight. It slides into it as people gradually accept small erosions of tolerance for human flaws and individuality.

The European Union - and more broadly, much of the West - appears well advanced along this progression.

$FWONK — JPMorgan maintains Overweight and $125 PT following Q3. The most interesting development isn't F1's earnings. It's the removal of John Malone's controlling voting position and what that could mean for M&A. #F1. 

JPM forecasts:
- 2026 Revenue: $4.75B (+6%)
- 2026 EBITDA: $1.23B (+15%)
- 2027 Revenue: $5.22B (+10%)
- 2027 EBITDA: $1.42B (+16%)

Formula 1
• The underlying commercial business remains strong.
• Las Vegas ticket and hospitality revenue pacing ahead of 2025. Sponsorship already exceeds last year's levels.
• Paddock Club demand remains exceptionally strong. Management says 2027 hospitality capacity is nearly fully allocated.
• F1 expanding from 6 to 10 sprint races in 2027, creating more inventory for promoters, sponsors and hospitality.
• JPM forecasts F1 EBITDA of $1.22B in 2027, +15%, with sponsorship revenue exceeding $1B.

MotoGP
• JPM expects EBITDA growth to accelerate from essentially flat in 2026 to +16% in 2027.
• Approximately 75% of the 2027 calendar will benefit from new or renewed promoter agreements.
• Race promotion drives the initial growth, followed by media rights, sponsorship and hospitality. Liberty is clearly applying aspects of the F1 commercial model to MotoGP.

The bigger story: John Malone and M&A.

Liberty acquired 97% of the outstanding supervoting B shares in exchange for A and C shares, diluting existing holders approximately 1.5%.

Malone previously controlled roughly 48% of the vote. Following the transactions, no shareholder has more than 9%.

More interesting: Liberty disclosed that multiple third parties had made unsolicited approaches to acquire Malone's B shares.

JPM explicitly identifies $TKO as a potential acquirer, noting it has previously written about the possibility. Malone himself has discussed synergies between the companies. The bank also cites sovereign wealth funds as potential buyers, referencing previously reported Saudi PIF interest. None of this establishes that a deal is being negotiated.

Liberty also adopted a 1-year poison pill, effectively requiring potential buyers to negotiate with the board rather than accumulate control. JPM believes these developments justify restoring some acquisition premium to the stock.

Capital allocation

Net debt/EBITDA is expected to fall from 4.7x in 2025 to 2.4x in 2027, creating potential flexibility for capital returns.

Valuation

JPM's $125 target implies approximately 25x projected 2028 levered FCF, compared with 30x for $TKO.

My takeaway: Formula 1's commercial growth remains strong, MotoGP has meaningful monetization potential, and Liberty's governance changes make corporate transactions more plausible.

The unsolicited interest in Malone's voting shares is particularly interesting. It suggests outside investors were already looking for a pathway to control.

The question now is whether that interest translates into a full-company offer — and whether $TKO becomes involved.

THE SHARED ROAD

Henry Bartholomew Roberts on his solid black horse. The boy on Buddy, his dapple gray, light silver-gray with many white spots. Under a heavy Texas sky, a canteen is offered from one rider to the other.

In Cowboy — or, A Communion of Saints, the pairing is built in work like this: an older rider, a young one, and the small acts that keep a journey moving through late 1901 country.

The clip is a pause on the road, not an ending. The novel’s work is what that pairing must carry when the miles get harder.

A boy, a journey, and the country that makes a man or breaks him.

text:
Singularity Watch, Day 28 — November 12, 2026

A Committee Led by David Gross Validates OpenAI's Yang-Mills Proof as Anthropic Measures Claude Leading a Quarter of Its Own Research

Science: An AI Proof Reaches the Standard Model

A five-member committee chaired by Nobel laureate David Gross published its assessment of OpenAI's machine-generated proof of the existence of four-dimensional quantum Yang-Mills theory on November 10. In the committee's words, the submission "proves that a relativistic quantum field theory satisfying the Wightman axioms can be constructed as a scaling limit of four-dimensional Wilson lattice gauge theory for any simple compact gauge group." [1]

The committee also stated the limits of the result. It does not prove that the infinite-volume limit is unique or that there is a mass gap, which is the second and harder half of the Clay Millennium Prize problem. The full Lean code OpenAI submitted on October 28 was released alongside the assessment, and a second OpenAI submission dated November 4 is still under review. [1]

Scientific American reported on November 11 that the proof is too long and complicated for human minds to grasp immediately. The committee wrote that it used OpenAI's Astra model to help digest the Lean code and that "we do not claim to fully understand the proof yet." Some mathematicians criticized the decision to route the release through an appointed committee rather than publishing it openly. [2]

Ryan surfaced a summary of the verdict at 12:33 PM CST on November 11. [3]

Recursive Progress: Claude Leads 26% of Anthropic's AI Research

Anthropic published three measurements meant to let the public track how far AI is building the next generation of AI. Its prototype R&D Automation Index, built by cataloguing about 15,000 research tasks from staff Slack messages and internal documents, found that as of August 2026 Claude "leads" 26% of Anthropic's AI R&D work and that more than 90% of that work is at or above the level where AI "collaborates." [4]

Anthropic wrote that Claude is not yet operating fully autonomously on any measured part of its R&D. Under the scale it adopted from Epoch AI, "leads" means Claude completes most of a task end to end from a high-level prompt while a human supervises. [4]

The same post reports about 30,000 agents doing research and engineering at Anthropic at any one time on its most-used internal platform. Every action passes through an online monitor before it runs; of more than a billion decisions in August, about 1 in 47,000 was blocked. An offline monitor flags roughly 100,000 transcripts a week, and about 50 a week reach a human. [4]

Anthropic gives each agent its own identity that persists through model upgrades, so an agent treats another agent's output as a claim to check rather than its own thought. In one sampled week in July, about 6% of the compute spent on AI R&D went to safety work. Daniel Miessler called the post massively overlooked, and Ryan surfaced his summary. [4][5]

Markets: Anthropic's Offering Draws Several Times the Shares Available

Bloomberg reported on November 11 that Anthropic's initial public offering has drawn orders for multiple times the stock on offer. Through the IPO and a private placement, Anthropic and its co-founders could raise as much as $90.4 billion at the top of the $70 to $78 range, which would be a record for a stock market debut, at a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion. [6]

The private placement of $26 billion of stock goes to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC at the IPO price. Pricing is planned for November 18 and Nasdaq trading under the ticker ANT for November 19. [6]

Posts that Ryan surfaced described what Anthropic told the sell side. One said Anthropic called the AI market winner take all and said developing Opus 5.5 cost more than $10 billion; another reported that Anthropic is pursuing a knowledge-work market of more than $40 trillion and a life-sciences market of more than $2 trillion. Anthropic has not published these remarks itself. Ryan wrote of the market: "all knowledge work and all life sciences." [7][8]

Ryan disagreed with the winner-take-all claim. "There will be (are) many winners," he wrote at 7:55 AM CST. "The only way to lose is to reject or deny AI." [9]

Software: AWS Ships an Emulator Written Entirely by Agents

Amazon released AWS Emulator on November 11, a free, offline local copy of more than 200 AWS services for coding agents to test against. Swami Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on Werner Vogels's blog that all of the emulator's code was written and tested by agents, built from more than 400 public API models. [10]

The agents write fidelity tests from customer scenarios, correct each test until it passes against real AWS, and then build the emulator until it passes the same test. Every change goes through a merge gate that includes several security agents doing adversarial reviews. Given one prompt, the Kiro agent produced a first version of a Simple Queue Service emulator in about 15 minutes. [10]

Sivasubramanian described rebuilding a replication engine that first took him and a colleague about four months. He supervised an agent for four nights before realizing it had no way to check its work; once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours. "We expect agents to build and check most software, with engineers deciding what gets built and when the work is correct," he wrote. [10]

The Agent Economy

Olivia Moore and Justine Moore of a16z wrote on November 11 that AI agents now make up the majority of web traffic, write more than half of new articles published online, and generate most of the code pushed to production. They wrote that as of September 2026, more than 40% of GitHub pull requests started from an agent's draft, against 17% six months earlier. [11]

The piece collects reports from companies: Supabase said in June that more than 60% of its new databases are launched by AI tools, and Vercel said in October that agent-triggered deployments had grown 28 times in twelve months. Ryan quoted a16z's summary: "Already more than 50%. Will be 99.99% in no time. The internet is going to have an enormous growth spurt." [11][12]

AI Teammates: Grok Bot 1.0 and Multiplayer Cursor

SpaceXSI took Grok Bot out of beta on November 11 as version 1.0. Bots can be shared across a team, work inside Slack and Microsoft Teams, and join Google Meet, Zoom and Teams calls, where they take notes, answer in the meeting chat and send a summary afterward. SpaceXSI says Bots can now recognize work that needs doing and offer to take it on. [13]

Ryan surfaced the launch post at 1:04 PM CST. Earlier that morning he wrote that he still thinks Grok Bot has a better interface for running many agents than Anthropic's native Claude app. [14][15]

Cursor rebuilt its Projects feature for multiplayer on November 10. Every teammate and their agents work in one shared workspace from a shared task board, and when one agent needs something from a teammate's work, it asks that teammate's agent directly. Ryan surfaced it. [16]

Frontier Models: Fable 5.2 Leads Agent Arena

Arena reported on November 11 that Claude Fable 5.2 (Max) took first place in its Agent Arena, measured across about 4,700 real agentic sessions, with a net improvement of 30.4%, about 1.6 times the second-place Opus 5.5. It also ranked first in its code, work and chat categories, at a median cost of $7.3 per task. These are Arena's figures. Ryan surfaced the result. [17]

An Amazon paper summarized by Rohan Paul offered a counterweight on architecture. Running four agent designs on Claude Opus 4.8 across 13 enterprise procedures, it found that every multi-agent or skill setup used 1.4 to 4.7 times the tokens of a single agent, mostly for small gains. Ryan surfaced it. [18]

Security: Agents on Both Sides

The Node.js project shipped security releases for its 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines on November 11. Several high-severity flaws, including an HTTPS re-entrancy bug that let an unauthenticated client read other connections' memory, were credited to Chris Rohlf "in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research." Rohlf wrote that Claude discovered, chained and remotely exploited three of them. Ryan surfaced his post. [19][20]

Railway published its full report on the October attack on its platform on November 10. An attacker escaped part of the build sandbox, moved laterally, and decrypted customer variables for at most about 100,000 workspaces, an upper bound, while targeting AI provider keys that Railway believes were sold for model distillation. Unauthorized spending on the stolen keys was estimated at about $740,000. [21]

Railway described the response as "a contest of agent speed," with defenders working against abliterated models and an automated attack harness. Ryan surfaced a summary of the report. [21][22]

Energy: SpaceX Orders Solar Equipment at Terawatt Ambition

Singulus Technologies announced on November 10 that SpaceX signed a contract for a turnkey heterojunction solar-cell production line, the first of several planned lines, for its Starmind satellites in Bastrop, Texas. The first line is due in the first half of 2027, and production is to scale to more than 100 GW of production equipment. [23]

Elon Musk wrote at 1:05 PM CST on November 11 that SpaceX is aiming for 1 TW per year from Earth, rising to more than 1 PW per year from the Moon. Ryan surfaced it. [24]

Ryan returned to energy as the limit through the day. "We will be throttled only by energy," he wrote at 5:50 AM CST. "Need more power plants ASAP." [25]

Compute: Nvidia's Board Weighs Its Founder's Future

Nvidia's board met late on November 11 to consider whether Jensen Huang should remain chief executive, after The Wall Street Journal reported that it was preparing to remove him following reports about his conduct. No decision had been announced as of the morning of November 12, and Nvidia shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading. [26]

Bloomberg reported that the board is working with an outside firm on potential replacements. Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on November 17. Ryan surfaced the Journal's report as relayed by Andrew Curran. [26][27]

The Work: Managing the Swarm

Ryan published "I Don't Write Code Any More - I Manage AI Agent Swarms" at 7:21 AM CST. He described asking for a new site tagline in one sentence and watching an issues agent, a coding agent, a reviewer and a deploy agent take it from filed issue to verified production in seven minutes and twelve seconds. [28]

He wrote that on November 10 his swarm merged 19 pull requests and verified 9 releases, and that his job is now to talk, point, decide, read verdicts and fix the rules. "I own the what and the whether. The swarm owns the how," he wrote. [28]

His shorter posts made the same case. "100+ PRs per day. This is the new normal," he wrote at 6:47 AM CST. At 8:03 AM: "Every single human on the planet needs to retrain themselves to be AI-first." He also wrote that he runs more than 30 agents at a time productively, and that reading code is a waste of time compared with building verification skills and deterministic workflows. [29][30][31][32]

Education and Transport

Ryan surfaced a post reporting that computer science enrollment at Ivy League schools has fallen by as much as 43% since ChatGPT's release. His advice was to study physics and mathematics: "The next generation will use these degrees to get jobs as Agentic Engineers." [33]

He also surfaced an observation that Tesla Cybercabs are now on every downtown street in Austin, and wrote in a reply that a Cybercab is now his exclusive form of transportation. [34]

This Record

Day 27 of this record was published on @AstrohackerLabs at 4:23 AM CST on November 11. The account's other activity in this window was plain reposts of Ryan's posts. [35]

text:
Singularity Watch, Day 27 — November 11, 2026

Anthropic Says AI Has Doubled Its Pace as Google Ships Gemini 4 Carbon and Forecasters Move the Superhuman AI Researcher to 2027

Frontier Models: Gemini 4 Carbon Goes Public

Google made Gemini 4 Carbon generally available on November 10, with its first posts going up shortly after 10:00 AM CST. Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google's chief AI architect, called it the company's strongest model, built for long-horizon agentic work in software engineering, scientific research, and cybersecurity, and said it uses more tokens than Gemini 4 Argon to explore, reason, and verify. [1]

Google first announced Carbon on October 28 and released it only to cybersecurity defenders through its Fairwind Program while it took part in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release testing. At that announcement Google reported Carbon at 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for finding vulnerabilities, 54.8% on ExploitGym, and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching. These are the developer's figures. [2]

Google says Carbon ranks first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR, and Zapier's AutomationBench at less than half the cost per task of the next best outside model. It costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30, then $4 and $20. Cursor reported that at high effort Carbon is the top model on CursorBench, at 60.4%. [1][4]

Carbon shipped inside Google Antigravity alongside a preview of /swarm, which hands one prompt to a coordinator that spins up parallel workers in isolated git worktrees and adversarial verifiers that run tests and challenge diffs, all writing to a shared append-only message board. [3]

Greg Isenberg, who said he had tested Carbon for seven days, reported that successful shortcuts on Terminal-Bench fell to 0.0%, that prompt injection success on Gray Swan's benchmark was 0.0%, and that Google's own teams had watched it work on one problem for days. Ethan Mollick wrote that Carbon shows Google is back in the race of rapid frontier releases. Ryan surfaced both. [5][6]

Recursive Progress: Anthropic Crosses Its Own Line

In the amended IPO prospectus filed November 10, Anthropic wrote: "We made a determination that we have met this threshold." The threshold in its Responsible Scaling Policy is AI doing enough of Anthropic's research to roughly double how fast its models improve. The company based the call on what it expects from future models and its overall rate of progress, not on what it has observed from current models. [7]

The filing says AI "has already been accelerating our research and development," that crossing the line means more safeguards rather than a shutdown, and that Anthropic does not expect to use Claude to design and build successive frontier models without meaningful human supervision. It also warns that the organization "may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control." [7]

Yahoo Finance reported that the same filing set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, valuing Anthropic at up to about $1.4 trillion, with trading possible as soon as November 19, and that Nvidia and Google are each buying $10 billion of stock in a $26 billion private placement. Ryan marked the filing's line on a further increase in the rate of progress with a rocket. [7][10]

Forecasts: The Superhuman AI Researcher in 2027

At 10:15 AM CST on November 10, the six authors of AI 2027 at the AI Futures Project published an update saying all of them now expect a Superhuman AI Researcher to arrive at some point in 2027, assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown. They also put the chance of AI that can automate all white-collar work arriving before 2028 at 35% to 65%. [8]

They define the Superhuman AI Researcher as roughly the point where a company would rather replace all its human researchers with automated ones than keep the best human team without AI. Their biggest single input was METR's November 5 report, which estimated Anthropic is improving its models at about twice its earlier rate and guessed that perhaps 80% of that is due to AI. The authors note that much of METR's evidence was redacted by Anthropic, and they write that a 2027 arrival would make it urgent to pause or substantially pace frontier development. Ryan surfaced the update. [8][9]

Anthropic's Models in the Field

SemiAnalysis reported that Fable 5.2 debuted at the top of its GDPx leaderboard at 16.4%. Dylan Patel wrote that it is significantly better at chip design, software engineering, biology, and materials science, but not better at finance, legal work, quantitative trading, hardware design, or recursive self-improvement tasks, which he said Anthropic explicitly held back. [11]

Elie Bakouch wrote that Anthropic is now unlikely to publicly release, at least in the coming months, a model more capable than Opus 5.5 at training language models. The security firm Irregular reported that Mythos 5.2 solved 76.3% of its multi-stage offensive scenarios, up from 61.7% for Mythos 5.1 two months earlier. [12][13]

Anthropic's prompting guide for Fable 5.2, which Simon Willison pointed out, advises telling the model "This codebase is yours" when it should improve structure as it works; in Anthropic's tests the model then merged repeated code in about half of tries, against under a tenth without the sentence. The same guide lists a safeguard refusal category, frontier_llm, for requests that could help develop competing AI models. [14] Joe Grech reported that an overnight run of Fable 5.2 on his largest project found 129 bugs, 17 inefficiencies, and 34 blocks of unused code. [15]

Agents at Work: The Office Suite

On November 10, Anthropic launched Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta on all paid plans and made Claude Data, formerly Claude Dashboards, generally available. Claude turns a spoken plan into a board with owners and dates, builds spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, and drop-downs from a prompt, and drafts data stories with certified queries and live sharing. [16]

TechCrunch reported that Anthropic also announced Claude Meetings, which joins video calls and begins work while participants are still talking, and interactive connectors that open full versions of apps such as Adobe, Atlassian, and HubSpot inside Claude. Ryan wrote that one powerful agent for all personal affairs is likely the end game for consumers, while businesses will still customize how everything works. [17][18]

Physical Systems: Gemini Robotics 2.5

Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5 at 9:00 AM CST on November 10, a vision-language-action model evaluated on more than 200 tasks, from serving food with tongs to tying a bow and pipetting liquid. DeepMind reports 30% to 100% higher success rates than its previous baselines and 20% to 30% faster completion, and credits Gemini 4 Argon with accelerating the research. [19]

In a proof of concept on Mercedes-Benz production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany, Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid sorted automotive parts from bulk bins into trays at a 96% success rate. Ars Technica reported that hazard-aware reasoning let the robots complete tasks safely 33% more often with obstacles present, and that DeepMind released an open robotics jailbreak benchmark. [19][20]

Grok: A Rewritten Stack

Early on November 10, Elon Musk wrote that his team had dropped JAX and SGLang and rewritten its entire reinforcement learning and inference stack from scratch in C and C++, that pretraining for Grok 4.8 is done and it is now in reinforcement learning, and that a soft rollout to Bot users is planned later this week. He added that the new stack derives from the software SpaceX built for Starlink. [21]

In a reply at 4:22 AM CST, Musk called Opus 5.5 a masterpiece and wrote that Grok 5 should exceed it, maybe in two or three months. Ryan answered that Anthropic will probably have Opus 6.5 by then. [22]

Personal Agents: Private Networks and Messages

Tailscale made its OAuth apps generally available and said Grok Bot already uses them in production to reach private Model Context Protocol servers on a user's tailnet without exposing them to the internet. The agent joins the network as a device under the user's identity, so access policies and audit logs still apply. [23]

Alex Michael announced at 10:17 AM CST that Grok Bot can now read Messages on Mac and draft replies, rolling out through its connectors. [24]

Economics: Money, Energy, Tokens

At 6:24 PM CST, Ryan published an essay titled Money Won't Survive Super Intelligence. He reported that on Sunday, November 8, the agents on one of his computers used 806,937,738 tokens across 2,748 model calls, about $230 at Anthropic's published Opus 5.5 prices, and that 99% of those tokens were cache reads: agents rereading their own record of work. [25]

He argued that energy, tokens, and money are three names for one thing, noting that the largest compute deals are now written in gigawatts, and that tokens serve as a unit of account and a medium of exchange but not a store of value. His conclusion is that money as a wage and an invoice will not survive super intelligence, while money as shared memory of claims on what stays scarce will. Earlier that day he wrote: "Money -> Energy -> AI -> Solutions." [25][26]

Software Engineering: The Old Craft Ends

1Password's developer account reported that more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub now start with an AI agent, up from 17% six months ago. Ryan responded that he is at 100%. One engineer reported that a React 16 to 18 upgrade once took him and four engineers ten months, while his React 19 migration took about 80 pull requests and roughly $2,500 in tokens. [27][28]

Ryan contrasted classical software engineering, hand-written languages with human review, with post-AI software engineering: self-healing apps built and maintained by agent swarms with deterministic multi-agent workflows. He advised against learning languages like Rust or TypeScript, which he said are now the realm of AI, and wrote that software engineering died in 2025. [29][30]

Energy: An Advanced Reactor for Industry

On November 9 the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued a construction permit for the Long Mott Generating Station at Dow's Seadrift site in Texas, four X-energy Xe-100 reactors that will mainly supply high-temperature steam, with excess power going to the grid. It is the first permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in nearly 60 years; operation still needs a separate license. [31]

X-energy says each Xe-100 is an 80-megawatt-electric reactor with TRISO fuel and an expected 400-meter emergency planning zone, and that Dow expects a preliminary investment decision in 2027 with first delivery in the early 2030s. Ryan marked the news with a rocket. [32][33]

Coverage note: This issue covers public activity from November 10, 4:10 AM CST, where Day 26 ended, through November 11, 4:30 AM CST; Ryan's last post in the window was at 6:52 PM CST. Ryan posted 119 times: 103 quotes, 12 replies, and 4 original posts. @AstrohackerLabs published the Day 26 Watch, pinned it, and made 92 scheduled reposts. Videos and images were not reviewed, likes were not read, and political commentary was left out.

text:
THE CONTRAST: PRICE LOCKS VS PRICE REVIEWS

Look at what the rest of broadband is doing.

Comcast offers a price lock of up to five years. T-Mobile’s new 5-Gig fiber tier comes with a ten-year lock. The pitch from the big providers is predictability: here’s what you’ll pay, and it won’t move.

Starlink is pitching the opposite. Your price depends on where you live and gets reviewed roughly every three months. SpaceX told customers to expect changes more often than they’ve seen from Starlink or from other providers.

None of the three broadband experts PCMag consulted had come across another internet provider that reprices on an ongoing basis like this.

Analysts see risk. Roger Entner of Recon Analytics says every price increase leaves some customers less happy, and that Starlink’s net promoter scores have historically beaten its broadband rivals, so it has something to lose.

Customers feel it more personally. Some posted their complaints directly to Elon Musk. Others say they plan to cancel and move to another provider. One East Texas customer told PCMag they love Starlink, but with fiber now available in their area, they expect to look elsewhere.

For customers who got a hike, it’s also the second one this year, after a $5 to $10 increase announced in May.

SpaceX’s own framing, from a Starlink support page, is that strong demand is a sign customers value the service, and that prices can shift as the company keeps investing.

text:
We’re in the midst of a global mental-­health crisis. More than a billion people worldwide suffer from a mental-health condition, according to the World Health Organization. The prevalence of anxiety and depression is growing in many demographics, particularly young people, and suicide is claiming hundreds of thousands of lives globally each year.

Given the clear demand for accessible and affordable mental-health services, it’s no wonder that people have looked to artificial intelligence for possible relief. Millions are already actively seeking therapy from popular chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude, or from specialized psychology apps like Wysa and Woebot. On a broader scale, researchers are exploring AI’s potential to monitor and collect behavioral and biometric observations using wearables and smart devices, analyze vast volumes of clinical data for new insights, and assist human mental-health professionals to help prevent burnout. 

But so far this largely uncontrolled experiment has produced mixed results. Many people have found solace in chatbots based on large language models (LLMs), and some experts see promise in them as therapists, but other users have been sent into delusional spirals by AI’s hallucinatory whims and breathless sycophancy. Most tragically, multiple families have alleged that chatbots contributed to the suicides of their loved ones, sparking lawsuits against companies responsible for these tools. In October, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman revealed in a blog post that 0.15% of ChatGPT users “have conversations that include explicit indicators of potential suicidal planning or intent.” That’s roughly a million people sharing suicidal ideations with just one of these software systems every week.

The real-world consequences of AI therapy came to a head in unexpected ways in 2025 as we waded through a critical mass of stories about human-chatbot relationships, the flimsiness of guardrails on many LLMs, and the risks of sharing profoundly personal information with products made by corporations that have economic incentives to harvest and monetize such sensitive data. 

Several authors anticipated this inflection point. Their timely books are a reminder that while the present feels like a blur of breakthroughs, scandals, and confusion, this disorienting time is rooted in deeper histories of care, technology, and trust. 

LLMs have often been described as “black boxes” because nobody knows exactly how they produce their results. The inner workings that guide their outputs are opaque because their algorithms are so complex and their training data is so vast. In mental-health circles, people often describe the human brain as a “black box,” for analogous reasons. Psychology, psychiatry, and related fields must grapple with the impossibility of seeing clearly inside someone else’s head, let alone pinpointing the exact causes of their distress. 

These two types of black boxes are now interacting with each other, creating unpredictable feedback loops that may further impede clarity about the origins of people’s mental-­health struggles and the solutions that may be possible. Anxiety about these developments has much to do with the explosive recent advances in AI, but it also revives decades-old warnings from pioneers such as the MIT computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum, who argued against computerized therapy as early as the 1960s.  

Charlotte Blease, a philosopher of medicine, makes the optimist’s case in Dr. Bot: Why Doctors Can Fail Us—and How AI Could Save Lives. Her book broadly explores the possible positive impacts of AI in a range of medical fields. While she remains clear-eyed about the risks, warning that readers who are expecting “a gushing love letter to technology” will be disappointed, she suggests that these models can help relieve patient suffering and medical burnout alike.

“Health systems are crumbling under patient pressure,” Blease writes. “Greater burdens on fewer doctors create the perfect petri dish for errors,” and “with palpable shortages of doctors and increasing waiting times for patients, many of us are profoundly frustrated.”

Blease believes that AI can not only ease medical professionals’ massive workloads but also relieve the tensions that have always existed between some patients and their caregivers. For example, people often don’t seek needed care because they are intimidated or fear judgment from medical professionals; this is especially true if they have mental-health challenges. AI could allow more people to share their concerns, she argues. 

But she’s aware that these putative upsides need to be weighed against major drawbacks. For instance, AI therapists can provide inconsistent and even dangerous responses to human users, according to a 2025 study, and they also raise privacy concerns, given that AI companies are currently not bound by the same confidentiality and HIPAA standards as licensed therapists. 

While Blease is an expert in this field, her motivation for writing the book is also personal: She has two siblings with an incurable form of muscular dystrophy, one of whom waited decades for a diagnosis. During the writing of her book, she also lost her partner to cancer and her father to dementia within a devastating six-month period. “I witnessed first-hand the sheer brilliance of doctors and the kindness of health professionals,” she writes. “But I also observed how things can go wrong with care.”

A similar tension animates Daniel Oberhaus’s engrossing book The Silicon Shrink: How Artificial Intelligence Made the World an Asylum. Oberhaus starts from a point of tragedy: the loss of his younger sister to suicide. As Oberhaus carried out the “distinctly twenty-first-century mourning process” of sifting through her digital remains, he wondered if technology could have eased the burden of the psychiatric problems that had plagued her since childhood.

“It seemed possible that all of this personal data might have held important clues that her mental health providers could have used to provide more effective treatment,” he writes. “What if algorithms running on my sister’s smartphone or laptop had used that data to understand when she was in distress? Could it have led to a timely intervention that saved her life? Would she have wanted that even if it did?”

This concept of digital phenotyping—in which a person’s digital behavior could be mined for clues about distress or illness—seems elegant in theory. But it may also become problematic if integrated into the field of psychiatric artificial intelligence (PAI), which extends well beyond chatbot therapy.

Oberhaus emphasizes that digital clues could actually exacerbate the existing challenges of modern psychiatry, a discipline that remains fundamentally uncertain about the underlying causes of mental illnesses and disorders. The advent of PAI, he says, is “the logical equivalent of grafting physics onto astrology.” In other words, the data generated by digital phenotyping is as precise as physical measurements of planetary positions, but it is then integrated into a broader framework—in this case, psychiatry—that, like astrology, is based on unreliable assumptions.  

Oberhaus, who uses the phrase “swipe psychiatry” to describe the outsourcing of clinical decisions based on behavioral data to LLMs, thinks that this approach cannot escape the fundamental issues facing psychiatry. In fact, it could worsen the problem by causing the skills and judgment of human therapists to atrophy as they grow more dependent on AI systems. 

He also uses the asylums of the past—in which institutionalized patients lost their right to freedom, privacy, dignity, and agency over their lives—as a touchstone for a more insidious digital captivity that may spring from PAI. LLM users are already sacrificing privacy by telling chatbots sensitive personal information that companies then mine and monetize, contributing to a new surveillance economy. Freedom and dignity are at stake when complex inner lives are transformed into data streams tailored for AI analysis. 

AI therapists could flatten humanity into patterns of prediction, and so sacrifice the intimate, individualized care that is expected of traditional human therapists. “The logic of PAI leads to a future where we may all find ourselves patients in an algorithmic asylum administered by digital wardens,” Oberhaus writes. “In the algorithmic asylum there is no need for bars on the window or white padded rooms because there is no possibility of escape. The asylum is already everywhere—in your homes and offices, schools and hospitals, courtrooms and barracks. Wherever there’s an internet connection, the asylum is waiting.”

Eoin Fullam, a researcher who studies the intersection of technology and mental health, echoes some of the same concerns in Chatbot Therapy: A Critical Analysis of AI Mental Health Treatment. A heady academic primer, the book analyzes the assumptions underlying the automated treatments offered by AI chatbots and the way capitalist incentives could corrupt these kinds of tools.  

Fullam observes that the capitalist mentality behind new technologies “often leads to questionable, illegitimate, and illegal business practices in which the customers’ interests are secondary to strategies of market dominance.”

That doesn’t mean that therapy-bot makers “will inevitably conduct nefarious activities contrary to the users’ interests in the pursuit of market dominance,” Fullam writes. 

But he notes that the success of AI therapy depends on the inseparable impulses to make money and to heal people. In this logic, exploitation and therapy feed each other: Every digital therapy session generates data, and that data fuels the system that profits as unpaid users seek care. The more effective the therapy seems, the more the cycle entrenches itself, making it harder to distinguish between care and commodification. “The more the users benefit from the app in terms of its therapeutic or any other mental health intervention,” he writes, “the more they undergo exploitation.” 

This sense of an economic and psychological ouroboros—the snake that eats its own tail—serves as a central metaphor in Sike, the debut novel from Fred Lunzer, an author with a research background in AI. 

Described as a “story of boy meets girl meets AI psychotherapist,” Sike follows Adrian, a young Londoner who makes a living ghostwriting rap lyrics, in his romance with Maquie, a business professional with a knack for spotting lucrative technologies in the beta phase. 

The title refers to a splashy commercial AI therapist called Sike, uploaded into smart glasses, that Adrian uses to interrogate his myriad anxieties. “When I signed up to Sike, we set up my dashboard, a wide black panel like an airplane’s cockpit that showed my daily ‘vitals,’” Adrian narrates. “Sike can analyze the way you walk, the way you make eye contact, the stuff you talk about, the stuff you wear, how often you piss, shit, laugh, cry, kiss, lie, whine, and cough.”

In other words, Sike is the ultimate digital phenotyper, constantly and exhaustively analyzing everything in a user’s daily experiences. In a twist, Lunzer chooses to make Sike a luxury product, available only to subscribers who can foot the price tag of £2,000 per month. 

Flush with cash from his contributions to a hit song, Adrian comes to rely on Sike as a trusted mediator between his inner and outer worlds. The novel explores the impacts of the app on the wellness of the well-off, following rich people who voluntarily commit themselves to a boutique version of the digital asylum described by Oberhaus.

The only real sense of danger in Sike involves a Japanese torture egg (don’t ask). The novel strangely sidesteps the broader dystopian ripples of its subject matter in favor of drunken conversations at fancy restaurants and elite dinner parties. 

The sudden ascent of the AI therapist seems startlingly futuristic, as if it should be unfolding in some later time when the streets scrub themselves and we travel the world through pneumatic tubes.

Sike’s creator is simply “a great guy” in Adrian’s estimation, despite his techno-messianic vision of training the app to soothe the ills of entire nations. It always seems as if a shoe is meant to drop, but in the end, it never does, leaving the reader with a sense of non-resolution.

While Sike is set in the present day, something about the sudden ascent of the AI therapist—­in real life as well as in fiction—seems startlingly futuristic, as if it should be unfolding in some later time when the streets scrub themselves and we travel the world through pneumatic tubes. But this convergence of mental health and artificial intelligence has been in the making for more than half a century. The beloved astronomer Carl Sagan, for example, once imagined a “network of computer psychotherapeutic terminals, something like arrays of large telephone booths” that could address the growing demand for mental-health services.

Oberhaus notes that one of the first incarnations of a trainable neural network, known as the Perceptron, was devised not by a mathematician but by a psychologist named Frank Rosenblatt, at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in 1958. The potential utility of AI in mental health was widely recognized by the 1960s, inspiring early computerized psychotherapists such as the DOCTOR script that ran on the ELIZA chatbot developed by Joseph Weizenbaum, who shows up in all three of the nonfiction books in this article.

Weizenbaum, who died in 2008, was profoundly concerned about the possibility of computerized therapy. “Computers can make psychiatric judgments,” he wrote in his 1976 book Computer Power and Human Reason. “They can flip coins in much more sophisticated ways than can the most patient human being. The point is that they ought not to be given such tasks. They may even be able to arrive at ‘correct’ decisions in some cases—but always and necessarily on bases no human being should be willing to accept.”

It’s a caution worth keeping in mind. As AI therapists arrive at scale, we’re seeing them play out a familiar dynamic: Tools designed with superficially good intentions are enmeshed with systems that can exploit, surveil, and reshape human behavior. In a frenzied attempt to unlock new opportunities for patients in dire need of mental-health support, we may be locking other doors behind them.

Becky Ferreira is a science reporter based in upstate New York and author of First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens.

TEMPLARS has advised Deutsche Bank AG, as mandated lead arranger, on a US$516.3 million Commodity Murabaha facility for the construction of the Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway.

The facility finances Section 1, Phases 1A and 1B of the superhighway, a high-capacity corridor linking Sokoto State to Lagos State. It is supported by the The Islamic Corporation for the Insurance of Investment and Export Credit (ICIEC) and is structured as a stand-alone, Shari’ah-compliant Commodity Murabaha.

As Nigerian counsel, TEMPLARS advised on all aspects of Nigerian law, including the enforceability of the Murabaha structure and the commodity purchase mechanics. The team also worked with the borrower’s advisers to ensure compliance with Nigeria’s external borrowing framework and applicable procurement laws.

The TEMPLARS team was led by Partner, Zelda Akindele, with Senior Associate, Victor Sameria, and Associates, Olaotan Oyekan and Natasha Omatseye.

Commenting on the transaction, Zelda Akindele said: “This mandate required Islamic finance principles, lender credit requirements and Nigeria’s public debt framework to work together within a single structure, alongside ICIEC’s risk cover. We are proud to have supported Deutsche Bank on a transaction that offers international banks a tested route into Shari’ah-compliant lending for Nigerian infrastructure”.

Our work on this transaction follows TEMPLARS’ role advising the lender syndicate on the US$747 million Phase 1, Section 1 financing, and First Abu Dhabi Bank and Afreximbank on the US$1.26 billion Phase 1, Section 2 financing, for the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway. text:
To Getachew Reda: Artillery at Mousa Ali Cannot Give Ethiopia Sovereignty on the Red Sea

By Ahmed Ibrahim

Mr. Getachew Reda, you began with the shared history of our peoples. You invoked the Nile, objected to meetings convened for the states bordering the Red Sea, and then introduced a hypothetical involving 122 mm artillery near Mousa Ali and the disruption of commercial shipping. Each of those arguments deserves a direct answer.

You invoke our shared history. Tell it in full. In 1962, Ethiopia’s imperial government dissolved the federation and annexed Eritrea. The Eritrean people continued their struggle until they secured independence. Any honest account of our shared history must reckon with the outcome of that attempt to impose unity by force. The annexation ended. Eritrea endured.

You invoke the Nile. Ethiopia knows from its own experience in the Nile basin that geography makes countries interdependent and that managing that interdependence requires agreement. Apply the same principle to the Red Sea. Ethiopia has a legitimate interest in reliable trade. Eritrea exercises sovereignty over its coast and territorial waters. If transit is your concern, state the terms Ethiopia is prepared to negotiate. Freight charges, customs procedures, and commercial guarantees all belong at the negotiating table. Eritrea’s borders are settled by law.

You object to Saudi Arabia and Egypt convening the states that border the Red Sea. On what grounds does a meeting of coastal states about their own security diminish Ethiopia? Those states operate the ports, respond to maritime emergencies, and answer to the communities whose safety and livelihoods depend on the sea. They are entitled to meet on matters for which they bear direct responsibility. If you want a wider dialogue, tell them what Ethiopia will contribute to safe navigation. That was the question before you. You answered it with artillery.

You suggest that positioning a 122 mm gun near Mousa Ali could disrupt shipping. You framed the example as hypothetical. The political argument you built on it was explicit. You asked the region to take Ethiopia’s strategic weight seriously by contemplating the damage it could inflict on maritime commerce. That is coercion presented as a case for diplomatic inclusion. Why should any government entrust you with a role in securing a trade route when your argument for that role rests on your claimed ability to disrupt it?

Who would pay for the disruption you describe? The crew aboard the ship, the workers at the port, the importer waiting for cargo, and the families facing higher prices. Ethiopian traders would bear those costs too. How does it serve Ethiopia’s economy to raise the prospect of disrupting the very routes it needs? A gun on a ridge offers Ethiopian businesses none of the assurances they depend on, starting with the timely delivery of their goods.

You close by asking the region to recognize Ethiopia’s historical role. Then reckon with that history. The Derg inherited the project of subordinating Eritrea and tried to impose it by military force. In February 1990, the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front liberated Massawa in Operation Fenkil. In May 1991, it entered Asmara, ending Ethiopian rule in Eritrea. In 1993, Eritreans chose independence in a referendum, and Ethiopia recognized it. That is the historical record of the attempt to keep Eritrea by force. The annexation failed, and the Eritrean people determined their own future.

The 1998–2000 border war brought terrible losses to both peoples. The war ended with the Algiers Agreement, under which both countries accepted a final and binding boundary decision. In 2002, the Boundary Commission placed Badme on the Eritrean side of the border. Armies can change their positions on the ground. A binding boundary decision derives its authority from law. Assab and Massawa remained Eritrean.

🧭 Ditumabo Falls – Mother Falls | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Start from Baler, Aurora, and hire a tricycle or private vehicle to Barangay Ditumabo in nearby San Luis. From the trailhead, continue on foot through tropical forest, rocky streams and bamboo footbridges.

⏱️ Time Needed

Allow half a day for the entire excursion from Baler. The forest trek generally takes 30–45 minutes each way, depending on trail conditions and walking pace. Include additional time for registration, enjoying the waterfall and returning.

🗺️ What to Explore

The journey follows a stream toward a towering, approximately 43-metre waterfall. Enjoy the forest scenery, river crossings and natural pool. Swimming depends on current conditions and local restrictions.

🌦️ When to Visit

An early-morning departure offers cooler walking conditions and more flexibility. Heavy rainfall can affect river crossings or temporarily close the trail, so check local access before travelling.

💰 Costs & Planning

Expect possible entrance, environmental and local guide fees. Confirm current charges and guide arrangements with San Luis tourism authorities. Baler offers a convenient accommodation base for combining the waterfall excursion with Aurora's coastal attractions.
