text:
$IREN: Why We’re Buyers Into the Texas Panic

$IREN is down 44% over the past month, with investors panicking over potential restrictions on data center development in Texas.

The market is pricing IREN as if its entire AI infrastructure expansion is at risk.

We believe the market is getting this wrong.

1. The Texas Situation

The proposed moratorium primarily threatens new approvals and grid connections, not necessarily existing energized capacity.

IREN already has significant infrastructure secured:

Sweetwater 1: 1,400MW
Childress: 750MW
Sweetwater 2: 600MW

That’s 2,750MW across Texas, although future development phases remain exposed to regulatory delays.

Our view is that restricting new capacity could make already energized infrastructure significantly more valuable.

2. The Fundamentals Are Accelerating

While investors focus on Texas, IREN’s underlying business continues expanding.

$20.3B contracted revenue backlog, up 22%.
Over $4B targeted ARR, fully contracted and funded.
$9.7B Microsoft agreement through 2031.
$3.4B NVIDIA agreement over five years.
$2.8B in additional AI contracts with major developers.

The latest quarter reinforces the opportunity:

Revenue: $228M, +66% QoQ
AI Cloud revenue: $200M, +182% QoQ
AI Cloud gross margin: 86%
Adjusted EBITDA margin: 29%, up from 14%

Contract pricing is also improving, up 11–12% across three- and five-year agreements.

3. Texas Isn’t the Entire Growth Story

IREN now reports approximately 5GW of secured power across the U.S., Canada, Spain, and Australia.

Around 68% of its latest reported revenue was booked outside the United States.

Additional developments in Spain, Canada, and Oklahoma provide even further geographical diversification.

The business isn’t solely dependent on future Texas approvals.

4. The Debt Looks Different Than Investors Think

IREN has approximately $10B in debt principal, but roughly $6.6B consists of convertible debt carrying a blended effective rate near 1.1%.

Its estimated blended financing cost is approximately 3.4%, equivalent to around $340M in annual interest against its targeted $4B+ ARR.

Only 19% of borrowings mature within two years.

Customers are also helping fund expansion through prepayments, while NVIDIA has the right to invest up to $2.1B in IREN shares.

Our interpretation is that IREN is using relatively cheap financing to build infrastructure backed by substantial contractual demand.

If the capacity comes online on schedule, the economics could look considerably different from what the market is pricing today.

5. What Matters Next

We’re watching three major developments:

December: ERCOT’s audit and the treatment of existing energized capacity.

January–February: Delivery milestones and the targeted $4B+ operational ARR run-rate.

Beyond Texas: Continued expansion in Spain, Canada, and Oklahoma.

Delays, contract reductions, or significantly higher financing costs would challenge our thesis.

Right no, we’re buyers into the fear.

A 44% correction, $20.3B in contracted backlog, 86% AI Cloud gross margins, and approximately 5GW in secured power.

The market sees political uncertainty and mounting debt.

We see an infrastructure business with substantial contracted demand, relatively cheap financing, and a significant advantage in a power-constrained industry.

Execution remains the deciding factor.

All of the charts used in this post are proprietary to us.

We’ve spent months building a platform designed to bring everything you need for financial research together.

Book a demo at https://t.co/eQcJNd3aD9 and see what the Terminal has to offer.

TO AND FOR THE NAYSAYERS

I WAS NOT PAID TO SPEAK. I WAS ASKED TO STOP SPEAKING.

I see the comments. "He must have been paid."

You don't know me. 

So let me introduce myself, once, with facts. Not insults. Facts.

While an undergraduate at the University of Ibadan, I would graduate with First Class Honours in Law — Top 3 in my set, the only male with a First Class in my set, with the highest CGPA in Year 1 Law at UI that year — 6.6/7.0 in a class of 150.

I did not get there on empty stomach and connections. I got there on scholarships I had to earn, again and again: Gani Fawehinmi Scholarship, @TotalEnergies Scholarship, @Chevron National Merit Scholarship, Faith Foundation Scholarship, and others I have named here before.

Let me be specific about what that meant. In Year Two, dropout was near. It was the Gani Fawehinmi Scholarship that saved me. I was the boy who hawked pastries until SS3. I am the first graduate and first lawyer on both sides of my family . Nothing in my story was handed to me.

A couple of years after that, I was a Commonwealth Shared Scholar at the University of Aberdeen, studying for my PG certification in Oil & Gas Law. I was fully funded — tuition, living expenses, return flight, visa — paid for, if memory serves right, by @DFID_UK and the University of Aberdeen.

I turned down a full-tuition Arthur Vanderbilt LLM Scholarship from NYU Law — about USD 70,000 at the time. 

I also turned down a full-tuition LLM scholarship from the University of Westminster, UK. I turned them down because I had already chosen a path that required discipline, not display.

I have been on @cnbcafrica twice .
First, on the foreign exchange regime during Emefiele, alongside a colleague from Olaniwun Ajayi LP, anchored by Wole Famurewa.

Second, alone with Christy Cole on the $11bn P&ID arbitration matter, produced by Kenneth Igbomor, facilitated at the Lagos studio by Temi Popoola, now Temi Badru.

At that time, I was the first Nigerian to raise the alarm on our liability exposure, through pieces in national dailies and on international arbitration platforms like Kluwer Arbitration and Business Day. Not after it became safe to talk. Before. When it was lonely to talk.

I have also served as General Counsel to a tier 1 maritime company and to a tier 1 oil servicing company. I got a partnership offer from a legacy firm that I turned down. I have never been desperate for a platform. I have walked away from platforms.

A year after I started that sensitization, on 17 March 2020 at 02:53 AM, while I was in Australia on a fully funded doctoral programme paid for by one of Australia's Group of Eight universities, the Federal Government reached out via a London communications agency — Portland Communications, Project Victoria team — advising the Government and its counsel on the communications aspects of the case.

Their words: "We noticed that you have spoken widely on the issue, and have a strong academic interest in Nigeria's natural resource allocation and judicial processes."

They asked me to soft-pedal my narrative and to discuss collaboration on the media aspect.

Read that again. They did not ask me to speak for them. They asked me to speak less.

I did not walk back my previous opinions. I did not recant. I simply stopped all publications on the matter until it was resolved in favour of the Federal Government. Which it was.

No noise. No parade. 
No press release about my sacrifice.

Australia gave me a fully funded PhD. In total, as I have shared here before, the funds I have received from scholarships and funding for studies and research are not less than N500M.

Now, same me — same boy from Ikire — filed the public interest suit at the Federal High Court, Lagos, on 12 February 2025, against 10 respondents, asking a simple constitutional question: once a police officer has ceased to be a serving member upon attaining 60 years or 35 years in service, can the National Assembly, by hurried amendment, keep him as IGP...

From the South to the United States: The full story of what those who do not know it are missing

🔷 A state that once existed..
Before 1990, there were two states on the map of the Arabian Peninsula: the Yemeni Arab Republic in the North with its capital Sana'a, and the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen in the South, with its capital Aden. They were both members of the United Nations, each with its own flag, army, and constitution.

🔷 Unity.. a dream that turned into a nightmare!
On May 22, 1990, the two states united. Southerners entered unity voluntarily, believing in an equal partnership. But they were surprised by dozens of assassinations, marginalization, and exclusion directed at the South, and in 1994, the partnership collapsed, the South declared disengagement, and the North responded with a comprehensive war that occupied the South.

🔷 What happened after 1994?
After the war, more than 120,000 Southern soldiers and civilian employees were dismissed from their jobs. Southern institutions were looted, its lands confiscated, and its political representation dropped from 50% to 0% in the presidency of the republic in 2011. The South turned from a partner into an occupied land.

🔷 The Southern Movement.. the voice of the people..
In 2007, Southern retirees came out in peaceful protests demanding rights. The regime ignored them, repressed them, and shed their blood, so the movement turned from reform demands into a clear demand: restoring the Southern state. It was not an emotional demand, but the result of a harsh experience.

🔷 2017: The birth of the Transitional Council..
On May 4, 2017, the South Arabian Transitional Council was founded to be the political representative of the Southern cause. It was not a political party, but an entity comprising armed forces, security apparatuses, and a broad popular mandate. Its goal: restoring the fully sovereign Southern state.

🔷 The Southern forces.. the region's safety shield..
Forces such as the Shabwa Defense, the Giants Brigades, and the Security Belt fought the Houthis for years, liberated Aden, Al-Dhale'a, Shabwa, and Abyan, and protected Bab al-Mandab. These forces were the first line of defense for the region and offered thousands of martyrs.

🔷 The alliance with Saudi Arabia.. then betrayal!
In 2015, Saudi Arabia entered the war against the Houthis. Southerners fought alongside it. But in December 2025, after the Transitional Council liberated Hadhramaut and Al-Mahra from the forces of the terrorist Muslim Brotherhood, Saudi Arabia turned against it: it launched more than 200 airstrikes on the Southern forces, imposed an air and sea blockade, and arrested the Council's delegation in Riyadh, where it remains detained to this moment.

🔷 What the South demands today?
Amr Al-Baidh, the representative of President Aidarous Al-Zubaidi for Foreign Affairs, calls on #Washington to support a political path leading to a referendum on the independence of the South, after a one-year transitional phase. And he says clearly: the option of restoring Sana'a militarily is no longer realistic.

🔷 Why a referendum?
Because Southerners want to determine their own destiny, not have it decided for them from closed rooms. A referendum is not an innovation, but a right guaranteed by United Nations covenants. It is the solution that ends the conflict, not the one that postpones it.

🔷 Conclusion..
The South is not a "secessionist movement" as it is portrayed. It is a people with a former state, a history, an identity, victims, and one demand: restoring their state. Whoever does not understand the story will deal only with the outcome.
#SouthVoice

Once conditions have stabilized, immigration may resume under much stricter terms that prioritize the preservation of Canada’s historical identity.

The Temporary Foreign Worker (TFW) program has no place in a modern, civilized economy. What started as a program to supplement seasonal agricultural employment has been transformed into a system to import an underclass of foreign labourers. Temporary workers are no longer just working in the fields picking strawberries, they’re working as delivery drivers and fast food workers; jobs that used to go to our young people and the elderly.
Canada must eliminate the TFW program in its entirety.This system displaces Canadian workers, suppresses wages, and undermines productivity. It benefits Big Business at the expense of the Canadian people. All temporary workers currently in Canada are to be returned to their countries of origin.
The International Mobility Program (IMP) is an even bigger scam. It lets employers skip the requirement to prove no Canadians are available, flooding the country with cheap foreign labour under flimsy excuses like “trade agreements” and “cultural exchange.” The IMP has ballooned into a back door for mass migration and must be abolished in full.
3. Restrict Birthright Citizenship
Canada currently has one of the most lax laws regarding birthright citizenship across the developed world. As it stands, children born to foreign diplomats, tourists, international students, temporary foreign workers, asylum seekers with unresolved claims, or illegal migrants on Canadian soil automatically receive citizenship. Our system is being taken advantage of by birth tourists.
We must amend the Citizenship Act to end automatic jus soli citizenship. Citizenship will only be granted at birth if at least one parent is a Canadian citizen. A new “Canadian-born non-citizen”status will be created for ineligible children, with strict cultural and civic requirements for future citizenship eligibility.
Retroactively impose these new standards, revoking citizenship from those who do not meet the new requirement and any resulted chain migration. Expand the definition of fraud to include those who intentionally gamed our immigration system through anchor babies and birth tourism.
4. Eliminate Pull Factors & Introduce Push Factors
Our government must prioritize the comfort and wellbeing of Canadians before those of immigrants. We must restructure Canada’s legal, social, and institutional environment to discourage long-term settlement by non-citizens. Key measures include:
A      national remittance tax on funds sent abroad;
Abolish      access to social services to all non-citizens including access to      healthcare, education, and any economic assistance;
A     ban on kosher/halal animal slaughter;
A ban      on foreign-language signage in government services and commercial      signage;
Strict      enforcement of French and English language laws;
A ban      on visible religious symbols for public employees and in publicly      funded spaces;
A     ban on employment for dual citizens in public service, elected office,      and national security-sensitive fields;
A ban      on new dual citizenships, and the eventual phase-out of existing dual      status.
Phase II: Remove Non-Citizens & Incentivize Voluntary Return
5.      Reform the Asylum System
Since 2015, Canada’s asylum system has expanded dramatically and become deeply dysfunctional. What was meant to provide temporary protection for genuine refugees has increasingly turned into a backdoor immigration channel, exploited by fraudsters, scammers, and unethical immigration consultants to bypass regular immigration pathways. Today, the system is overwhelmed, with a backlog of roughly 300,000 unresolved claims, leaving many applicants in legal limbo for years while imposing major costs on taxpayers.
This broken system must be shut down and fundamentally reformed. Any permanent residency or citizenship obtained through fraudulent or abusive asylum claims should be reviewed and revoked.Going forward, asylum processing should be conducted outside Canada’s borders, following models such as the UK’s Rwanda plan, with secure third-country facilities where claims can be assessed and individuals can be housed safely before returning home. Canada must end the abuse of its asylum system and restore its integrity.
6. Revocation of Permanent Residency
Terminate existing permanent residency status and conduct a full scale audit. Offer citizenship to those who meet new citizenship standards — economically productive, culturally integrated — remove those who do not.
Amend the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) to eliminate the presumption of indefinite residence for permanent residents. Establish a new provision under IRPA that allows for the revocation of permanent resident status and subsequent removal from Canada at the discretion of the Minister of Public Safety or the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, without the need to prove inadmissibility under existing categories (e.g., criminality, security, misrepresentation).
Repeal or amend IRPA Sections 44–46 to remove procedural constraints related to admissibility determinations. Remove access to appeals through the Immigration Appeal Division (IAD) for any revocation of permanent residence not based on humanitarian grounds. 
 
 Modify or suspend the application of Section 7 of the Charter for permanent residents through the Notwithstanding Clause, allowing for removal without extended judicial review. Grant the federal government full statutory authority to terminate permanent residency for any non-citizen, with removals carried out on a categorical or individual basis, regardless of conduct, tenure, or country of origin.

7. Mass Deportations
Following the end of immigration programs and PR revocation, initiate a nationwide removal operation targeting:
All      Temporary Foreign Workers, estimated at approximately 3,000,000,     following the abolition of the program;
Revoked      birthright citizenships under new laws, estimated between 175,000      and 250,000;
Permanent      Residents, estimated at roughly 2,200,000, whose status has      been revoked under new legislation;
Illegal      migrants, estimated between 20,000 and 500,000 according to      government sources (likely much higher);
Holders      of expiring temporary visas (students, workers, visitors), totaling      approximately 2.1 million individuals currently in Canada;
Fraudulent      Asylum Claimants, estimated between 600,000 and 700,000     including those currently in the system and those wrongly awarded      citizenship or permanent residency.
Estimated total: 5 to 9 million deportations. Deportations will be carried out in phases using updated removal infrastructure, chartered flights, and bilateral repatriation agreements. Appeal processes will be suspended or narrowed, and overstayers will face mandatory identification and removal.
8. Voluntary Repatriation Program
Establish a federal program for naturalized citizens who wish to renounce their Canadian citizenship and return to their country of origin. Participants will receive a one-time financial repatriation package and assistance resettlement logistics. The program will be promoted as a peaceful, non-punitive option for individuals with weak ties to Canada or enduring identification with their country of origin.
Phase III: Rebuild a Cohesive & Sovereign Nation
9.      Adjust and Expand Rules for Revoking Naturalized Citizenship
Amend the Citizenship Act to restore and expand the federal government’s authority to revoke naturalized citizenship on the basis of national interest, loyalty, and cultural compatibility—not solely fraud. New grounds for revocation will include:
Public       allegiance to foreign states or ideologies hostile to Canada;
Participation       in foreign-aligned political agitation or demonstrations on Canadian       soil;
Engagement       in subversive or anti-Canadian activity, whether violent or ideological.
The legal definition of fraud will be expanded to encompass concealment of political, ideological, or civilizational loyalties incompatible with the duties of Canadian citizenship, as well as common means of abusing existing systems including birth tourism, anchor babies, and dishonest asylum claims.
A Citizenship Integrity Tribunal will be established to adjudicate revocation cases through an administrative process. Charter protections will be overridden where necessary using the Notwithstanding Clause, and revocation will be followed by removal from the country.
10. Penalize Institutions That Enabled Mass Immigration
Conduct a full investigation into government agencies, non-governmental organizations, academic institutions, and corporate entities that enabled, promoted, or profited from mass immigration. Defund and dismantle publicly funded organizations that facilitated demographic replacement under the banner of multiculturalism, refugee resettlement, or "diversity" policy.
Audit immigration consulting firms, legal aid networks, and taxpayer-funded NGOs for abuse, fraud, and collusion with foreign interests.
Ban former senior officials from IRCC, CSIS, CBSA, and related departments from working in the immigration sector post-tenure.
Introduce criminal liability, financial penalties, and debarment for institutions that engaged in systemic misrepresentation, trafficking, or political subversion under the guise of humanitarian or economic necessity.
 
The goal is to dismantle the infrastructure of mass immigration and ensure that those who undermined national sovereignty are held legally and politically accountable.
11. Repeal the Multiculturalism Act

Repeal the Canadian Multiculturalism Act and remove all references to multiculturalism from federal law, policy, and Charter interpretation. Replace it with a new National Cohesion Act that affirms Canada’s founding as a historically European, Christian, and bicultural (English and French) nation with a common civic identity.
End all public funding for multicultural programming, ethnic lobbying organizations, and diversity-based hiring or procurement initiatives. Redefine national culture as something to be preserved and transmitted, not diluted or redefined.
Public institutions—including schools, media, and the civil service—will be required to promote assimilation, unity, and shared national values, not group-based identity politics. This marks the formal end of multiculturalism as a state ideology and the re-establishment of Canada as a coherent, rooted, and self-determined nation.
Public institutions will be required to promote cultural unity, not pluralism." https://t.co/TpCw5hNha0

text:
From the South to the United States: The full story of what those who do not know it are missing

🔷 A state that once existed..
Before 1990, there were two states on the map of the Arabian Peninsula: the Yemeni Arab Republic in the North with its capital Sana'a, and the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen in the South, with its capital Aden. They were both members of the United Nations, each with its own flag, army, and constitution.

🔷 Unity.. a dream that turned into a nightmare!
On May 22, 1990, the two states united. Southerners entered unity voluntarily, believing in an equal partnership. But they were surprised by dozens of assassinations, marginalization, and exclusion directed at the South, and in 1994, the partnership collapsed, the South declared disengagement, and the North responded with a comprehensive war that occupied the South.

🔷 What happened after 1994?
After the war, more than 120,000 Southern soldiers and civilian employees were dismissed from their jobs. Southern institutions were looted, its lands confiscated, and its political representation dropped from 50% to 0% in the presidency of the republic in 2011. The South turned from a partner into an occupied land.

🔷 The Southern Movement.. the voice of the people..
In 2007, Southern retirees came out in peaceful protests demanding rights. The regime ignored them, repressed them, and shed their blood, so the movement turned from reform demands into a clear demand: restoring the Southern state. It was not an emotional demand, but the result of a harsh experience.

🔷 2017: The birth of the Transitional Council..
On May 4, 2017, the South Arabian Transitional Council was founded to be the political representative of the Southern cause. It was not a political party, but an entity comprising armed forces, security apparatuses, and a broad popular mandate. Its goal: restoring the fully sovereign Southern state.

🔷 The Southern forces.. the region's safety shield..
Forces such as the Shabwa Defense, the Giants Brigades, and the Security Belt fought the Houthis for years, liberated Aden, Al-Dhale'a, Shabwa, and Abyan, and protected Bab al-Mandab. These forces were the first line of defense for the region and offered thousands of martyrs.

🔷 The alliance with Saudi Arabia.. then betrayal!
In 2015, Saudi Arabia entered the war against the Houthis. Southerners fought alongside it. But in December 2025, after the Transitional Council liberated Hadhramaut and Al-Mahra from the forces of the terrorist Muslim Brotherhood, Saudi Arabia turned against it: it launched more than 200 airstrikes on the Southern forces, imposed an air and sea blockade, and arrested the Council's delegation in Riyadh, where it remains detained to this moment.

🔷 What the South demands today?
Amr Al-Baidh, the representative of President Aidarous Al-Zubaidi for Foreign Affairs, calls on #Washington to support a political path leading to a referendum on the independence of the South, after a one-year transitional phase. And he says clearly: the option of restoring Sana'a militarily is no longer realistic.

🔷 Why a referendum?
Because Southerners want to determine their own destiny, not have it decided for them from closed rooms. A referendum is not an innovation, but a right guaranteed by United Nations covenants. It is the solution that ends the conflict, not the one that postpones it.

🔷 Conclusion..
The South is not a "secessionist movement" as it is portrayed. It is a people with a former state, a history, an identity, victims, and one demand: restoring their state. Whoever does not understand the story will deal only with the outcome.

text:
Two engineers in Baku, on the same monthly salary.
🇦🇿 One pays 905 manat of income tax on it.
The other pays 2,225.

The salary is 10,000 manat a month, about 5,880 dollars or 5,310 euros. Which tax scale applies depends on the employer's sector.

The first engineer works for a private company outside oil and gas. Since January 2026 its staff pay 3 percent up to 2,500 manat a month, 10 percent up to 8,000 and 14 percent above that.

The second works for a state body, on the general scale. 14 percent up to 2,500 manat a month, 25 percent above that.

On this salary the gap is 1,320 manat a month, 15,840 a year, about 9,300 dollars or 8,400 euros. The gap grows as the salary grows.

The private scale is rising too. Its 3 percent entry rate becomes 5 percent in 2027 and 7 percent in 2028, both already law. On 10,000 manat, the private engineer's tax goes to 955 a month, then 1,005.

Social insurance is charged on top under both scales and is not in these figures.

I have coded 1,334 special tax regimes in 228 jurisdictions. My read: this is a tax rate that depends on who employs you, not only on what you earn, and the state charges its own staff the higher one.

If you are weighing a job offer in Baku, check which scale the employer is on before you agree the gross salary.

Would you take a lower gross salary from a private Baku firm to be taxed on the private scale?

With its strategic proximity to Bengaluru, connectivity through National Highway 48, access to the international airport and its position along the Chennai–Bengaluru Industrial Corridor, Tumakuru possesses all the advantages necessary to become a major manufacturing powerhouse.

The proposed industrial township spread across approximately 8,484 acres in phases, together with established industrial ecosystems at Vasanthanarasapura and the Machine Tool Park, provides a strong foundation for attracting investments in precision engineering, electronics, electric mobility, aerospace components, pharmaceuticals, logistics and food processing.

If Bengaluru represents the power of ideas and innovation, I envision Tumakuru becoming one of the great manufacturing centres where those ideas are transformed into products for the world.

Our Industrial Policy 2025–30, which targets investments of ₹7.5 lakh crore and the creation of 20 lakh jobs, reflects our commitment to translating this vision into tangible economic opportunities. We are focused on faster approvals, better infrastructure, industry–academia collaboration, emerging technologies, green manufacturing and creating an ecosystem where businesses can establish, expand and succeed with confidence.

But I want to emphasise one important principle: the true measure of an investment summit is not merely the value of agreements signed, but the factories established, the enterprises created, the jobs generated and the lives transformed.

Every major investment must contribute to the larger aspirations of our people. Industrial growth must create opportunities for our youth, strengthen local enterprises, empower women, support regional development and improve the standard of living of our citizens.

To investors across India and around the world, I extend an invitation to become partners in Karnataka's next chapter of growth. We offer not only an attractive investment destination but also a long-term partnership built on skilled talent, innovation, policy support and a shared commitment to prosperity.

I am confident that Invest Karnataka 2027 will mark another defining milestone in our State's industrial history, enabling Karnataka to strengthen its global leadership while bringing the benefits of economic progress to every district.

Our aspiration is that Karnataka must become a State where global investments create local opportunities, where innovation drives industrial prosperity and where economic growth transforms the lives of ordinary people.

Together, let us make Karnataka the place where the world's ambitions meet India's possibilities. (2/2)

text:
Sixteen seconds. That is the entire length of the clip, and it holds more than most hour-long documentaries manage to say.

It is easy to watch it once and move on. It is much harder to watch it and not start asking questions. How does a person get within reach of a wild creature that was built to keep its distance? What does a day look like when your next meal depends entirely on what you can find, approach and carry home? And who teaches a human being to do that?

The people in this video are the Hadza, also called the Hadzabe. They live in northern Tanzania, around the shallow, salty waters of Lake Eyasi, and they are one of the last communities in Africa that still get most of their food by hunting and gathering. No shops. No fridge. No delivery window. No second chance if the day goes wrong.

I am not going to tell you how this particular story ends. The clip is too short to explain and deserves to be seen without a spoiler attached. What I can do is give you the context that makes sixteen seconds feel a lot longer.

Read on, then press play. You will notice different things.

Let's start with the people, because the people are the story.

The Hadza live in dry woodland and thornscrub in the Rift Valley of northern Tanzania. Estimates vary, but they number roughly a thousand in total, and only a few hundred of them still live mainly by foraging. Their diet is built from wild plants, tubers, berries, honey and animals they hunt themselves. For a very large part of human history, that was simply what a human diet looked like. Today it is almost unheard of.

Their language, Hadzane, is classified as a language isolate. It has no known living relatives, and it uses click sounds that most people in the world cannot easily produce. Linguists have argued about its origins for decades without reaching an answer everyone accepts. Genetic studies have placed the Hadza on a very old branch of the human family tree, though scientists are careful to add a warning: no living people are a window into the past. Every community alive today has had exactly as many years of history as yours.

That warning matters, because here is what gets lost when a clip like this travels. The Hadza are not a relic. They are not a museum exhibit or a costume or a time machine. They are contemporary people who share this century with you and who have made a long-standing choice about how to live on a particular piece of land. Their way of life is not primitive. It is specialized, in the way a surgeon's or a pilot's life is specialized, except that the training starts in early childhood and the classroom is the bush itself.

Ethnographers who have spent years with the community describe children who forage for themselves at an age when children elsewhere are still being fed by hand. Small kids dig for roots, collect fruit and wander farther from camp than most visitors would dare. Boys make small bows and practice on small targets long before anyone expects them to bring back anything that matters. Competence is not lectured into them. It is built by doing, failing and doing again.

Keep that in mind. Whatever you see in the clip is the visible tip of something that began when the person in it was around the size of a backpack.

Now, the word everyone reaches for when they see something like this: skill.

It is a lazy word. It sounds like talent, like a gift some people are born with. What it actually describes here is closer to the opposite: an enormous, slow accumulation of small corrections.

Ethnographers describe Hadza men making their own bows and arrows from local materials, shaped to fit the person who will use them. A hunter's equipment is not bought, it is made, and it is tuned by the one who has to trust it. That alone is a different relationship with a tool than most of us will ever have. When was the last time you depended on something you built yourself, with a result that mattered that day?

But the bow is the easy part. Here is the fact that changes how you should look at any scene involving one: a bow is a short-range tool. It does not forgive distance the way a modern firearm does. Every bit of the difficulty lives in the stretch before the shot, in the approach. The weapon is simple. The craft is everything that has to go right so that the weapon gets its chance.

And "everything that has to go right" is a long list. Hunters in foraging societies, the Hadza among them, read what most of us never notice. Wind direction, because scent travels. The angle of the light, because a shadow can announce a person long before a person arrives. The sound of their own footsteps on different ground. How other animals behave, because a sudden silence among birds is information and so is the opposite. Where water is, where shade is, which time of day brings which animal to which place.

None of that lives in a book. It lives in bodies, handed down by watching, copying, being corrected and getting it wrong in front of people who are hungry.

One snapped twig, one shifted shadow, one badly judged step, and a whole morning of work can vanish. The margin for error is small and the feedback is immediate. Nobody sends a polite email telling a hunter what he did wrong. The bush simply says no.

Think about what that does to a mind. The loudest thing in a modern life is a notification. The loudest thing in a hunter's day is a twig.

I want you to carry that into the clip. Not as a stunt, not as a trick, but as a piece of work performed inside a very narrow window by someone for whom the stakes are not abstract.

Then there is the other side of the equation: the animal.

When people talk about hunting, they imagine the person. The animal is usually treated as scenery. But the animal is half the problem, and in a place like this, it is a problem with millions of years of engineering behind it.

Africa has birds that make the point about scale very clearly. The marabou stork is one of them. It stands up to roughly a meter and a half tall, about as high as a ten-year-old child. Its wingspan is commonly cited at around two and a half meters, and sometimes more, which is wider than a standard doorway is tall. It carries a heavy, dagger-like bill, a bare head and neck, and a pouch of skin that hangs from the throat. It has earned the nickname "undertaker bird" for its dark, hunched, cloaked look and for its habit of feeding where other animals have died.

It is, by any honest standard, an unsettling thing to see up close. It is also an extremely successful survivor. Marabous live across sub-Saharan Africa, scavenge at carcasses alongside vultures, and thrive near human settlements as easily as in open savanna. A species does not manage that by being slow, naive or easy.

That is the point. A wild animal of that size is not a prop. It is awake, wary and well equipped. Its eyes are better than yours. Its sense of danger is older than any human culture. Whatever happens when a person and an animal like that meet in open country, it is not a one-sided event.

And that is exactly where the tension in a clip like this comes from, whichever way you think it will go. You are not watching a person act on a passive world. You are watching two sets of survival instincts, one human and one wild, occupy the same few seconds.

Which one has the advantage? That depends on a great many things that sixteen seconds cannot tell you. I will leave that part for your eyes.

Here is something the highlight-reel version of hunting never mentions: most days, nothing happens.

Researchers who have studied foragers in this region have long pointed out that big-game hunting is a gamble. Hunters can walk for hours and return without meat. Not once, but repeatedly, across weeks. It is one of the reasons the daily calories in Hadza camps lean so heavily on what is gathered, tubers and berries and baobab fruit and honey, much of it collected by women, and much of it far more dependable than anything with a pulse.

So why hunt at all?

Scientists genuinely argue about this. One camp says meat is nutritionally precious and socially explosive: a rare, dense, valuable food that changes the mood of an entire camp. Another says hunting is partly about reputation, that a man who provides is a man whom others notice. A third says it is some tangled combination of both, plus the plain fact that it is what Hadza men have always done and what they are good at. The debate is still open, and it should be. Anyone who offers you a tidy one-line answer is selling something.

What most observers agree on is what happens after a successful day. Meat is shared widely. In many foraging societies, a hunter does not get to keep his catch the way a shopper keeps a purchase. Anthropologists have described strong norms of sharing among the Hadza, strong enough that the ideal is for the whole camp to eat, not just the person who made the effort. It works as a kind of insurance. Today it is your good fortune. Tomorrow it is someone else's, and you will want the same generosity back.

Consider how different that is from the way most of us think about food. We tend to treat a meal as a private transaction. In this system, a meal is closer to a public event, something that happens to a group, and that quietly decides who feels secure and who does not.

Hold that thought. It changes the weight of everything on screen. When the outcome of a few seconds does not only feed one person, the stakes are not personal. They belong to a camp.

If you think this is a story only about the past, the science has some bad news for you.

Over the last few decades, the Hadza have become some of the most studied people on Earth, and what researchers found has quietly rewritten several things we thought we knew about our own bodies.

Start with energy. In a well-known 2012 study, anthropologist Herman Pontzer and colleagues measured how many calories Hadza adults burn in a day. These are people who walk many kilometers, dig, climb and carry as a matter of routine. The expectation was obvious: they must burn far more than a person who sits at a desk. Instead, once body size was taken into account, their daily energy expenditure looked remarkably similar to that of adults in Western countries. That result unsettled a lot of assumptions about exercise and weight. It suggested that the story of modern health is not simply that we move less, and that diet and other factors may carry more of the weight than most of us were told.

Then there is the gut. In a 2017 study published in Science, researchers who followed Hadza gut bacteria across the seasons found something striking. The microbial communities shifted with the wet and dry seasons, with some bacterial groups fading and reappearing over the course of a year, tracking what was available to eat. Compared with people in industrialized countries, the Hadza showed greater microbial diversity, and certain bacteria common in industrial populations were scarce. Scientists are still working out what that means for health. But it is hard to look at that data and not wonder what we traded away, without noticing, for convenience.

And then there is the strangest partnership of all.

Hadza honey gatherers are known for a working relationship with a small wild bird called the greater honeyguide. The bird knows where wild bees nest. The humans know how to open a nest the bird cannot. Researchers have documented that people and birds communicate, with humans using calls to recruit the bird and the bird leading people to the hive, and that both sides benefit. The honeyguide is not a pet and not a trained animal. It is a wild creature that has been negotiating with human beings, in its own way, for what may be an extraordinarily long time.

Why do I bring all this up? Because it shows what kind of knowledge sits behind a few seconds of video. This is a community whose relationship with the living world is not casual, not romantic, not performative. It is practical, reciprocal and deeply specific. They do not only take from the wild. They have learned its terms.

So let's talk about what sixteen seconds actually is.

A short clip is a compression algorithm for a life. It takes hours of walking, watching and waiting, years of apprenticeship and a lineage of inherited knowledge, and it presses all of that into a thumbnail-sized window. What survives the compression is the moment with the most motion. What is lost is everything that made the motion possible.

We do this to everything now. We pull a few seconds out of a process that took a lifetime and we call it content. Sometimes that is fine. Sometimes it is how a stranger on the other side of the planet gets to glimpse a way of living they never would have known existed. The risk is that we mistake the glimpse for the whole. That we see a few seconds of action and conclude that it was easy, or sudden, or simple, when the truth is that nothing about it was.

Think about the preparation that would have to exist before any scene like this. The knowledge of ground, season and weather. The equipment, made by hand and understood in detail. The decision about when to go and when to stay put. The quiet judgment about what is worth the effort and what is not. The community that expects, or does not expect, anything to come back.

You will not see any of that in the clip. That is exactly why I am describing it here.

There is one more thing worth saying, and it is the one I find hardest to shake. The attention required for this kind of life is not a mood you can summon. It is a trained state of mind, available for hours, in heat, with real consequences for lapses. Most of us have to schedule a retreat to approximate it. For a Hadza hunter it is simply Tuesday.

I do not say that to idolize anyone. People everywhere are capable of extraordinary focus when the situation demands it. I say it because the video is a rare chance to watch focus without a screen in it. And after a day of scrolling, that is oddly rare.

Before we go further, let me retire a few myths, because clips like this attract them.

Myth one: that people like the Hadza live in a state of constant, desperate struggle. The honest picture is more complicated. Anthropologists have debated for decades how hard foragers actually work. Early estimates for some foraging societies suggested surprisingly modest hours spent on food, and later researchers argued that the answer depends heavily on what you choose to count as work. Both sides agree on this much: it is neither a permanent crisis nor a permanent paradise. It is a life with real hardship, real leisure and a rhythm set by seasons rather than by a calendar.

Myth two: that a community without a government is a community without rules. The Hadza are widely described as strongly egalitarian. They have no chiefs in the sense most of us would recognize. Camps are small, often only a few dozen people, and they are fluid. People move between camps, and whole camps relocate several times a year. Influence is earned by being useful and trusted, and it can disappear the moment it is abused. When a person cannot stand the company, the usual answer is not a lawsuit. It is walking away.

Myth three: that "traditional" means "unchanged." Nothing alive is unchanged. The Hadza have encountered traders, missionaries, researchers, tourists, neighbors with very different economies and governments that have wanted them to live differently. They have adapted, resisted, borrowed and negotiated all along. A foraging life is not a frozen photograph. It is an ongoing decision, renewed every day by people who know exactly what the alternatives look like.

I mention all this for a simple reason. When you watch a short video of any group, you are tempted to fill the gaps in your knowledge with a story you already own. The noble savage. The harsh survivalist. The vanishing tribe. Every one of those is a costume, and none of them fits a real person. Try to watch without one.

Now consider something that rarely gets credit: the breadth of what a forager has to know.

We celebrate expertise in modern life, and we are right to. A surgeon, a pilot, an engineer, a chess grandmaster: each has gone very deep into one narrow field. But a forager's expertise runs in the other direction. It is wide. Ethnographers working with foraging peoples describe detailed knowledge of plants, which ones feed, which ones heal, which ones hurt and when each is in season. Knowledge of animals, their tracks, their habits, their moods at different times of year. Knowledge of terrain, water, weather and the thousand small signs that tell you the weather is about to turn. Knowledge of people, because every one of those skills has to be coordinated with others.

Then add the manual skills: making tools, repairing them, building shelter, starting fire, preparing food, caring for children while doing all of the above.

No single person holds all of it, but each person holds an astonishing share. A useful comparison: imagine being dropped, alone, into a landscape with nothing but your own memory and your own hands, and being asked to feed yourself, safely, for a week. Most of us would last only a short while before the gaps in our knowledge became painful. Not because we are foolish, but because we are specialists in a system that handles everything else for us.

That is not an insult to modern people. It is a trade, and a good one in many ways. But it makes one thing clear. The ability to walk through a place and understand it, to see opportunity and danger in a landscape that looks like empty ground to a visitor, is not ordinary. It is among the oldest forms of intelligence our species has produced, and almost nobody is still practicing it at this scale.

So when you press play, you are not just watching an event. You are watching a fluent speaker of a language most of the world has forgotten.

Now let me be honest about the thing some of you are already thinking.

This is a video about hunting. A wild animal is part of it. Some people will feel uneasy watching that, and that reaction is legitimate. Others will feel nothing but admiration for the skill involved. Both reactions are human. Neither one makes you a better or worse person.

What I would gently ask is that you do not let the discomfort decide too quickly. Most of the meat people eat in the modern world arrives hidden. It passes through systems designed, in part, to keep the origin out of sight. A visible version of the same chain, where a person must personally face the cost of a meal, tends to produce stronger feelings than a package in a supermarket. That is worth sitting with. Not because it settles the argument, but because it reveals one.

The question underneath is an old and serious one: what do we owe the thing that feeds us? Many foraging peoples answer with restraint, respect, use of everything that can be used, and an unwillingness to take more than a day requires. I am careful not to speak for the Hadza on what they believe about it. I can only say that researchers describe a practical, hunger-sized relationship with animals, one in which taking is tied to need and eating is shared widely. You can agree or disagree with where they land. It is a very different thing from hunting as a hobby, a trophy or a post.

There is another conversation hiding here, too. As interest in the Hadza has grown, so have the visitors, the researchers and the cameras. People who care about the community disagree, sincerely, about what that attention does for them. Some see income and visibility. Others see intrusion and a life turned into a spectacle. If you share this clip, it is worth remembering that you are looking at real people who did not necessarily sign up to be anyone's entertainment. Watch the way you would want to be watched: with curiosity, and with some humility.

That does not mean looking away. It means looking properly.

There is a reason this kind of footage feels a little urgent, even when nobody says so.

Foraging peoples across the world have been under pressure for generations, and the Hadza are no exception. Their land has long been wanted by others. Farmers and herders have moved into areas where the Hadza hunt and gather. Wild game that once roamed widely has declined in many regions of Africa. Outside institutions have repeatedly encouraged, or pushed, communities like theirs toward settlement and agriculture. Securing land rights has been a recurring, difficult struggle, and it is the kind of struggle that rarely makes it into a sixteen-second video.

A way of life that depends on open land cannot survive without open land. That sounds obvious. It is also the whole problem. You cannot practice the knowledge of a place if the place is fenced, ploughed, grazed to dust or simply no longer yours.

I do not want to turn this into a lecture, and I certainly do not want to tell you how to feel. The Hadza are not asking anyone to rescue them from their own lives. Like any community, they have their own views, their own disagreements and their own ideas about what to keep and what to change. What outsiders can reasonably do is smaller and harder: pay attention honestly, avoid turning people into symbols, and notice when a way of living that took thousands of years to refine is being squeezed out in a handful of decades.

Here is the uncomfortable symmetry. We live in a world where food is abundant and attention is scarce. In the bush the equation is reversed, and attention is what makes food possible. Two entirely different economies, two entirely different relationships with time. And both of them are available on the same screen, in the same thumb-swipe, a few inches apart.

So what should you watch for?

Not the obvious thing. The obvious thing is the moment you will notice no matter what I say. The less obvious thing is what the people involved treat as ordinary. What they do not hurry. What they do not waste. How little noise there is around the effort, and how much knowledge seems to be sitting inside the quiet.

Watch how the work is shared. A single decisive moment in a clip can look like a solo performance, but this kind of life is rarely solo. Look for who is nearby, who is waiting, who is watching, and what their faces and bodies seem to know before you do.

Watch the scale difference between the two sides of the encounter, and ask yourself which of them looks like the underdog. Then ask whether you are sure.

And watch what is missing: the rifle, the vehicle, the engine, the shortcut. A very large amount of modern life exists to remove risk and effort from the act of getting a meal. Here, none of that is in the frame. The risk is real and the effort is real, and that is exactly why the sequence feels so heavy for something so brief.

I will not tell you what it all adds up to. Sixteen seconds is not a lot of time, but it is enough for a question to land and an answer to begin forming. Whatever you decide you saw is yours.

One last thing before you go.

After you watch, notice where your attention went first. To the person? To the animal? To the open land around them? There is no correct answer, but there is a revealing one. Where your eyes land first is a small portrait of what you tend to value and what you tend to overlook. Some viewers see courage. Some see vulnerability. Some see the ground itself and wonder how much of it is left. All three are looking at the same sixteen seconds.

That is part of why the clip travels. It does not hand you a conclusion. It hands you a mirror, and then it ends before you have finished looking.

Let me end where I started, with that small number.

Sixteen seconds is shorter than the time it takes most of us to decide what to watch next. It is shorter than an advertisement. It is shorter than the pause before a text that we were not sure we should send. And somewhere inside it sits a life lived by a standard most of us would find almost impossible to meet: total attention, total honesty, no padding, no reset.

We spend enormous effort building tools that save us time. The Hadza spend their time building knowledge that cannot be saved, only inherited, practiced and passed on. One of those approaches gives you a faster day. The other gives you a deeper place in the world. Neither is simply right. But only one of them is vanishing.

If a clip ever deserved two viewings, it is this one. The first time, you will watch what happens. The second time, you will watch who it is happening to, and what it took for them to be standing there at all.

And if you keep only one thing from all of this, keep this: the next time you see a few seconds of someone doing something that looks effortless, ask what had to be learned, lost and learned again for it to look that way. Effortless is almost always the last stage of a very long effort.

Press play now, and see for yourself exactly what sixteen seconds can hold.

Cross River State Governor, Senator Bassey Otu has welcomed the employment of 20 youths by Skyrun International and the company’s admission of forty additional candidates into its third training cohort under the state’s Skills-in-the-Hands Initiative.

The 20 beneficiaries completed electrical and electronics training in the first two batches of the programme, a partnership between the Ministry of Youth Development and Skills Acquisition and the Chinese household electronics manufacturer operating in the Calabar Free Trade Zone. Skyrun offered automatic employment to every graduate from those cohorts.

Governor Otu, represented by the Chairman of the House Committee on Youth and Sports Development, described the outcome as evidence of the administration’s emphasis on human-capital development, skills acquisition, and sustainable employment. He congratulated the new employees and urged them to maintain discipline, integrity, and professionalism. He also expressed support for the expanded third intake and pledged continued government patronage of Skyrun products in recognition of the firm’s investment in local capacity building.

Commissioner for Youth Development, Barr. Udom-Ijom Ukam stated that the 100 per cent placement rate demonstrates the effectiveness of industry-linked training models. 

Skyrun Chairman Chief George Wu reaffirmed the company’s long-term commitment to manufacturing and job creation in Nigeria, noting that the Calabar facility now functions as a state internship and employment centre. The company employs more than one thousand Nigerians, the majority of them from Cross River State.

The Skills-in-the-Hands Initiative forms part of the state government’s broader strategy to equip young people with practical, market-relevant skills and direct pathways into employment within the industrial sector.

text:
@JustGrok, 
No, that claim is not correct.

What actually happened: On or around Armistice Day (11 November 2026), Major General Karl Harris CBE signed the Armed Forces Covenant with Dr Tariq Sheikh of Tariq Halal Meats (a major UK/European halal meat supplier) at the company’s Wembley HQ. The Covenant is a standard pledge by organisations to support serving personnel, reservists, veterans and their families (e.g., no disadvantage in employment, flexibility for training/postings, possible job support for leavers). Reports from outlets such as The Nation and Daily Pakistan describe the signing, historical remarks about South Asian soldiers in the British Indian Army, and the company’s plans to display the Covenant and encourage recruitment/support for the forces. There is no mention of any meat supply contract or change in Army catering.⁠Nation⁠Dailypakistan

The claim that “the majority of meat now used by the British Army will be Halal-certified” and that there is “no need to provide a ‘Halal Option’ as most of the meat is Halal” originates from social media posts (notably from accounts like UNN / Unity News Network). It is not supported by the factual reporting of the Covenant signing or by official policy.⁠Facebook

Official MoD position (parliamentary answer, October 2025, to a question from Rupert Lowe): Halal food is not the default option for the Ministry of Defence, military academies, or the Armed Forces. There are no Defence institutions where Halal is the only option. Suppliers must accommodate the inclusive dining offer for all personnel, including religious and other dietary needs. Similar earlier answers and FOI responses have confirmed Halal is available via contractors (and in some ration packs) but that the MoD does not treat it as default and does not centrally hold detailed volume figures (those sit with the contractors).⁠Parallelparliament

In short: the Covenant signing is real and concerns support for the armed forces community. The assertion that it means the majority of British Army meat is (or will be) Halal-certified, rendering separate options unnecessary, is unsupported.

Revolutionary Snipers: Washington’s Frontier Commandos Whose Marksmanship Forged a New Way of War and Helped Win the Revolution
- by Patrick K. O'Donnell

From the bestselling and award-winning author of The Indispensables and The Unvanquished, the dramatic untold story of the Continental Army's first soldiers and special operators, whose marksmanship and irregular warfare altered the outcomes of crucial battles and turned the tide of the Revolutionary War

In Revolutionary Snipers, acclaimed military historian Patrick K. O’Donnell vividly brings to life for the first time the exploits of Washington’s finest frontier com mandos, whose legendary deadeye shooting offered the Continental Army an evolving and unconventional tactical advantage in the War of Independence. Snipers such as Daniel Morgan, Timothy Murphy, and Samuel Brady were rugged frontiersmen armed with long rifles, a path-breaking American technology that allowed them to attack from a significant distance.

The snipers, the very first members of the Continental Army, quickly struck terror among British troops besieged in Boston in the summer of 1775 by picking off targets. However, their success was checkered by mutiny, an epic journey through the Maine wilderness, and heart-wrenching failure at the gates of Quebec. O’Donnell follows unforgettable characters, including a white slave to a rifle-wielding female camp follower, in a riveting Band of Brothers–style narrative. Despite the setbacks, Washington and his officers perceived a new approach to waging war could emerge from the combined arms of pairing sniper groups with traditional units. The riflemen played vital roles in many pivotal battles—from protecting Washington’s army during its retreat from Manhattan, when some 25 snipers repelled an amphibious landing of hundreds of British soldiers at Throggs Neck, to energizing the momentum-shifting battles at Saratoga and later, in the South, at King’s Mountain and Cowpens.

Unearthing unpublished letters, diaries, and other participant documents, O’Donnell puts readers dramatically in the moment as riflemen prevented a British charge at Trenton that could have ended the war, employed irregular warfare to counter enemy attempts to re-supply during the critical yet obscure “Forage War” in spring 1777, and contested large swaths of the frontier, at times disguised as Native Americans.

Placing the riflemen front and center throughout the war, Revolutionary Snipers illuminates an unknown aspect of the conflict and is an important addition to our understanding of how the Revolution was won and of an emerging new way of war.

🇺🇦🇷🇺🇺🇸 PETRAEUS DELIVERS A STUNNING WARNING: UKRAINE IS FIGHTING THE WAR NATO COULD FACE NEXT!

Former CIA Director and US General David Petraeus has offered a striking assessment of Ukraine's military capabilities, Russia's mounting losses and the urgent lessons Western armies must learn from the battlefield.

Speaking to SpyCast, Petraeus described Ukraine as having Europe's largest and most innovative army, arguing that its resistance is preventing a much wider security crisis.

His warning was explicit: if Russia achieves its objectives in Ukraine, Moldova could become its next target, with Lithuania potentially following.

But some of his most revealing observations concerned the extraordinary transformation of modern warfare.

Petraeus warned that Western militaries cannot simply purchase drones, attach them to existing tank formations and assume they are prepared for the next conflict.

Ukraine has demonstrated that entire military structures, tactics and weapons systems need to be reconsidered. Equipment that Western armies have relied upon for decades could struggle to survive on today's Ukrainian battlefield.

And Russia is learning too.

Petraeus acknowledged that Moscow has sometimes developed new battlefield capabilities ahead of Kyiv, while China, Iran and North Korea are closely studying the conflict.

The implications extend far beyond Europe.

Ukraine is not merely defending itself. It is helping reveal what the next generation of warfare will look like, while NATO is being forced to reconsider some of its most fundamental assumptions.

Petraeus also presented a grim assessment of Russia's military and economic position.

He cited approximately 1.5 million Russian personnel killed or wounded, comparing that figure with American casualties during the Second World War.

According to the Ukrainian estimates he referenced, Russia suffered roughly 46,000 casualties last month while recruiting approximately 30,000 replacements.

He described captured Russian soldiers who had received less than two weeks of military training before being sent into combat.

On the economic front, Petraeus highlighted Ukraine's long-range strikes against Russian oil infrastructure, saying refineries within 3,000 kilometres of Ukraine's border had been targeted, some repeatedly.

He also cited Russian oil production falling below nine million barrels per day, growing fuel shortages and pressure on Moscow's National Wealth Fund, which he warned could be exhausted by the end of the year.

These are Petraeus's assessments and cited figures, rather than independently established outcomes.

He urged Europe and the United States to transfer frozen Russian reserves to Ukraine to help sustain its defense.

There was also a personal dimension to his interview.

During a recent visit to Ukraine, Petraeus witnessed the aftermath of a Russian jet-powered drone striking a locomotive on a neighbouring railway track. He described the fear experienced by passengers, many of whom were women and children.

And he spoke about Kyrylo Budanov, whom he knows personally.

Petraeus praised Budanov's direct military assessments and argued that his appointment to head Ukraine's Presidential Office gives Zelenskyy a close adviser with exceptional knowledge of frontline operations.

He recalled first speaking with Budanov while the Ukrainian intelligence chief was near the Russian border, commanding an early operation on Russian territory.

Despite his admiration for Ukraine's military innovation and resilience, Petraeus emphasized that Ukrainians are exhausted and facing another difficult winter.

That may be the most important contrast in his assessment.

Ukraine has demonstrated remarkable military adaptability while enduring enormous human and economic pressure.

Petraeus's message carries a warning for the West: Ukraine is gaining battlefield experience that NATO cannot afford to ignore, but learning from Ukraine means little if its partners fail to provide the resources it needs to survive.

To allow Huang to resign rather than fire him speaks volumes imo. This reduces their exposure immensely to a wrongful suit and liability. This allows him to find work within the circular arrangement of Blackrock and Big Tech. The backstory might be the chain of Commerce, Treasury and White House in terms of corruption. Here's the AI take:

Congress can compel a private citizen to testify. Being unemployed doesn't make you immune to Article I investigative power. The House Foreign Affairs Committee's demand for the November 18 closed-door briefing doesn't evaporate because he's no longer CEO — if anything, the committee gets more interested, because now there's no corporate spokesperson filter between them and him.

And if he shows up and pleads the Fifth, that's its own headline. There's no version where this quietly goes away.

A CEO's testimony binds the company. If Jensen sits in that closed-door briefing and says something false or something damaging, Nvidia owns it. Remove him, and whatever he says becomes a former employee's statements. The company gets to say "we've moved on, we're cooperating fully, we've taken remedial action" — which is the single most valuable sentence in any DOJ or BIS penalty negotiation.
Remediation is currency. BIS penalty guidelines explicitly weigh cooperation and corrective action. Firing the CEO is the most expensive, most legible remedial gesture a board can make. It buys down the fine before the fine exists.
The Delaware exposure is theirs, not his. Directors who've worked alongside him for decades and got rich doing it are the ones facing Caremark claims — did the board have a monitoring system, did it ignore red flags. Firing him is a defense exhibit.
Securities exposure runs through the filings. Nvidia publicly denied diversion to Chinese entities. If that was false, the board signed off on it. The CEO's head is the cheapest thing to put on the altar.

A sitting CEO has every incentive to absorb the hit and protect the institution — his identity is the institution. A fired CEO has no reason to keep carrying its secrets. He loses the company's legal cover, loses indemnification for conduct that turns out to be willful, and becomes a defendant shopping for a cooperation deal. DOJ's favorite witness is a freshly terminated executive who knows where every document is. The story stops being about the company and starts being about who told him what, and when.

The second affair is the one that's a corporate violation: a relationship with a direct report, filmed at a company conference, with security offering the witness an NDA. That's the thing that creates the Delaware and securities exposure. That's the thing that makes him radioactive. Again in my opinion this is why they allowed him to say he resigned. They could have easily fired him and gotten away with it. So there's more there there than we know at this point.

Wachtell and Joon Kim are serious people. They're also retained by the board whose members are the potential defendants. That's not independence — that's a shared-interest arrangement with a prestigious letterhead.

And a private law firm can't subpoena Alice Huang, can't read the classified Rubio memo, can't compel testimony, can't execute a warrant, and can't reach anything in China. The investigation's actual function is to produce a defensible narrative and a document trail — not to find out what happened.

They're letting him resign so that whatever he says next belongs to him alone. Job offers at this point exposes corporate malfeasance intentions and poor judgment and responsibility to stockholders. Could backfire on those companies as Americans are sick of blatant corruption and the wealthy committing crimes they are never responsible for. BDS rings a bell.
