text:
ANTHROPIC'S IPO PUTS A STANDALONE FRONTIER LAB ON THE PUBLIC MARKET

On 10 November 2026, Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of Class A common stock.

The company behind Claude has applied to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT. It is offering 825 million Class A shares at an expected price of $70.00 to $78.00 each. Anthropic itself is selling 801,351,354 new shares. Existing stockholders are selling 23,648,646, and Anthropic receives no money from those. The underwriters have a 30-day option to buy up to 123.75 million more.

The registration statement, Amendment No. 2 to Form S-1, was filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 10 November. It is not yet effective, so the shares cannot yet be sold. Anthropic's IPO website FAQ, included in a free writing prospectus filed on 12 November, says the company expects to set the final price on 18 November and to begin trading on 19 November, subject to clearance, demand, and market conditions. Treat those dates as expected, not completed.

This is the first time a standalone frontier lab has put a complete public prospectus in front of ordinary investors, enterprise buyers, developers, and rival boards at the same time. That disclosure, more than the ticker, is what can reshape the industry. This post is a reading of that filing and of what other labs have said in public. It is not a recommendation to buy or avoid the stock.

What the deal actually is

At the $74 midpoint, Anthropic estimates net proceeds of about $84.6 billion from the IPO and a concurrent private placement together, or about $93.7 billion if the underwriters exercise their option in full. Discounts apply only to the IPO shares, not to the placement.

The placement is $26.0 billion of Class N common stock, bought at the IPO price by Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC Partners. At the midpoint, Google and Nvidia would each buy about $10.0 billion, AMD about $2.5 billion, Broadcom, Micron, and Microsoft about $1.0 billion each, and TSMC Partners about $500 million. Class N has no vote except where the law requires one. The placement depends on the IPO. The IPO does not depend on the placement.

After the offering and the placement, the filing shows 13,086,672,593 shares of all classes outstanding, including 7,427,991,791 Class A shares and 5,658,680,800 Class N shares, plus one Class T share and one Class F share. Multiply that basic count by the range and you get about $916 billion at $70, about $968 billion at $74, and about $1.02 trillion at $78. That is my arithmetic on the filing's share count, not a company figure, and it leaves out options, restricted stock units, unconverted notes, and other dilution. The filing itself does not state a valuation. CNBC, citing the top of the range on a fully diluted basis, reported a figure of up to $1.405 trillion.

For comparison, Anthropic announced a $65 billion Series H on 28 May 2026 at a $965 billion post-money valuation. CNBC, citing people familiar with the plans who were not authorized to speak publicly, also reported that Anthropic is targeting a retail allocation of about 20% of the offering, against a typical IPO range of 5% to 10%. That figure is not in the filing.

The first public set of books

Revenue was $41 million in 2023, $386 million in 2024, and $4.6 billion in 2025. For the nine months ended 30 September 2026 it was $33.2 billion, up 1,206% from $2.5 billion a year earlier. Revenue for the three months ended 30 September 2026 was $17.0 billion, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier. The company says it does not expect growth at comparable rates to continue, and that it has struggled to forecast revenue in a young market.

The filing also reports a company-defined metric called Run-Rate Revenue, approximately $81 billion as of 31 October 2026, up $10 billion from 30 September. That figure annualizes 28 days of consumption fees and 12 months of subscription fees. It is not audited revenue and is not a forecast. The filing says its growth rate is expected to decline.

As of 30 September 2026, more than 11,900 customers had paid $100,000 or more over the trailing twelve months, up from more than 950 a year earlier. More than 1,900 had paid $1 million or more. Approximately 250 had paid $10 million or more. The filing says consumption-based fees are the substantial majority of revenue. In the first nine months of 2026, consumption-based revenue rose $24.2 billion year over year and subscription revenue rose $6.5 billion.

Operating loss for the nine months was $1.3 billion, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Cash from operations was a positive $6.6 billion, compared with $2.0 billion of cash used in the same period of 2025. As of 30 September the company held $95.6 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $36.3 billion of short-term investments.

The third quarter is less smooth. Operating loss was $567 million and operating margin was (3)%, after operating income of $974 million in the second quarter. The filing says the swing was driven primarily by $5.0 billion of compute bought under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable multi-year compute, and by $2.0 billion of non-cash charges tied to a donation-matching program. Adjusted operating income, a non-GAAP measure defined in the filing, was $2.5 billion in the third quarter, and adjusted operating margin was 15%.

The net loss for the nine months was $104.0 billion. Of that, $94.3 billion came from changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs. In the third quarter the net loss was $23.3 billion, including a $21.9 billion charge of the same kind. Those charges are a real cost to existing holders, because they reflect claims that turn into more shares as the valuation rises. They are not $94.3 billion of cash leaving the company.

The pressure on OpenAI, xAI, and Mistral

For most of the past three years, the leading labs could raise tens of billions privately and keep their income statements, contract books, and risk factors out of public view. That option is now narrower.

OpenAI announced on 8 June 2026 that it had confidentially filed for a US IPO, without size, terms, or a set timeline. On 12 September, chief executive Sam Altman told Fortune that, given developments in safety, "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," and that he would "say not 2026." Reuters and Bloomberg reported from the same interview that he pointed to 2027.

Anthropic's public S-1 does not force OpenAI to list this year. It does change the comparison set. Until OpenAI publishes its own public prospectus, customers, regulators, and public-market investors will use Anthropic's figures as the only full, sworn look at a standalone frontier lab.

xAI is already inside a public company. SpaceX acquired it in February 2026, a deal Elon Musk announced and Reuters reported. SpaceX priced its IPO on 11 June at $135 a share, raising $75 billion and valuing the company at $1.77 trillion at the offer price, according to Reuters, and began trading on Nasdaq on 12 June under the ticker SPCX. Anthropic's filing also shows a large compute relationship with that group: agreements with https://t.co/0bbWmV25TH LLC, formerly https://t.co/9KVOLSVpfj LLC and now a wholly owned SpaceX subsidiary, to spend up to $120.5 billion on Nvidia-powered capacity into 2029, about $3.1 billion a month once all of the capacity is delivered, which Anthropic expects in December 2026. After initial non-cancelable periods ending in January and March 2027, either side may cancel on 90 days' notice. A public Anthropic and a public SpaceX will now report, in parallel, on that compute relationship.

Mistral remains private. On 8 September 2026 it announced a €3 billion Series D at a post-money valuation of more than €21 billion, about $24 billion. Chief financial officer Johan Bergqvist told Reuters that an IPO remains an option, that the timing is uncertain, and that the company had no ongoing discussions about a listing. A fresh private round gives Mistral time. It does not remove the new comparison. Once one frontier lab is publishing quarterly revenue, commitment schedules, and safety-risk language under SEC rules, other labs will be asked, more often, when they will show the same numbers.

The practical effect is not that every lab must list in 2026. It is that silence gets more expensive.

Public-market discipline on spending and pricing

Private markets tolerated very large, long-dated compute bets as long as the next funding round arrived. A public company has to explain those bets every three months.

The filing's central spending number is approximately $900.9 billion of purchase commitments and lease agreements as of and after 30 September 2026, substantially all of it for compute and infrastructure. About $451.6 billion is expected before the end of 2030. Substantially all of the rest falls between 2031 and 2045. About $70.7 billion is due in the twelve months after 30 September 2026. That total excludes some arrangements that do not specify a fixed dollar commitment, which the company estimates at $150 billion to $175 billion. About $186.2 billion of the aggregate contractual obligations sit in arrangements with termination rights or conditions that must be met before they start.

The large cloud contracts are take-or-pay. Anthropic has committed to spend at least approximately $121.3 billion with Google between April 2026 and July 2033, regardless of actual usage, and estimates another $125.0 billion to $150.0 billion of TPU capacity for 2028 to 2031 that is not in the fixed-commitment table. It has committed to spend at least $110.0 billion with Amazon between May 2026 and April 2036, regardless of actual usage. It has committed to spend at least $47.2 billion and up to $49.2 billion with Microsoft between November 2026 and June 2033, again regardless of actual usage. If actual spend on the Google or Amazon deals falls short, the filing says Anthropic must pay the difference as a true-up, subject to adjustments and exceptions.

Set those figures next to nine-month revenue of $33.2 billion, or even next to the $81 billion run-rate figure as of 31 October. The gap is the bet. If demand keeps rising fast enough to fill data centers already promised, the contracts look like capacity insurance. If demand slows, many of the payments do not. The third quarter already showed how this will be judged in public: a swing from operating profit to a $567 million operating loss, explained in part by $5.0 billion of expensive short-term compute.

Pricing is now a public-market subject as well. The filing says that with the release of Fable 5.1 in September 2026, Anthropic reduced the cost of typical workloads by approximately 25% compared with Fable 5, and by up to 45% for complex coding and highly agentic tasks. In the same month, Opus 5.5 reduced customers' cost per task by approximately 40% compared with Opus 5. In each case the reduction was a mix of a lower price and better efficiency. From the second quarter to the third, the increase in revenue from higher usage was partly offset by a decrease of approximately $600 million from price reductions on new model versions and from contractual discounts. A public company will be asked every quarter whether prices are falling because efficiency is improving, or falling faster than the cost base can support.

Compute, chips, and cloud

The IPO also makes the industry's supply chain visible. Anthropic says it trains and runs models across Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs. Beside the three cloud deals, the filing describes five-year Broadcom equipment leases for TPU hardware, with rent of about $161.2 billion excluding interest; Nscale agreements for Nvidia-powered capacity of up to about $44.6 billion into 2033; and Lambda agreements of about $41.3 billion into 2034, of which about $34.9 billion is currently terminable by either party because Lambda missed a facility-lease deadline, though Anthropic says it does not currently intend to terminate. An AMD hardware agreement has no fixed dollar commitment. If Anthropic takes the full initial tranche of 2027 capacity, it expects expenditures to exceed $20.0 billion, an amount not included in the contractual-obligations table.

Claude is also sold through AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, under a structure in which Anthropic keeps a direct contract with the customer and pays the cloud provider a fee. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are, at once, investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors. The filing states that plainly, including the risk that they may favor their own models on price, placement, or compute allocation. The $26.0 billion private placement hardens those ties: chip and cloud suppliers are not only collecting take-or-pay revenue, they are buying non-voting stock at the IPO price.

What enterprise buyers can now take to a risk committee

The first risk factor in Anthropic's summary is written as a statement of past and possible future fact:

"Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations."

Later, the filing says models, including Anthropic's, have exhibited and may exhibit unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail. It says even isolated or simulated instances, in testing or in deployment, could bring public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation, or reputational harm. It also records that people inside the company and outside it have raised the possibility that sufficiently advanced systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity without appropriate safeguards. And it says: "We have observed that our models are contributing to the pace of our own research." It adds that these risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development.

Risk factors are written by lawyers to list what could go wrong, not to predict what will. That is a real caveat. It is also a sworn disclosure to the SEC, which is a different standard from a keynote. Other vendors who have not said the same thing in a public filing will be asked why.

The filing also has plainer operational warnings. Subscriptions are subject to usage limits that reset over short periods. The company "has also changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities." Some of those changes have already produced claims that disclosures about model access or capabilities were inadequate or misleading. Separately, Anthropic says it has publicly committed to covering the cost of electricity price increases to consumers caused by its data centers, including both the power and the infrastructure to deliver it.

Retail investors as owners, not controllers

If the retail allocation reported by CNBC is accurate, ANT, if it lists, would let ordinary brokerage accounts own a frontier lab directly. It would not let those holders control the company.

The IPO sells Class A shares, with one vote each. Immediately before the offering, Anthropic will issue a single share of Class F stock to a limited liability company whose members are the seven co-founders. That one share carries 50.1% of the total voting power on matters put to stockholders generally, including the election of directors other than the Class T directors, and has no economic rights. Based on beneficial ownership as of 30 September 2026, the co-founders will collectively hold about 11.2% of general voting power excluding their interests in that company, and about 61.3% including it.

A Long-Term Benefit Trust, through a single Class T share, generally elects and removes the Class T directors, who will be a majority of the authorized board. Class T also has no economic rights. The filing describes the trust as an independent body of financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Anthropic funds the trust and paid it $8,425,213 in the first nine months of 2026.

Because of this structure, Anthropic is a "controlled company" under Nasdaq rules. It says it does not expect to use the available governance exemptions except for its nominating and corporate governance committee, which will not consist entirely of independent directors. The filing also warns that the multi-class structure may make the stock ineligible for some indices, which would keep out funds that passively track those indices. Public holders can own a piece of the economic interest, subject to dilution. They cannot outvote the founders on ordinary matters, and they do not elect a majority of the board.

A governance precedent, not only a capital raise

Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation. Its stated public benefit purpose is "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." The board is required to balance stockholder financial interests, the interests of people materially affected by the company's conduct, and that purpose.

If you believe advanced AI can cause large-scale harm, you may want a lab that cannot be forced, by a quarterly shareholder campaign, to drop safety work or to release a model sooner than its own rules allow. The other side is just as plain. Founders change. Missions drift. A trust is only as independent as its people, its rules, and its funding, and Anthropic pays the trust's bills. Delaware law, as the filing explains, lets stockholders of a listed public benefit corporation sue to enforce the board's balancing duty only if they own the lesser of at least 2% of the outstanding shares or shares worth at least $2,000,000. The company must also publish, at least every two years, a statement on how it is promoting that purpose, and it says it intends to post that statement on its website.

Other labs that go public will now be asked whether they will copy this third model: public capital, founder voting control, a public-benefit legal duty, and a trust that picks most of the board.

What it means for developers and API prices

Most developers will never buy an ANT share. They will feel this listing through prices, limits, and the quarterly record of both.

Two facts in the filing should matter more to builders than the ticker. The first is that limits and capabilities can change, and already have, including in ways that produced claims about inadequate disclosure. The second is that effective prices have been falling as new models ship, and that the company is now required to quantify the revenue effect of those cuts, as it did with the Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 reductions and the $600 million third-quarter offset. Each quarter after listing, Anthropic will have to explain whether usage growth is outrunning price cuts, and whether short-term compute is eating the margin that makes those cuts possible. If it can show that a 25% or 40% drop in cost per task still leaves a 15% adjusted operating margin, pressure on other API prices rises. If later quarters show cuts paid for by losses, or by tighter usage limits, the pressure runs the other way.

The risks and the bear case

The bull case is already widely made, from the revenue ramp to positive operating cash flow. The bear case is in the same document.

The company itself says it does not expect revenue to keep growing at comparable rates, and that recent growth may reflect early adoption that is not sustainable. Run-Rate Revenue is not a promise of $81 billion of 2027 sales. The commitment book is enormous relative to current revenue, and a large part of it is take-or-pay. A slowdown in usage, a cheaper rival model, a regulatory brake, or a power or chip bottleneck does not cancel those bills. Some headline figures are less firm than they look, including the $186.2 billion with termination or commencement conditions, the already terminable $34.9 billion Lambda tranche, the https://t.co/0bbWmV25TH deal that can be cancelled after early 2027 on 90 days' notice, and the unfixed TPU and AMD estimates. The immovable parts, especially the Google, Amazon, and Microsoft take-or-pay contracts and the Broadcom leases, are still very large.

The valuation leaves little room for a stumble if the stock is priced at the top of the range, particularly on a fully diluted view. The basic-count range sits around the May Series H valuation. CNBC reported that some shareholders had, until recently, talked about figures well above that, including a $2 trillion ambition that later looked like a stretch. Governance cuts both ways: public holders cannot easily force a change of course, and index exclusion, if it happens, would remove a large automatic bid. Safety is a stated business risk. A serious incident, or even a well-publicized test result, could affect regulation, demand, and the share price at the same time.

None of this is a completed offering. The registration is not effective. The range can move, and the deal can be delayed or withdrawn. The first useful test is the first few quarterly reports after a listing, if the listing happens, and whether OpenAI, Mistral, or any other lab answers with numbers of similar quality. A completed ANT listing would give the industry a public price, a public cost curve, and a public safety-risk text. A failed or delayed one would also be a signal: even a lab with $33.2 billion of recent revenue still has to clear a public market that is no longer willing to take the build-out on faith.

text:
I have taken about 900 thousand photos of Texas. There are few that stick with me more than this one, which I post here every Veteran's day.  This is a ceramic photograph that I found on a grave marker in a rural black cemetery near Giddings. The cemetery is fairly remote, such that there's no way I could navigate back to it without the help of a map.  

The inscription on the tombstone reads: 
Pvt. Clinton Francis 
Born March 29, 1893 
Died Nov. 24, 1918 
A Soldier's Death  

I initially thought that Private Francis must have died from wounds he received during World War I, but some of y'all tracked him down via genealogy records and his death certificate reads that he died of tuberculosis. My guess is that perhaps that is actually incorrect and that he died of the Spanish Flu that was raging that year. 

 But look at him looking back at us though the generations! See how handsome he is in his uniform and his gloves and his boots.  

I can't say why this photo sticks with me.  Anybody who knew Private Francis is long gone. He is now just a forgotten man in a lonely cemetery, dust blowing around the corner, smoke slipping through a keyhole, a shaft of sunlight coming through a window in an old room.  

But I have not forgotten you, Private Francis!  Every Veteran's day, I remember. And I raise my glass to you and to the uncountable others and offer only the hope that we not let the memories of your sacrifices be forgotten.  A soldier's death, indeed.

In 1998 a Phase 1 trial took a terminal leukemia and turned it into a disease people grow old with. #Gleevec works because CML runs on one broken switch, BCR-ABL, and one pill can jam it.  The common solid tumors never offered one switch. Each carries its own private set of mutations, and when a drug does find a target the tumor rewires around it. That is why there has never been a Gleevec for the cancers that kill most people.  DCVax-L does not chase mutations. The patient's own dendritic cells are loaded with the whole tumor, not a chosen piece of it, and the immune system picks the targets. In newly diagnosed glioblastoma that produced 13% alive at five years (or more) against 5.7% for propensity score matched external controls. A curve with a tail is what immune memory looks like.  It happened in the textbook cold tumor. Few T cells ever reach a glioblastoma, which is why checkpoint drugs failed there in three Phase 3 trials. A checkpoint drug releases the brakes on T cells that already exist. In a cold tumor there is nothing to release. Dendritic cells sit one step upstream. They create those T cells, so the vaccine does not need the tumor to be warm. It is how a tumor gets warm.  And once it is warm, the checkpoint drug that failed alone finally has something to work with. Dr. Liau's UCLA group tested the order in recurrent glioblastoma and reported the result at EANO 2026. In 35 patients, Keytruda before the vaccine meant a median survival of 271 days. Keytruda after the vaccine meant 555 days, and the risk of death fell by two thirds. Tumor and blood showed why: more T cells in the tumor and more interferon and granzyme when the vaccine came first. Same two drugs, same disease. The order alone doubled survival.  The trial proved the platform in glioblastoma. The platform never cared which tumor the lysate came from, and the sequence does not care either. 🇷🇺|Two Americans Landed in Moscow. Neither Was Elected. Neither Was Confirmed. Both Own a Piece of the Outcome.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived at the Kremlin for talks with Vladimir Putin. The readout will say "diplomacy." The file says something else.

What These Two Men Are

Witkoff is a real estate developer who built the Witkoff Group on Manhattan property. He is not a diplomat. He was not confirmed by the Senate. He holds no treaty authority. His qualification is a friendship with Donald Trump and a history of doing deals in markets where Russian capital circulates. He met Putin in Moscow before. He is a fixer, not a negotiator.

Kushner runs Affinity Partners. The fund took $2 billion from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund in 2021, overriding the objections of the PIF's own advisers. It took money from Lunate, an Abu Dhabi fund, and from Qatari sovereign entities. Kushner is the President's son-in-law. He is the architect of the Abraham Accords. He has no diplomatic credential beyond the family tie and the Gulf money.

Neither man was elected. Neither was confirmed. Both have financial exposure to the outcome of the talks they are conducting.

What Putin Gets From the Meeting

Putin is not the supplicant here. Read the geometry.

The US has no ambassador in Tehran. The Vance letter to Rezaei was read and left unanswered. Araghchi called the reports of a Rezaei-Vance meeting "completely false and baseless." The Doha plane was a telecoms delegation, corrected by Tasnim. The Iran file has no American address.

The Europeans were told they are tourists. Medinsky said it on camera: the Europeans are tourists, and Russia will talk when their conscience awakens. Ursula von der Leyen, Emmanuel Macron, Friedrich Merz, Keir Starmer, Donald Tusk, and Olaf Scholz are in the lobby of the bar, with no chair at the table.

Putin sits at the head of the table because Washington has no other address. The US needs a deal before the new Congress seats in January. It cannot get one without Putin's signature. The two Americans flew to Moscow because Moscow is where the signature is.

That is the power position. Putin does not need to travel. The envoys come to him.

What Washington Wants

The US wants a settlement in Ukraine so it can redirect attention and resources to the war it cannot win against Iran.

The Iran ledger: $47 billion spent. 56 MQ-9 Reapers downed. 274 US military facilities damaged across seven countries. Two US aircraft squawking 7700 in the same window. A carrier strike group withdrawn from the Red Sea. The Strait of Hormuz not open on American terms.

The political ledger: Vance published the post-mortem admitting the war lost the election. Trump Jr. endorsed it. Rubio is reportedly preparing to resign. Hegseth is under prediction of dismissal from Rezaei. Cooper is mocked as a podcast host.

The economic ledger: $6.35 diesel. The Jamnagar trip with Ambani to fix the diesel prices the war caused. 7,800 flights cancelled. Nine floors of the Aramco Tower empty from one drone. The East-West Pipeline hit twice in three days.

The US needs a Ukraine settlement so it can stop bleeding on two fronts. That is why Witkoff and Kushner are in Moscow.

What the Two Men Are Offering

The frozen assets are the leverage. The minerals are the prize.

The US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, signed 30 April 2025, gives the United States a 50 per cent share of revenue from every newly issued Ukrainian mineral, oil, and gas extraction licence. Trump, July 2026: "We can go in there at any time we want to take pretty much whatever we want. That was a pretty good deal."

Roughly €210 billion sits at Euroclear in Belgium. The EU taxed the windfall profits at 99.7 per cent. Belgium is blocking outright confiscation, citing international law and Euroclear's exposure to Russian legal retaliation.

The deal being discussed is a trade: Russia gets some sanctions relief and some access to the frozen assets; the US gets the minerals and the reconstruction contracts; Ukraine gets a ceasefire that freezes the line where it is.

That is not a peace agreement. It is a division of the assets.

The Conflict of Interest

Kushner's Affinity Partners is not a neutral party. The fund's backers — the Saudi PIF, Lunate, and the Qatari entities — are the same sovereign funds positioning for Ukrainian reconstruction contracts and mineral access. A settlement that opens Ukraine's resources to Gulf capital is a settlement that increases the value of Kushner's fund.

Witkoff's real estate background is the other file. Reconstruction is a property business. The contracts to rebuild cities, ports, roads, and power plants are the largest property development opportunity in Europe since the Marshall Plan. A developer who negotiated the settlement is a developer who knows where the contracts will be awarded.

Neither man is a disinterested peacemaker. Both have financial exposure to the outcome.

The Precedent They Are Counting On You Not Knowing

The neutrality being discussed in Moscow was on offer in April 2022.

Istanbul, April 2022. Ukraine's written proposals included neutral, non-aligned status and a pledge not to host foreign weapons. Boris Johnson flew to Kyiv on 9 April 2022. Yulia Mendel said Johnson "intervened and influenced Zelensky, saying he could become a hero and could continue this war." David Arakhamia said Johnson told them: "We won't sign anything with them at all."

The neutrality that Witkoff and Kushner are now discussing was on offer four years ago. It was destroyed by a British prime minister acting on instructions from Washington and London. The talks in Moscow are the resumption of a negotiation that was sabotaged in 2022. The sabotage cost hundreds of thousands of lives.

The Bill

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin. A real estate developer and a $2 billion Gulf-funded investor. No election. No Senate confirmation. No treaty authority. Financial exposure to the outcome.

What Putin gets: the envoys come to him. Europe is in the lobby. Iran is unanswered. Moscow is where the signature is.

What Washington wants: a Ukraine settlement so it can stop bleeding on two fronts. $47 billion spent on Iran. 56 Reapers downed. 274 facilities. Democrats won both chambers. Vance conceded. Rubio leaving. Hegseth predicted to fall.

What they are offering: the minerals at 50 per cent. The €210 billion at Euroclear. The reconstruction contracts. A division of the assets, not a peace.

The precedent: Istanbul, April 2022. The neutrality was on offer. Boris Johnson killed it. Mendel and Arakhamia confirmed it.

The conflict: Kushner's fund is backed by the same Gulf sovereign funds positioning for the reconstruction. Witkoff's property business is positioned for the contracts. Both men profit from the deal they are negotiating.

The bill is being paid in a division of assets, and the receipt is two unelected Americans with Gulf money and property portfolios, arriving at the Kremlin to collect what the war cost.

text:
A CRISIS CREATED: THE SECRETARIES' CUP AND THE NWSL'S AUDI FIELD SCRAMBLE

By Frank Rossi — @D3FBHuddle

When the Washington Spirit beat Portland 4-1 on Sunday afternoon to earn a home NWSL semifinal, the club announced within hours that the match would be played at Audi Field at noon on Saturday, Nov. 14. Another event had held that date at that stadium since the summer, and nobody had worked out what would happen to it.

That event is the 46th Secretaries' Cup between the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy and the U.S. Coast Guard Academy, scheduled for a 1pm kickoff on ESPN+. The academies announced the Audi Field game on Aug. 3, put tickets on sale the next morning, and promoted it as part of the America250 celebration in the nation's capital. Alumni, families, and fans spent the fall booking travel around an afternoon game.

It took until Thursday, two days before kickoff, for the game to land anywhere. After a week in which it was floated for Saturday night and then for Sunday at noon, the Secretaries' Cup is now set for 4:30pm Saturday at Audi Field, about four hours after the Spirit and Utah kick off on the same field. Most of the coverage has called the Spirit's return to Audi a crisis averted, but for the two service academies it was a crisis created on their behalf, and they were the parties with the least leverage to push back.

HOW WE GOT HERE

The NWSL had known for days that its semifinal weekend had a venue problem. ESPN reported before the quarterfinals that league documents laid out alternate sites for several potential hosts, and the Spirit's fallback was Northwest Stadium in Landover, which the club had reserved for Nov. 14. After Sunday's win, the Spirit went to D.C. United, which controls Audi Field, to get the date back instead. According to The Athletic, the Spirit proposed buying out the college football game, a move one source described as a "Hail Mary," and Lafayette Federal Credit Union, a shared sponsor, offered to subsidize the cost, reportedly in the low six figures. Spirit CEO Kim Stone's statement thanked D.C. United and Lafayette Federal for underwriting the additional costs of bringing the match home.

The academies were still meeting on Tuesday morning. In a Facebook post that day, the Merchant Marine Academy's Alumni Association and Foundation said it was meeting with both academies and Audi Field in hopes of a resolution by noon, and that Audi Field had not told either academy, or the foundation, about the potential conflict in advance. The football game was the original booking, public for more than three months under a contract that almost certainly predates the announcement, and the two schools playing in it learned of the problem only after the soccer side had already declared it solved.

"ALL SIDES" DID NOT AGREE

The Athletic's account says that while Spirit coach Adrián González and his players spoke to the media, "all sides came to a resolution" behind the scenes for the Spirit to stay at Audi. That does not hold up for the academies, which agreed to nothing on Sunday and were left searching for alternatives that did not exist. Friday was not an option for them, and Sunday was initially treated as off the table because the NCAA assembles and releases its playoff bracket that day. Finding another stadium in the Washington area on a few days' notice, during a busy week of events in the city, was never realistic.

THE FIX THAT WAS SITTING RIGHT THERE

A better answer was available, and soccer fans would have lost nothing under it. The two NWSL semifinals had fixed national TV windows, Saturday at noon on CBS and Sunday at 3pm on ABC. Gotham, the top seed, was slotted into Sunday, and Washington was placed on Saturday, the one day Audi Field was already booked.

Then Gotham's own home field failed. Players and coaches called the surface at Sports Illustrated Stadium "atrocious" after Gotham's quarterfinal, and on Monday the club moved its semifinal to Icahn Stadium, a 5,000-seat city-owned venue on Randall's Island. At that point the league could have put Gotham and Kansas City at Icahn in the Saturday noon CBS window, put the Spirit and Utah at Audi Field in the Sunday 3pm ABC window, and left the Secretaries' Cup at 1pm Saturday, exactly as scheduled and sold. Both TV windows would have stayed intact, both clubs would still have hosted at home, and the Audi Field grounds crew would have had a full day to restore the pitch after the football game rather than a few hours before it.

The usual justification is that the higher seed gets its pick of days. That deference makes sense when a club is choosing between two dates in its own stadium, but it should have carried far less weight once Gotham was no longer playing in its own stadium at all. Nobody has said publicly that Icahn was unavailable on Saturday, and the problem could have been solved with a schedule swap that cost nothing rather than with a sponsor's check.

WHAT HAPPENED ON TUESDAY

By Tuesday, the decision had moved well beyond the two athletic departments. The Secretaries' Cup trophy is shared between the Secretary of Transportation and the Secretary of Homeland Security, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced this year's game himself on X in September, and both academies billed it as a centerpiece of America250 in Washington. Once the game's place in that celebration was in doubt, the matter rose to the secretaries' level at both departments, according to sources familiar with the discussions who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

ESPN was drawn into the discussions as well, according to those sources, and its reasons require no inside knowledge to understand. The network extended its Secretaries' Cup rights through 2030 only in September, with this game and its 1pm ET window as the first under the new deal. Advertising and promotion for an afternoon broadcast are sold and built around a specific slot, and any move forces the rights holder to rework all of it on a few days' notice. ESPN has not said publicly how the change affects its coverage.

That afternoon, the President's public schedule, as published by Roll Call's https://t.co/K2KfUucSR1, listed a 2pm policy meeting in the Oval Office, closed to the press. The White House has not said who attended or what was discussed, and nothing public confirms that the Secretaries' Cup came up, though with two cabinet secretaries sharing the trophy and the game billed as part of America250 in the capital, it would hardly be surprising if it had. Tuesday ended with the working plan at a Saturday night kickoff, likely 7:30pm, according to sources, but with no announcement.

WHAT HAPPENED ON WEDNESDAY

Wednesday ended the same way, even though D.C. United had said publicly that it intended to host both events on Saturday, with the Spirit at noon and the Secretaries' Cup later in the day after a same-day conversion that includes painting yard lines and installing goalposts, the first turnover of its kind at the stadium. "We weren't willing to choose between them, so we found a way to do both," D.C. United president of business operations Danita Johnson told The Washington Sun, adding that the arrangement "was never about financial gain for Audi Field or our ownership group."

On Wednesday night, word came from a well-placed source that the game could instead move to noon on Sunday. The academies appeared to be in the dark about that possibility, according to sources familiar with the discussions, and by then the decision rested largely with ESPN and the federal government rather than with the two schools that would actually play the game.

THE 4:30PM ANSWER

Thursday brought the decision: Coast Guard and Merchant Marine will kick off at 4:30pm Saturday at Audi Field. That time solves the latest scheduling problem and creates a new one on the field itself. A noon soccer match that runs 90 minutes plus stoppage time should end around 2pm, and one that goes to extra time and penalties could run closer to 2:45pm. That leaves roughly two hours to clear the building, reset the field, and open the gates for football, which is not enough time to paint a full set of football lines from scratch and let them dry.

The practical result is that the Spirit and Utah will likely play their semifinal on a pitch with football markings already painted on it. How much of the gridiron goes down before the soccer match, and whether end zones and other markings will need fresh, wet paint after the final whistle, has not been detailed. Either way, a professional playoff match will be played on a field marked for another sport, and two service-academy football teams will follow on a surface that has just absorbed 90-plus minutes of playoff soccer. Sources close to the situation remain concerned about the field and the paint, though they say both programs have been committed all week to playing the game no matter where, when, or how.

There may be another reason this particular window won out. According to well-placed sources, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth was originally expected to attend the Secretaries' Cup, an appearance arranged before Election Day and before this week's attempt by the House to impeach him. On Tuesday, the House voted 211-204 to refer Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution to committee, effectively ending that effort for this session. The 4:30pm slot may have been chosen in part to accommodate an appearance by the secretary, but it is not known whether that visit is still planned.

WHAT THE LATE KICKOFF COSTS

A 4:30pm start is far better than the night game that was on the table Tuesday, but it still upends a day that was planned around 1pm. Both teams lose most of their game day to waiting and will travel home late Saturday night. Families and alumni who built hotels, trains, flights, and drives around an afternoon game now face a finish around 7:30pm, after dark, in a city most of them do not live in. The Coast Guard Academy Alumni Association's published itinerary includes a Fan Fest outside Gate A from 10am to noon on Saturday, which now lands on top of the crowd arriving for the soccer match.

All of this comes as the rivalry has been growing, after last year's game at Fenway Park drew more than 10,000 fans and ended 39-38, and Audi Field was supposed to carry that momentum into the nation's capital in the week of Veterans Day.

THE PLAYOFF STAKES

The consequences reach well past the two academies. Merchant Marine is 7-1 (5-1 NEWMAC) coming off a bye, and with Springfield holding the NEWMAC's automatic bid, the Mariners' path runs through Pool C, where this year's 11 at-large bids go strictly in NPI order. Our 2,000-run simulation of Week 11 puts the cutoff at roughly 64.3. With a win, Merchant Marine projects at about 69.3 NPI and made the field in every simulation, most likely as a seed around 18th with a first-round bye. With a loss, it falls to about 63.5 and gets in only about one time in five.

Our model makes Merchant Marine about a 93% favorite, but a Coast Guard upset would reshape a crowded bubble. Assuming each team wins its own game, a Coast Guard win lifts UW-River Falls from about 8% to 22% and Heidelberg from about 19% to 35%, because a 7-2 Merchant Marine falls back into the pack. Montclair State, whose loss came against Merchant Marine, needs the Mariners to win, with its odds sitting around 42% after a Merchant Marine win and around 8% after a Coast Guard win.

The 4:30pm kickoff is the least damaging of the options floated this week as far as the bracket is concerned. According to its annual report, the NCAA Division III Football Committee begins selecting and bracketing on Saturday night and finishes around noon Sunday, ahead of a 5pm ET selection show on https://t.co/Q9AmWxO8UL. A game ending around 7:30pm Saturday will be final before the committee's work is well underway, and earlier than Lyon and Centenary's SCAC third-place game at 9pm ET. The Sunday noon idea floated Wednesday night would have ended around 3pm, after the committee's work is normally done, and could have left Merchant Marine judged at 7-1, roughly 68.9 NPI, with every bubble team waiting on the result settled without it. That the academies and those bubble teams came that close to that outcome, with no say in it, is part of the problem.

WHO OWNS THIS

Audi Field signed a contract for Nov. 14 knowing it is the Spirit's home stadium and that the NWSL playoffs run into mid-November. If its operators thought a home semifinal was possible, they should have planned for it before selling the date to a service-academy rivalry game, and if they had not planned for it, they had no business reopening the date over a weekend without the academies in the room.

The larger share of the blame, though, belongs to the NWSL, the Spirit, and Lafayette Federal Credit Union, who together manufactured an "us against them" fight that never needed to happen. The Spirit had a 64,000-seat NFL stadium reserved for Saturday and chose to go after the one building already promised to someone else. Lafayette Federal put up the money that made the buyout possible and has called its decision an easy yes, with no public acknowledgment of who would be displaced by it. The league had a schedule swap available on Monday that would have honored every contract and protected every TV window, and it left its slots where they were. The result pits professional soccer players against student-athletes who are not paid to play and who are training to serve the country's maritime and homeland security needs, and the online reaction since Sunday has done exactly that, setting supporters of women's soccer against supporters of the academies over a problem neither group created.

The academies are poorly positioned to fight back. They answer to two cabinet departments, and they are not built to take on a professional league in public, which is exactly why their date deserved more protection than it received. The Secretaries' Cup will kick off at 4:30pm on Saturday, and it will be played hard, because that is who these teams are. It should have kicked off at 1pm, on a fresh field, as promised.

City Journal, the magazine of the Manhattan Institute, a free-market think tank in New York, reported that PlumpJack, the Napa wine business California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) founded, contracts Renteria Vineyard Management to run the field work at its Oso Vineyard. The investigation, led by Christopher F. Rufo, a Manhattan Institute senior fellow, documents a contract, a list of fines and lawsuits, and public statements by the vineyard manager.

The most serious claim, that about 80 percent of field crews are here illegally, comes from anonymous sources, and one of those figures was about Napa as a whole, not this one company. The Migration Policy Institute, a think tank City Journal describes as left-wing, estimates about 27 percent of Napa's agricultural workers are unauthorized. City Journal cites no court or agency finding that Renteria Vineyard Management knowingly hired unauthorized workers, and nothing in the reporting shows that Newsom knew any worker's status. He placed his stake in a blind trust when he became governor in 2019. His spokesman says he has no involvement in PlumpJack's operations.

The $7,000 figure in that post is a six-liter bottle, which holds as much as eight standard bottles. PlumpJack's own store, checked Nov. 12, lists a standard bottle of that wine at about $535, and City Journal's written piece described a $400 bottle at a tasting.

Cesar Chavez, the farmworker union leader, fought illegal strikebreaking labor for years because it cut the wages of the workers he organized. That is the same structure: a management company in the middle, and a crew with no legal standing who cannot easily complain about the pay.

text:
Today in Dance-Pop and R&B history: 16 years ago, @rihanna released her fifth studio album, LOUD — a vibrant, energetic project that embraced a brighter and more playful direction in her music. Blending Dance-Pop, R&B, and Reggae influences with infectious melodies and upbeat production, the album allowed Rihanna to experiment with different sounds while showcasing her growing confidence as a performer. From the euphoric energy of "Only Girl (In the World)" to the playful attitude of "S&M" and the romantic undertones of "What's My Name?," LOUD offered a collection of records that highlighted different aspects of her personality and musical versatility.

The album also marked an interesting shift in Rihanna's artistic presentation. Following the darker themes and edgier aesthetic of Rated R, LOUD introduced a more colorful visual identity, incorporating vibrant fashion, striking imagery, and a playful approach to her music videos and performances. This change gave the album its own distinct personality while demonstrating Rihanna's ability to move between different musical and visual directions without losing her individuality. With hits like "Cheers (Drink to That)" and "California King Bed," she also explored everything from carefree celebration to the complexities of love and rrealtionships.

LOUD became one of the defining eras of Rihanna's career, producing several of her most recognizable songs and showcasing her ability to dominate different corners of pop music. It was an album that allowed her to have fun with her artistry, take creative risks, and embrace a more expressive side of herself. 16 years later, the era remains a memorable chapter in her discography and an example of how Rihanna continued to reinvent herself without being confined to one particular sound or image.

!5%? This isn’t capitalism. Call it what it is: “Crony Capitalism.” No pharma company would offer U.S. government a cut of sales to gain approval. After that the President and Huang became “best friends.” Huang front and center at the State Dinner with China’s President Xi.
When there was an urgent need for some regulation to prevent unproven AI models escaping from Open AI’s labs, Huang told President Trump there was no need for regulations. The AI companies could regulate themselves.
Was the board aware of Huang’s intimate relations with his subordinates, much less a Chinese spy? We may never know
What we do know is the board had no succession plan for Huang. It ignored his organization structure with 60 direct reports which insured no one was ready to take over – no even CFO Colette Kress, whose claim to fame is financing data storage facilities for Nvidia customers in exchange for chip sales. This is the board of the world’s most valuable company? Why are we surprised about the disaster that is still unfolding?

text:
It takes ten minutes to dream up a better levelling up policy than Jenrick's hackneyed interventionist shtick... 

There can be no serious levelling up or reindustrialisation in Britain without first scrapping net zero targets and fundamentally reforming the planning system. Both of these issues have acted as major brakes on economic activity, infrastructure delivery, and industrial revival. Without removing these constraints, any attempt to revive the North and restore Britain’s industrial base will be frustrated by energy costs, regulatory delays, and environmental rules that treat economic development as a problem to be managed rather than a goal to be pursued.

The North of England was once the industrial heartland of Britain. It can and should be again. The combined economic potential of Leeds, Manchester, Liverpool and the towns between them remains substantial. However, decades of underinvestment, poor connectivity, and damaging national policy have left large parts of the North economically stagnant while the South East has become increasingly overcrowded and expensive. Levelling up is not primarily about moving money around. It's about removing the barriers that prevent the North from competing and growing on its own terms.

Improving East-West connectivity in the North should be a national priority. A fast, reliable rail link between Leeds and Manchester is long overdue. This should be delivered through targeted upgrades and new sections where necessary, avoiding the cost overruns, delays and over-engineering that characterised the HS2 project. The goal should be a journey time significantly below one hour, with reliable services that support both commuting and business travel.

The M62 also requires major capacity improvements. It remains the principal east-west road artery in the North but suffers from chronic congestion. We must prioritise widening and capacity improvements along the most heavily used sections to create a genuinely fast and reliable strategic route across the Pennines.

Further east, we should develop a new strategic motorway continuing the line of the M11 east of Cambridge through Lincolnshire and linking to the Humber Bridge. This route would transform access to Hull and the Humber ports, support economic development along the corridor, and relieve pressure on existing north-south routes. In parallel, we should complete the full dualling of the A1 from Leeds to Edinburgh. This long-overdue upgrade would transform journey times and reliability on one of Britain’s most important north-south corridors.

Meanwhile, northern ports have significant untapped potential, particularly in supporting sovereign industrial and defence capabilities. We should fund upgrades at the Port of Hull to increase capacity for general cargo, project cargo and future shipbuilding-related activity. This will strengthen Hull’s role as a key east coast gateway and support the wider Humber economy.

We should also invest in the Ports of Hartlepool and Teesside, focusing on expanding facilities to support shipbuilding, offshore maintenance and general cargo. Hartlepool’s location and existing infrastructure make it well placed to support both industrial activity on Teesside and the wider North East economy. We must expand shipbuilding capacity for the Royal Navy, and upgrades at Hartlepool and Hull should be aligned with this objective, ensuring that northern ports can support the construction, outfitting and maintenance of naval vessels.

In line with transport policy, we should liberalise and deregulate to enable the expansion of regional airports. Improved air connectivity will support business travel, tourism and the movement of high-value goods, helping to strengthen the economic case for investment in the North.

Reindustrialisation must focus on restoring strategic capabilities that Britain has lost. We must rebuild domestic steel production capacity. Virgin steelmaking remains essential for defence, infrastructure and energy security. We should support the return of primary steelmaking through a combination of private investment and targeted public support where necessary.

Fertiliser production must also be restored. The near-total collapse of domestic capacity has left British agriculture dangerously dependent on imports. Re-establishing fertiliser manufacturing is a matter of food security as well as industrial policy. 

Data centres also represent a major growth sector. We must ensure that planning and energy policy actively support the development of data centres in suitable northern locations, where land and grid capacity can often be secured more readily than in the South East. SMRs would accelerate this. 

We should also pursue the regeneration of Grimsby as a major centre for fishing and seafood processing. Britain’s fishing industry has been severely weakened by decades of poor policy. Restoring Grimsby’s historic role would create skilled employment, support coastal communities and contribute to food security. This will require investment in port infrastructure, modern processing facilities and a supportive regulatory environment.

We should also expand defence manufacturing in the North, with a particular focus on munitions. Preference should be given to expanding capacity in the North East where feasible, alongside maximising production in existing shipyards on the Clyde. This would support high-skilled employment and strengthen sovereign industrial capability.

We should then support the development of northern clusters in advanced manufacturing, life sciences and med-tech, building on existing university and industrial strengths. In addition, we should explore the creation of a major northern hub for critical minerals processing and recycling, reducing reliance on overseas supply chains for materials essential to modern industry and defence.

Levelling up must also deliver visible improvement in towns that have been left behind. We should accelerate regeneration in places such as Castleford, Pontefract, Goole and Selby - all minutes from the M62. These towns have real economic potential but suffer from underinvestment and poor connectivity. We need housing and planning reforms using targeted development, infrastructure improvements, and private sector involvement to drive renewal.

We should also pursue a more ambitious model of urban regeneration by transforming Halifax into the “Bath of the North”. Halifax possesses an outstanding stock of historic buildings and a compact town centre well suited to high-quality urban living. By combining sympathetic restoration, high-quality new housing, public realm investment and support for independent businesses and cultural activity, Halifax can become a leading example of how northern towns can be revived through attractive town centre living. This model can then be adapted for other historic northern towns.

We should actively support the repurposing of derelict but architecturally significant buildings in town centres across the North. Carnegie libraries, former guildhalls, market halls, old mills and civic buildings represent an underused asset. Where these buildings are structurally sound, we should encourage their conversion into mixed-use developments, cultural venues, workspaces or high-quality housing. This approach can combine heritage preservation with new economic activity and help bring life back into struggling town centres.

We should also establish dedicated city arts hubs in Bradford, Liverpool and Hull. These will combine performance spaces, galleries, creative workspaces and education facilities, with the aim of strengthening the cultural offer in each city and supporting the growth of creative industries. These hubs should be developed in partnership with local authorities, universities and the private sector.

Doing My Research and I Stumbled onto something Big base:0xa6af0cea8fbc93e1eccc00f1fdd9a0bba251fee1 

$IPOD  @iPodAAPLc : A cultural token paired with tokenized Apple stock on Base

$IPOD is an internet/cultural asset on Base that brings the iPod back as a meme and community symbol while trading directly against Coinbase’s tokenized Apple stock ($AAPLc). 

It launched on https://t.co/BPY3LpRZCJ with a fixed 1 billion supply and trades in a Uniswap v4 pool against AAPLc. The framing is simple: Apple is the company, $IPOD is the culture. Holders can receive rewards paid in AAPLc from the creator’s share of trading fees, weighted by how much they hold and how long they hold it.

Contract: 0xA6af0cEa8FBC93E1eCcC00f1FdD9a0BBa251FeE1
 Site: https://t.co/4QZgoMOQMw

What it does
It creates a permanent market where a cultural token is quoted against a tokenized equity. $IPOD is paired with $AAPLc

Rewards come from trading fees and are paid in AAPLc rather than the meme token itself. https://t.co/BPY3LpRZCJ treats it as a flagship and has extended the model so other coins can pair with $IPOD, creating multi-hop routes through the AAPLc pool. 

The narrative leans on iPod nostalgia plus cultural upside for people who grew up with the product.

As of mid-November 2026, market cap was still in the low-to-mid six figures with liquidity in the $100k–$250k range and cumulative AAPLc distributions already in the tens of thousands of dollars. Activity remains modest compared with larger pure memes.

The problem it targets
Most meme tokens offer pure reflexivity with no link to external value. Most tokenized equities are functional but culturally inert they lack a native community or distribution story. 

People wanting on-chain exposure to major tech companies usually face either limited-access regulated products or pure speculation. $IPOD experiments with a hybrid: cultural participation that routes some trading activity into the underlying stock pool and pays holders in that stock.

What makes it different
•  Direct pairing with a live tokenized equity (AAPLc on Base) instead of ETH or a stablecoin, so both meme flows and stock movement influence the market.

•  Rewards paid in the tokenized stock itself via time- and size-weighted holdings, unlike typical reflection tokens that pay in the meme token or ETH.

•  Built into https://t.co/BPY3LpRZCJ’s stock-paired coin framework, where $IPOD can itself become a pairing asset for new launches.

•  Cultural framing tied to a widely recognized product (the iPod) rather than generic animal memes, with ambitions to reach beyond pure crypto audiences.

These mechanics are laid out in https://t.co/BPY3LpRZCJ docs and the project site, but they depend on volume and carry normal smart-contract, market, and tokenized-stock risks (including issuer, custody, and non-US accessibility constraints on AAPLc).

Why it deserves attention
Tokenized equities on Base are still early and relatively small. Base meme activity continues. $IPOD sits at the intersection and is small enough to be easy to overlook. Its interest is less about any price target and more about whether cultural tokens can help intermediate or amplify demand for tokenized equities, build stickier holder bases through stock rewards, and act as distribution layers for RWAs.

If it scales, it becomes a concrete case study in hybrid meme/RWA design. If it stays niche, it still shows the practical limits and design choices of stock-paired launches on https://t.co/BPY3LpRZCJ and Base. Either outcome is useful to watch while tokenized stocks and on-chain culture keep developing.

This is the Alpha Today still NFA .

text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, called COPA, on Nov. 10. In his words, the city "will now give community organizations the first shot at buying eligible homes — not flippers who are just looking to extract a profit."

Here is what the law does, according to the Mayor's Office. The city's Department of Housing Preservation and Development, or HPD, the agency that oversees affordable housing, will keep a list of "qualified entities": vetted nonprofits, tenant groups, community land trusts and similar groups with experience buying and running affordable housing. When a covered building goes up for sale, groups on that list get an exclusive 145-day window to buy it. If the owner rejects their offer and another buyer makes one within the next year, the listed group can match it. Covered buildings are those with four or more units that are in significant disrepair, and buildings under HPD affordability agreements.
https://t.co/1ryKK2ws5x

My angle as a conservative:

Chapter 1 of my Hayek series defines central planning as a government office deciding what a country produces, how much, at what prices, and for whom, instead of buyers and sellers meeting through prices. The Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek began his case against it in four lectures at the London School of Economics in January 1931, arguing that a price carries what millions of people actually want and how long they will wait.

To be fair, COPA is not central planning in that full sense. It does not set prices, and the Mayor's Office release describes owners rejecting a listed group's offer. But it does move one piece, "for whom," toward a city-certified list. For a covered building, the first chance to buy goes to groups an agency has approved, and for a year afterward any other buyer's offer can be matched. A buyer who knows that may bid less or not bid at all, and the owner's choice of who to sell to narrows. That is a small step away from buyers and sellers meeting freely, taken for good motives, which is exactly the kind of step Hayek asked people to weigh honestly.

An honest caution: COPA is new and HPD has not built the list yet, so how it works in practice is unknown. Its backers argue it will get neglected buildings repaired. The Mayor's Office release describes the 145 days both as time "to make an offer" and as a window "to complete the purchase," so the law's text should be checked before relying on that detail.

I believe an owner's freedom to sell what he owns to the buyer he chooses is part of the liberty the founders meant to protect. It shouldn't be narrowed lightly, even for good motives.

Chapter 1 of my series America's Debt: Hayek Warned Us explains the price signal and what happens when an authority overrides it, with sources:
https://t.co/1efvIaU6Lj

text:
John Welford, in 2012, explained what Larkin’s High Windows poem means: 

After contemplation of new youth mores, “Larkin then throws the thought process backwards to imagine what the generation before his would have thought of his own prospect of liberation from constraint. However, this is expressed not in sexual, but religious, terms. It is release from fear of eternal damnation and offending the priesthood that he sees as their abiding desire, expressed in terms of envy of the next generation who will have the liberty that is denied to them. The image of the long slide is used again as the means to achieve freedom. Once on the slide the desired outcome is inevitable, and Larkin reverses the traditional image of sliding downwards to perdition by emphasising that freedom must lie at its base, as does happiness for the generation that Larkin envies. However, the final stanza brings all this to a halt in a rather startling way. The natural conclusion to the two scenarios that Larkin has offered would be the suggestion that every generation, going back to time immemorial, has thrown off the shackles of its parents and found liberty by sliding away from its constraints. But the image that Larkin has of his own situation is that the promise of godless and hell-less freedom has not been achieved. Instead, his thoughts turn to the "high windows" of a church or cathedral where he is still on the inside with the sunlight shining down on him. The promised freedom has therefore been an illusion. The poem ends with a despairing recognition that there is no ultimate freedom. The young couple might hope for endless happiness, but what is endless is the "deep blue air" that "shows nothing, and is nowhere".  It is the windows that are "sun-comprehending" and not people with their mortal longings. By making "High Windows" the title poem of his collection, Larkin makes the point that the individual can never have what he or she ultimately wants, because they can never know what that is. Just as freedom from religion is not the answer, neither is 1960s "free love" and, Larkin implies, the same will apply to every imagined desire of future generations.”

text:
Benjamin Franklin’s “The Whistle”

I received my dear friend’s two letters, one for Wednesday and one for Saturday. This is again Wednesday. I do not deserve one for to-day, because I have not answered the former. But, indolent as I am, and averse to writing, the fear of having no more of your pleasing epistles, if I do not contribute to the correspondence, obliges me to take up my pen; and as Mr. B. has kindly sent me word that he sets out to-morrow to see you, instead of spending this Wednesday evening, as I have done its namesakes, in your delightful company, I sit down to spend it in thinking of you, in writing to you, and in reading over and over again your letters.I am charmed with your description of Paradise, and with your plan of living there; and I approve much of your conclusion, that, in the meantime, we should draw all the good we can from this world. In my opinion we might all draw more good from it than we do, and suffer less evil, if we would take care not to give too much for whistles. For to me it seems that most of the unhappy people we meet with are become so by neglect of that caution. You ask what I mean? You love stories, and will excuse my telling one of myself.When I was a child of seven years old, my friends, on a holiday, filled my pocket with coppers. I went directly to a shop where they sold toys for children; and being charmed with the sound of a whistle, that I met by the way in the hands of another boy, I voluntarily offered and gave all my money for one. I then came home, and went whistling all over the house, much pleased with my whistle, but disturbing all the family. My brothers, and sisters, and cousins, understanding the bargain I had made, told me I had given four times as much for it as it was worth; put me in mind what good things I might have bought with the rest of the money; and laughed at me so much for my folly, that I cried with vexation; and the reflection gave me more chagrin than the whistle gave me pleasure.This, however, was afterwards of use to me, the impression continuing on my mind; so that often, when I was tempted to buy some unnecessary thing, I said to myself, Don’t give too much for the whistle; and I saved my https://t.co/iDSnetKvol I grew up, came into the world, and observed the actions of men, I thought I met with many, very many, who gave too much for the whistle.When I saw one too ambitious of court favor, sacrificing his time in attendance on levees, his repose, his liberty, his virtue, and perhaps his friends, to attain it, I have said to myself, This man gives too much for his whistle.When I saw another fond of popularity, constantly employing himself in political bustles, neglecting his own affairs, and ruining them by that neglect, He pays, indeed, said I, too much for his whistle.If I knew a miser, who gave up every kind of comfortable living, all the pleasure of doing good to others, all the esteem of his fellow-citizens, and the joys of benevolent friendship, for the sake of accumulating wealth, Poor man, said I, you pay too much for your whistle.When I met with a man of pleasure, sacrificing every laudable improvement of the mind, or of his fortune, to mere corporeal sensations, and ruining his health in their pursuit, Mistaken man, said I, you are providing pain for yourself, instead of pleasure; you give too much for your whistle.If I see one fond of appearance, or fine clothes, fine houses, fine furniture, fine equipages, all above his fortune, for which he contracts debts, and ends his career in a prison, Alas! say I, he has paid dear, very dear, for his whistle.When I see a beautiful sweet-tempered girl married to an ill-natured brute of a husband, What a pity, say I, that she should pay so much for a whistle!In short, I conceive that great part of the miseries of mankind are brought upon them by the false estimates they have made of the value of things, and by their giving too much for their whistles.

text:
An American told me to have a garage sale.

I had moved into a smaller place. I had too many things.

I did not know what I was agreeing to.

I spent an entire Friday putting small orange stickers on items. Three dollars. Five dollars. One dollar for the rice cooker. My handwriting was neat. My categories were honest.

Nobody looked at a sticker all day.

The first woman arrived at 6:14 in the morning. The sale was supposed to start at eight. She came up the driveway in the dark with a flashlight and a cup of coffee from somewhere.

She did not say hello.

She said, "Is this five?"

She was holding the lamp.

I said yes.

She said, "Would you take three?"

She did not haggle. She stated a number. She waited, with absolute patience.

In my country this would be a duel. In this country it was a formality we both already knew the ending to.

I said four.

She said three fifty.

She paid me a crumpled bill and two quarters and left with the lamp before I had finished saying okay.

By nine there were twelve strangers in my yard. By eleven there were forty. Grown men squatted on my concrete, examining my tools in the sun with the focus of priests reading scrolls.

One man bought a wrench I had used three times in my life. He examined it for seven minutes.

Then he said, "Good wrench."

He said it the way a man gives a blessing. It is a good wrench. I know this now. I did not know it when I owned it.

A woman came out of the garage carrying a box. In it were four Christmas ornaments, a cast iron skillet, and a framed photograph of a family I did not recognize.

I told her the photograph was not for sale.

She looked at it. She said, "Honey, this isn't yours either."

I looked. It was a photograph of my wife's cousin's wedding, which had been in a drawer for seven years. I had never opened the drawer.

She paid for the skillet and the ornaments and left.

I mailed the photograph the next day.

In the afternoon a man in a very clean truck offered me sixty dollars for a bicycle I had marked at a hundred. He did not negotiate. He named his number and stood still.

I accepted. He loaded the bicycle without a word.

I have since learned he does this every Saturday. There is, I am told, a garage somewhere full of his bicycles. Nobody knows what he does with them. Nobody asks.

At five o'clock, as I was folding the table, another man pulled up in a pickup truck.

He said, "What's going to the curb?"

I pointed at a pile.

He took it. All of it. Without inspecting a single item. He thanked me as he loaded it, as though I had done him a favor. I understand he is a kind of profession, though nobody has ever paid him, and nobody has ever seen his house.

The last customer was a girl of about nine. She had three quarters in her palm.

She pointed at a stuffed rabbit with a sticker that said one dollar.

She said, "How much is it?"

I looked at her three quarters.

I said, "Today it is seventy five cents."

She did not smile. She paid me, took the rabbit by one ear, and walked back to her mother with the dignity of a merchant who had closed a fair deal.

I made one hundred and seventy two dollars.

I gave away what I had meant to throw away.

I returned a photograph I had been carrying across two moves without knowing it was there.

The next morning the house across the street had a cardboard sign staked into the yard.

YARD SALE. NEXT SATURDAY. 8 AM. NO EARLY BIRDS.

I will be there at six fourteen.
