🇷🇺🇦🇫|A Russian Government Aircraft Landed at Kabul Airport. On Board: A Deputy Prime Minister and Seventy Businesspeople. The Cargo Was Not a Demand. It Was an Offer.

The aircraft carried Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk, more than 70 business representatives from Russian companies in transport, logistics, agriculture, and pharmaceuticals, and Zamir Kabulov, Russia’s Special Envoy for Afghanistan. They met Mullah Abdul Ghani Baradar, the Taliban’s deputy prime minister for economic affairs, at the presidential palace.

The Western headline was written before the plane landed: Russia legitimises the Taliban. The actual manifest was a trade mission, and the numbers are the indictment of the Western model.

The Transaction: What Russia Brought and What It Asked For

Overchuk stated trade between Russia and Afghanistan reached approximately $350 million in the first eight months of 2026 more than double the same period last year. Russian imports of Afghan fruit and vegetables have begun.

The Taliban’s offer was specific. Baradar invited Russian companies to extract copper, zinc, and chromite in partnership with Afghan firms, and to invest in factories, industrial parks, special economic zones, dry ports, and specialised hospitals.

The Taliban’s shopping list: Russian cars, grain, fertilisers, medicines, and equipment.

Read the structure. Russia is buying Afghan produce and offering to build industrial capacity in partnership with Afghan firms. The Taliban is buying Russian goods and inviting Russian investment. It is a two-way transaction goods for goods, capital for minerals, expertise for infrastructure. The growth is shared because the deal requires the Afghan side to be a partner, not a supplicant.

The Looting Model: What Washington Left Behind

The United States spent $2.3 trillion in Afghanistan over twenty years, lost 2,400 service members, and withdrew in August 2021. It then did three things.

It froze the money. Roughly $7 billion in Afghan central bank reserves were frozen after the Taliban took power. US and international economists have publicly urged Washington to return the funds, stating the refusal is worsening the economic collapse.

It cut the aid. US assistance inside Afghanistan ceased altogether in 2025. The aid that had sustained the economy was switched off.

It kept the sanctions. The unilateral sanctions cut Afghanistan off from the international banking system, choking the foreign exchange the country needs to import food and medicine.

That is the looting model. It does not send a delegation. It sends a freeze order. It does not build a factory. It blocks the bank account that would pay for one. The result is a country with $1 trillion in untapped minerals; lithium, copper, iron ore, rare earths and a population that cannot access its own money.

What Washington Wants Now: The Bagram-for-Lithium Offer

The record shows Washington’s actual model, and it is not reconstruction. Reporting in August 2026 documented the Taliban offering the Trump administration access to Afghanistan’s estimated $1 trillion in minerals: lithium, gold, copper, rare earths in exchange for sanctions relief and the return of frozen assets.

The framing of the offer was reported as Bagram for lithium and gold. The United States is not being asked to build a factory. It is being asked to return the money it froze and lift the sanctions it imposed in exchange for access to the resources.

That is the extractive model stated as a transaction: give us the minerals, and we will give you back your own money. The Taliban is offering it because the blockade has left no other path.

The Comparison, Stated as Arithmetic

Washington’s balance sheet in Afghanistan: $2.3 trillion spent, $7 billion frozen, aid cut to zero, sanctions maintained, no ambassador in Kabul, and a proposed deal that trades mineral access for the release of the frozen reserves.

Russia’s balance sheet: $350 million in trade in eight months, doubled year-on-year, 70+ companies on the ground, a delegation led by a deputy prime minister, an embassy that never closed, and a partnership offer on mining, factories, industrial parks, and hospitals.

One side froze the assets and cut the aid. The other side flew in seventy businesspeople and doubled the trade. One side’s model requires the country to stay poor so its resources can be accessed on favourable terms. The other side’s model requires the country to trade so the resources can be developed with a local partner.

The Bill

The aircraft: a Russian government aircraft at Kabul Airport. Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk. 70+ business representatives in transport, logistics, agriculture, and pharmaceuticals. Zamir Kabulov.

The trade: $350 million in eight months, double the previous year. Afghan fruit and vegetables entering Russia. Russian grain, fertilisers, and medicines entering Afghanistan.

The investment offer: copper, zinc, chromite in partnership with Afghan firms. Factories, industrial parks, special economic zones, dry ports, hospitals.

The Western model: $7 billion frozen. Aid ceased in 2025. Sanctions maintained. No ambassador. A $1 trillion mineral offer framed as a trade for the release of Afghanistan’s own reserves.

The Western headline: Russia legitimises the Taliban. The Western model is the one that froze the money, cut the aid, and left the country to negotiate access to its own resources while it starves. The Russian model is the one that landed a plane full of businesspeople and doubled the trade. The bill is being paid in frozen reserves and blocked bank accounts, and the receipt is a trade mission the Western press will report as a threat while the Afghan central bank’s $7 billion sits in a US account.

What if the two most dangerous builders on Earth joined the same team?

Elon Musk, who builds rockets, EVs, AI models, and now his own chip fabs.

Jensen Huang, who spent 33 years turning NVIDIA into the engine of the AI age.

If those two ever worked side by side… what would still be impossible?

Today, that fantasy got one step closer to a headline.

NVIDIA has announced that Jensen Huang resigned as President, CEO, and board member, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.

And when someone on X asked Musk if he would hire Jensen, he replied with four words:

“That would be an honor.”

No offer has been made. No talks have been reported. This is still just a reply, a screenshot, and a very loud imagination.

But the pieces fit almost too well. xAI needs compute. SpaceX is reaching into space computing. Terafab needs exactly the kind of mind that has run a chip empire for three decades.

So here is the question the whole industry is now quietly asking:

Is Jensen Huang about to become the most shocking free agent in tech history?

Philip J. Klass
Electrical engineering degree from Iowa State University Journalist and researcher Born in Des Moines, Iowa, USA (1919-2005)
Klass’ first job was working on aviation electronics systems for General Electric during World War II.He is credited with coining the term “avionics” and went on to become the first avionics editor of Aviation Week & Space Technology, the premiere journal of the aviation industry.

Klass is largely considered the most famous skeptic within ufology and wrote several books critical of UFOs. Perhaps because of his immersion in the reality-based world of aviation and science, Klass did not automatically give credence to claims of flying saucers and alien abduction which first began proliferating in the late 1950s and early 60s.

Klass inspires polarized appraisals in both the ufological and skeptical communities, and had a reputation as  the “Sherlock Holmes of ufology”. In 1999, Skeptical Enquirer named him number five on their list of top skeptics of the 20th century.

In 1966, Klass offered a $10,000 reward if certain conditions proving UFOs were met, which remained unclaimed at his death.  Klass left a particularly damning statement towards his critics titled The Last Will and Testament of Philip J. Klass, originally published in Saucer Smear in October 1983:

“To ufologists who publicly criticize me, … or who even think unkind thoughts about me in private, I do hereby leave and bequeath: THE UFO CURSE: No matter how long you live, you will never know any more about UFOs than you know today. You will never know anymore about what UFOs really are, or where they come from. You will never know anymore about what the U.S. Government really knows about UFOs than you know today. As you lie on your own deathbed you will be as mystified about UFOs as you are today. And you will remember this curse.”

text:
Monday, Nov 16: Iowa DOR expects to publish its first vapor products directory. Once it's out, only listed vapor products may be sold or offered for sale in Iowa.

For Iowa retailers, distributors, subjobbers and delivery sellers, that day's list sets what can stay on the shelf.

What the DOR page says:
• The directory takes effect as soon as it's published
• First 21 business days: DOR focuses on education
• Penalty enforcement expected to start Thu, Dec 17
• DOR calls these dates an estimate, subject to change

How a product gets listed (Iowa Code 453A.52):
• The manufacturer holds an FDA marketing order, or
• The product was on the market by Aug 8, 2016, with a PMTA filed by Sept 9, 2020 that's still pending
• Certification fee: $100 per product, renewed each Aug 1

Parts sold on their own (empty tanks, batteries, coils, cases) don't need a listing. Sold in a bundle at one price, the vapor product in it must be listed.

Selling unlisted products can bring civil and criminal penalties, including fines and permit suspension or revocation.

An Iowa man placed just over $300 in bets on DraftKings using a loophole in its own betting rules. His bets could have paid him more than $14 MILLION, but the sportsbook canceled them and returned his money.

> His name is Nicholas Bavas

> He is a bettor from Iowa who noticed a potential loophole in how DraftKings priced certain wagers.

> He found a way to structure bets that could profit regardless of the outcome, based on the odds offered by the sportsbook.

> So he placed just over $300 across the wagers.

> If DraftKings had honored the bets as written, he stood to collect more than $14 MILLION.

> But DraftKings voided the bets, citing its house rules on pricing errors.

> Instead of paying the potential winnings, the company simply refunded his original stake.

> Bavas decided to fight back and filed a 39 page lawsuit accusing DraftKings of breach of contract.

> His argument was that DraftKings accepted the bets, making the wagers binding agreements.

> The case was moved from an Iowa state court to federal court in Des Moines.

> As of the latest public reporting available in the account, there was no final ruling on whether Bavas was entitled to the $14 MILLION.

He found a loophole that could have made him $14 MILLION but DraftKings reminded him why the house always wins

text:
Why Did Kate and William's Remembrance Appearance Carry Such a Serious Message? 🌺
The Royal British Legion's Festival of Remembrance and the national service at the Cenotaph invite people to reflect on duty, loss, and public gratitude. William and Catherine participated in the November 2026 commemorations, while George, Charlotte, and Louis did not join them at the Cenotaph on Remembrance Sunday. It would be misleading to write as though all five family members appeared there. The family story on such an occasion is about adults honoring national responsibilities, not about creating a scene for viral drama. Royal coverage can make distant occasions feel immediate for viewers who will never attend them. The camera brings the architecture, crowds, and atmosphere close, while familiar faces provide a point of connection. Catherine's family is especially recognizable, but the footage should remain a record of a public event rather than an excuse to speculate about private life. Keeping that boundary makes the experience more enjoyable for everyone. The quiet symbolism of remembrance needs careful language. People across Britain and the Commonwealth bring personal histories to these ceremonies, and those experiences are far more important than speculation about what a royal expression might mean. The history of the Prince and Princess of Wales gives their appearances a wider resonance. Longtime royal followers have watched the couple take on new duties while the public role of the monarchy continues to evolve. Their children add another generational layer to that story. But a wider historical narrative should not overshadow the immediate occasion. Sometimes the right question is not what a moment predicts about the future, but whom it honors today and what viewers can learn from it. The public sometimes assumes that the absence of a family member must have a dramatic explanation. Usually, that assumption is not justified by the event alone. Different occasions have different attendance arrangements, and young children do not join every engagement. Without an official explanation, it is best not to attribute the decision to a dispute, an illness, or a private concern. The occasion can still be meaningful when only part of the family attends. It is reasonable to be interested in how children respond to a public ceremony, but unreasonable to treat that response as an examination of their character. A child who seems quiet may be listening; one who looks around may simply be curious. A short clip offers no basis for sweeping claims about manners or private upbringing. Protecting that perspective makes royal storytelling both kinder and more credible. For Catherine and William, the public demands of royal life sit alongside an understandable desire to preserve family boundaries. That is not unusual for parents, although their level of scrutiny is exceptional. Public appearances reveal something about ceremonial participation but little about home life. The distinction is especially important for children. A warm family-centered story can recognize this without making claims about the decisions taken behind closed doors. Above all, the event deserves to be understood as a public gathering with its own purpose, not simply as a stage for familiar faces. That approach gives viewers something substantial to discuss after the first burst of attention has passed. Viewers may disagree about the monarchy while still appreciating careful context. The significance of a public occasion is always richer than its shortest highlight. A royal event belongs to its organizers and participants as well as its guests. The wider story deserves much more thoughtful attention from viewers across Britain and America at this meaningful public moment. Which part of a remembrance occasion touches you most: the silence, the tradition, or the stories of those being honored? 🌺

Fly from Port Moresby to Buka Airport, located on neighbouring Buka Island. Cross the Buka Passage by local boat to reach Bougainville Island. Arrange onward road transport with a trusted local operator and confirm flight schedules before departure.

Expect hot, humid weather and substantial rainfall throughout the year. Tourism infrastructure is limited, so arrange transfers and accommodation in advance.

#fiction #cozymystery #dogs  
Standalone Myteries Versus Series
 A mystery reader’s bookshelf can hold two very different kinds of comfort. In the question of **standalone mysteries versus book series**, one book offers the pleasure of a complete case wrapped up by bedtime, while the other invites readers back to familiar streets, familiar suspects, and perhaps one very determined dog with a nose for trouble.

Neither choice is better for every reader or every moment. Sometimes you want a fresh town, a new puzzle, and a satisfying farewell. Other times, you want to check in on the people and animals who already feel like neighbors. The real joy is knowing what each type of mystery does especially well.

## What Makes a Standalone Mystery Special?

A standalone mystery tells its full story in one volume. The crime, the clues, and the main character’s emotional journey generally reach a meaningful resolution by the final page. There is no need to remember what happened three books ago, and no pressure to keep reading if one adventure is all you have time for.

That makes standalones wonderfully inviting for readers in between commitments. A vacation, a rainy weekend, a book club selection, or a busy month can all be perfect occasions for one complete whodunit. You meet the sleuth, learn the lay of the land, gather clues, and get the answer without needing a map of past events.

Standalones also give authors room to take a big creative swing. A new setting can have its own personality: an old inn with a locked library, a coastal town preparing for a festival, or a quiet neighborhood where everyone seems to know everyone else’s business. The author can build a mystery around a particular event or historical detail, then leave that world behind once the case is closed.

There is a lovely finality to that approach. A good standalone can feel like a warm visit with a fascinating stranger. You may not see them again, but you remember the conversation.

### The Trade-Off of One Complete Case

The same quality that makes a standalone easy to pick up can make it harder to leave. Readers only have so many pages to get to know the detective, their friends, their home, and their heart. A talented author can make those pages count, but there is less time for gradual changes and long-running friendships.

For readers who enjoy watching a character grow through several seasons of life, one book may feel a little brief. The ending can be satisfying and still leave you wishing there were another porch conversation, another town gathering, or another chance for a favorite animal sidekick to investigate something suspicious.

## Why Book Series Keep Readers Coming Back

A mystery series offers a different promise: the next case may be new, but the heart of the story remains familiar. Returning to a favorite fictional town can be as cozy as visiting a beloved local café. You know who makes the best pie, which neighbor is likely to gossip, and which trusted sleuth will notice the clue everyone else missed.

Series mysteries are especially satisfying in the cozy tradition because community matters. Each installment can introduce a new crime, while continuing the relationships that make readers care about the outcome. A sheriff may become more trusting. A shy neighbor may find courage. A rescue pet may settle into a permanent home. These changes do not need to rush. They can unfold naturally, book by book.

For animal lovers, a series has another special reward. Dogs and cats are not simply decorations in the background. They can become companions whose habits, quirks, and loyalty deepen over time. A clever canine might recognize a scent that does not belong, react to a nervous visitor, or lead a human sleuth toward a detail nobody thought to question. That is not magic. It is observation, instinct, and sometimes a warm snout in exactly the right place.

The Doc and Daisy Mysteries use that lasting connection to bring readers back to small-town Florida, where canine forensics, local history, and Daisy’s lively point of view keep each new puzzle feeling fresh.

### The Trade-Off of Returning to the Same World

A series can ask a bit more from its readers. While many cozy mysteries are designed so each book works on its own, a new reader may wonder whether they have missed an earlier relationship, an old feud, or an important personal milestone. Starting with book one often gives the richest experience.

Authors also face a cheerful but real challenge: keeping the setting recognizable without making it repetitive. Readers want the comfort of a favorite town, yet they also want an unpredictable mystery. The best series balances both. The diner can still serve its famous peach cobbler, but the next crime should not feel like the last one wearing a different hat.

A long series may also leave readers waiting for favorite storylines to develop. That patience can be part of the fun, like tending a garden and watching what comes up in the next season. Still, readers who prefer quick resolution may be happier with a standalone when they want every major thread neatly tied.

## Standalone Mysteries Versus Book Series: Choose by Mood

The easiest way to choose is not to ask which format is objectively best. Ask what kind of reading companion you need right now.

Choose a standalone when you are craving a clean start and finish. Perhaps you want a single satisfying puzzle for a flight, a book club, or a weekend curled up with a cat at your feet. You may be trying a new author or a new mystery style and want a low-commitment introduction. A standalone lets you sample freely.

Choose a series when you want to settle in. Maybe life has been busy, and you would rather return to characters who already know their way around the town square. Maybe you enjoy noticing small changes in friendships and romances alongside the central investigation. Or maybe you simply want more time with a dog narrator who has earned your trust, even if their opinion of the mail carrier remains a work in progress.

There is also a practical difference. Readers who borrow books, travel often, or have unpredictable reading schedules may appreciate that a standalone never leaves them halfway through a larger story. Readers who like to keep a dependable pile of books ready for the next cozy evening may find a series especially comforting. Once you discover a world you love, you already know where to go next.

## What Readers Get From Both

Despite their differences, strong standalones and strong series share the same essentials. Both need fair clues, memorable characters, a setting that feels alive, and an ending that rewards attention. In a cozy mystery, they also need a sense of safety and heart. The crime may shake up a community, but the story should leave room for kindness, humor, and the belief that careful observation can bring truth to light.

Both formats also benefit from a sleuth with a reason to care. The most engaging investigators are not merely solving a puzzle for sport. They are protecting a friend, seeking justice for a neighbor, preserving the peace of a town they love, or following a clue that will not stop scratching at the back of their mind.

That emotional connection is what makes readers remember a mystery long after they have guessed the culprit. A clever reveal is delightful. A clever reveal that matters to people we have come to care about is even better.

## A Reading Life Has Room for Both

There is no rule saying a reader must pledge loyalty to one kind of mystery. A standalone can refresh the palate between installments of a beloved series. A series can provide a welcome homecoming after several one-book adventures. Many readers happily switch between the two without giving it a second thought.

Think of the choice as matching a book to a moment. Some days call for a complete little journey, with one map, one mystery, and one tidy destination. Other days call for an open invitation to return, sniff around familiar corners, and see what trouble has found the neighborhood this time.

The best next mystery is the one that makes you want to pour something warm, settle into your favorite chair, and turn just one more page.

text:
In the late 9th century AD, more than five centuries after Christianity began receiving imperial support, the Hellenes of the mountainous Mani Peninsula were still worshipping the Hellenic Gods of their ancestors.

These were descendants of the ancient Hellenes, inhabiting one of the most isolated regions of Greece, where their traditions had survived centuries of religious and political change. Modern genetic research has revealed remarkable continuity between Deep Maniot genetic lineages and the ancient populations of Greece, with limited influence from later migrations.

During the reign of Emperor Basil I (867–886 AD), a ruler of Armenian family origins who rose to power within the multiethnic Christian Roman Empire, the imperial authorities sought to extend their religious domination over the Hellenes of Mani and replace the ancestral worship of their Greek Gods with Christianity, a religion that worships a Jewish God and is rooted in the religious traditions of ancient Israel.

This was an imperial establishment whose rulers and officials came from various ethnic backgrounds, asserting authority over Greeks who had preserved and practised their ancestral faith for centuries. The fact that the Empire spoke Greek did not make every imperial ruler a descendant of the ancient Hellenes, nor did it make Christianity the ancestral religion of Greece. An emperor of foreign descent could command armies, rule Greek lands and enforce his laws, but none of this gave him the moral right to determine which Gods the Hellenes could worship.

Emperor Constantine VII, Basil's own grandson, distinguishes the inhabitants of Maina from the Slavic settlers of the Peloponnese, identifying them with the region's ancient Greek population and recording that they were known as Hellenes because they had preserved the religious practices of the ancient Greeks.

Long before Christianity existed, the Hellenes had worshipped Zeus and the other Hellenic Gods. Their religion had produced sanctuaries, festivals, sacred traditions, philosophy, and an understanding of the divine deeply rooted in Hellenic civilisation. The sacred landscape of Mani itself bears witness to this inheritance. The ancient Greek writer Pausanias recorded the sanctuary of Poseidon at Cape Tainaron, the sanctuaries of Demeter and Aphrodite at Kainopolis, the worship of Apollo Karneios at Oitylo, and the oracle of Ino at Thalamae, where bronze statues of Helios and Pasiphae stood.

What right did an emperor in Constantinople have to interfere with that inheritance? Why should Greeks who had preserved the worship of their forefathers for centuries be expected to abandon their Gods simply because the imperial authorities had embraced a religion originating outside Greece?

The wider history of Christian imperial rule makes the question of religious freedom impossible to ignore. Under Justinian, imperial legislation required unbaptised Hellenes to submit to Christian instruction and baptism, threatening those who refused with the loss of property, civil rights and exile. Those discovered secretly practising prohibited sacrifices or returning to ancestral worship after baptism could face death.

This was not the peaceful preaching of a new religion. The Maniots left no surviving account explaining the circumstances of their Christianisation. What survives is the testimony of imperial authorities who celebrated their conversion, not the voices of the Hellenes whose religious traditions were being displaced.

The Maniots also faced threats beyond the religious demands of Constantinople. During the 9th century, Arab forces based in Crete launched maritime raids across the Greek seas, threatening coastal settlements throughout the Peloponnese. Maintaining relations with Constantinople and its naval forces could therefore offer practical advantages to vulnerable communities, regardless of their religious beliefs.

The Christianisation of Mani was not an overnight transformation. Christian communities had existed in some coastal settlements for centuries, with basilicas at Kyparissos and Alika generally dated to the 6th or 7th century, although their precise construction dates remain uncertain. The basilica at Cape Tigani, originally dated to the 7th century, was later reassessed and placed in the late 10th or early 11th century. Archaeological research has identified no Christian structures in Mani's interior dating before the 10th century. The existence of coastal churches does not establish that the surrounding Hellenes had abandoned their ancestral Gods.

According to Constantine VII, ancestral Hellenic religious practices survived among the inhabitants of Maina into the 9th century. Christian missionary activity continued across the southern Peloponnese during the late 10th century, and some historians have argued that ancestral Hellenic worship may have endured until around 1000 AD.

The Greek religion did not disappear when Constantine embraced Christianity, nor when Theodosius prohibited traditional sacrifices or Justinian imposed further restrictions. Centuries later, descendants of the ancient Hellenes were still worshipping their ancestral Gods in southern Greece.

The conversion of an empire does not prove the willing conversion of every people within it. The history of Mani demonstrates that the decline of the Hellenic religion cannot be explained merely as a peaceful transition from one faith to another. It must also be understood through imperial authority, religious persecution, and the survival of Hellenic worship for centuries despite the state's efforts to suppress it.

text:
Vasco Da Gama was guided by a 'Gujarati Canaca' (Muslim ?) ജോനകര്‍ / Jonakan / Sonakar

---------------

On his first voyage (1497–1499), he deliberately sailed up the East African coast after rounding the Cape of Good Hope. He reached the Swahili ports, encountered hostility in Mombasa, and then arrived at the friendlier port of Malindi (present-day Kenya) around 14 April 1498.

There the local ruler (Sultan of Malindi) welcomed him, provided supplies, and arranged a skilled pilot—described in Portuguese chronicles as a Gujarati “Moor” called Malemo Cana (or Malemo Canaca/Canaqua). This pilot, experienced in the monsoon winds and Indian Ocean routes, guided da Gama’s fleet across the open ocean. They left Malindi on 24 April and sighted the Indian coast near Calicut (Kozhikode) around 18–20 May 1498—a crossing of roughly 23–26 days.

-------------------

More Details:

The Sultan (or King/Sheikh) of Malindi :
In April 1498, after a hostile reception at Mombasa, Vasco da Gama’s fleet reached Malindi (present-day Kenya), a Swahili Muslim trading port. Contemporary Portuguese accounts (especially the anonymous Roteiro / journal of the voyage and later chroniclers such as João de Barros) describe a notably friendly reception:

> Da Gama arrived around 14–15 April 1498 (on or near Easter).

> The ruler of Malindi (usually called “the king” or “sultan” in the sources; his personal name is not recorded in Portuguese accounts) welcomed the Portuguese. He was in rivalry with Mombasa and saw the newcomers as potential useful allies.

> He sent gifts (including sheep) and offered food, fresh water, and other supplies.

> He agreed to provide a pilot for the crossing to India.

> There were exchanges of courtesies and presents. Da Gama, following royal instructions not to leave his ship lightly, met the ruler’s representatives (and possibly the ruler himself in some accounts) with ceremony. Festivities, including music and displays, took place during the roughly 9–10 days the fleet stayed.

> As a mark of the agreement, da Gama was permitted to erect a padrão (stone pillar with a cross and Portuguese arms). Most historians place the erection of the surviving Vasco da Gama Pillar on the return voyage in 1499, though one early chronicler (Gaspar Correia) places it at the end of the April 1498 visit. The pillar still stands in Malindi.

Malindi remained Portugal’s main ally on the East African coast for much of the 16th century.

> The Pilot: Malemo Cana (Malemo Canaca / Canaqua)

The pilot was arranged through the Sultan of Malindi. The main Portuguese sources are consistent on the essentials:

> Name:
João de Barros (Décadas da Ásia) calls him Malemo Caná, a “Moor of the Guzerat nation” (Gujarati). Other chroniclers (Castanheda, Góis) use variants such as Malemo Canaca, Canaqua, or Malemocanaqua.

> Etymology:
“Malemo” is the Portuguese rendering of Arabic muʿallim (“master” / “teacher” / chief navigator). “Cana” / “Canaca” is linked to Sanskrit/Indic kanaka (associated with astrologers or sailing masters).

> Origin:
Gujarati (from Gujarat in western India). He was almost certainly one of the experienced Muslim or Gujarati pilots then present in Malindi with the Indian Ocean trading ships.

> How he was engaged:
Barros says he was among those who visited the Portuguese ships. He took pleasure in talking with them and, wanting to please the King of Malindi (who was seeking a pilot), agreed to go. Da Gama was impressed when the pilot showed him a detailed chart of the Indian coast drawn “in the Moorish fashion” (with fine meridians and parallels).

> Navigation skill: He used the monsoon winds expertly. The crossing from Malindi to the coast near Calicut took about 23 days (departed 24 April 1498; sighted India ~18 May; anchored near Calicut/Kappad ~20 May). Portuguese accounts note he used instruments (including a kamal, a simple latitude device with a wooden card and knotted string) that the Portuguese had not previously seen in this form. Some of da Gama’s men reportedly thought he was “telling the distance by his teeth” when using the kamal.

> Role: He guided the fleet across the open ocean and later helped in the early contacts at Calicut.

On identity:
Later traditions sometimes identify him as the famous Arab navigator Ahmad ibn Majid. Most modern historians reject this (chronological problems, lack of contemporary Portuguese evidence, and the clear Gujarati attribution in the chronicles). The true personal name beyond “Malemo Cana” remains unknown; he was a skilled professional Gujarati pilot of the Indian Ocean monsoon routes.

In short:
the Sultan of Malindi actively facilitated the voyage by supplying the fleet and securing a competent Gujarati pilot who already knew the established monsoon route to the Malabar Coast. This local knowledge, not Portuguese discovery of the ocean itself, enabled the final leg to India.

---------------

Aḥmad ibn Mājid (Arabic: أحمد بن ماجد), also known as the "Arab Admiral" (أمير البحر العربي, ʿAmīr al-Baḥr al-ʿArabī) and the "Lion of the Sea",[1] was an Arab navigator and cartographer born c. 1432[2] in Julfar, the present-day Ras Al Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates.[3][4][5] He was raised in a family famous for seafaring; at the age of seventeen he was able to navigate ships. The exact date is not known, but Ibn Mājid probably died around 1500. Although long identified in the West as the navigator who helped Vasco da Gama find his way from Africa to India, contemporary research has shown Ibn Mājid is unlikely even to have met Da Gama.

Ibn Mājid wrote several books on marine science and the movements of ships, which helped people of the Persian Gulf to reach the coasts of India, East Africa and other destinations. Among his many books on navigation, Kitāb al-Fawā’id fī Uṣūl ʿIlm al-Baḥr wa’l-Qawāʿid (The Book of the Benefits of the Principles and Foundations of Seamanship) is considered one of his best.[7] It is an encyclopedia, describing the history and basic principles of navigation, latitude and longitude by way of celestial navigation,[8] lunar mansions, loxodromes, the difference between coastal and open-sea sailing, the locations of ports from East Africa to Indonesia, accounts of the monsoon and other seasonal winds, typhoons and other topics for professional navigators. He drew from his own experience and that of his father, also a famous navigator, and the lore of generations of Indian Ocean sailors. The book encompassed the entire science of navigation in the Indian Ocean at the time.

Ibn Mājid was known as a muʿallim (“teacher”, the title for pilots), i.e. teacher of navigation. Most of his navigational calculations depended on sophisticated astronomical observations, especially using the lunar mansions (manāzil al-qamar) and the thirty-two stellar rhumbs (akhnān).

Although Ibn Mājid was long held to have helped the Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama cross from Africa to the Indian subcontinent, contemporary research has shown that he would have been in his seventies at the time of Da Gama’s trip. The actual pilot who sailed with Da Gama was a Gujarati and may have returned to Portugal with da Gama.

text:
Duke faces SIU-Edwardsville after first loss
Friday, 8:00 CW

I expect Duke to figure out a way to get the five guys on the court playing in unison again, and the first opportunity is against  SIU-Edwardsville tomorrow night at Cameron Indoor Stadium.

The  Blue Devils have had little time to reflect on their loss to Michigan State in a game that was not Duke's best showing.  This is where Duke really starts to build chemistry, after a disappointing effort.

It will likely start with building better habits, as Duke had both offensive and defensive lapses against the Spartans.

We'll see if Duke coach Jon Scheyer tinkers with his lineup a bit.  At this point, it's on the players to step up and take on their roles with more certainty in their play.

Nobody around Duke basketball is worried the season is off the rails.  Some were, however, knocked back pretty good with what looked like an uncharacteristic effort from the players. 

Duke will look to better develop their half-court offense against 2-2 SIU Evansville, a team that is not made to hang with the Blue Devils.

So, yeah.  I think getting back to what Duke basketball normally looks like is the goal.  Duke will begin to heal before their matchup with a big and old Illinois team in the game while resetting their competitiveness a notch.

The lessons learned in early November are quite valuable.  An early loss or few often makes teams tougher after the experience.

Right now, Duke has some roles to offer guys who can step into them.  It is on the staff to get across to players that you sometimes have to play roles that help collectively.  That means doing some things better that are not your cup of tea, because it is a missing component the team needs.

Duke will rebound against a decent Cougars team that won 19 games a season ago.  Then they're back in the fire against an equally talented and hungry Illini team that is coming off their own upset loss.

And while on a hunger, that is the name of the game to improve and to win.  Duke needs some hungry players to start showing off what they can do while playing together.  Do that, and you earn a role on the journey ahead.

For the September 24, 1960 game, the Oregon Ducks traveled to Michigan by airplane, landing at Willow Run Airport

The Airport Bribe Attempt. That arrival at Willow Run became famous for a major off-field scandal. Shortly after the Ducks' plane landed, a 27-year-old gambler from Brooklyn named David Budin approached Oregon junior halfback Mickey Bruce in the airport terminal. Budin offered Bruce $5,000 to help rig the game against Michigan. Bruce immediately reported the bribe to head coach Len Casanova, sparking an FBI investigation and eventually leading to U.S. Senate subcommittee hearings.

text:
🔭 ASTRONOMY PICTURE OF THE DAY

🌌 Discover the cosmos, one extraordinary image at a time. Every day, explore a different corner of our fascinating universe through a remarkable astronomical image, accompanied by insights from a professional astronomer.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌌 NOVEMBER 12, 2026

🌖 MOON, VENUS AND SPICA MEET

Not all those who wander are lost. In the night sky, planets wander among the stars, creating beautiful celestial encounters that remind us of the intricate choreography of our solar system.

📸 IMAGE CREDIT: Włodzimierz Bubak

✨ THE COSMIC STORY

The word planet comes from an ancient Greek expression meaning "wandering star." Unlike the distant stars, which appear fixed in their positions, planets continually shift their locations against the background of the night sky.

Occasionally, from our perspective on Earth, these celestial wanderers appear to draw remarkably close to other astronomical objects. Such apparent meetings are called conjunctions.

They are not random encounters. They are beautiful demonstrations of celestial mechanics, governed by the precise and predictable movements of objects through space.

Today's photograph, captured in Poland, presents one such enchanting encounter.

Above the magnificent Tatra Mountains, a delicate crescent Moon hangs in the evening sky. Nearby shines brilliant Venus, appearing somewhat lower toward the horizon.

But there is another celestial participant in this gathering.

To the left of Venus shines Spica, one of the brightest stars in the night sky and the most prominent star in the constellation Virgo, the Maiden.

Located approximately 250 light-years from Earth, Spica is an extraordinary stellar system.

For centuries, astronomers observed it as a single point of light. Then, in 1890, observations revealed something remarkable: Spica was actually a binary star system, consisting of two massive blue stars orbiting one another.

And they move at an astonishing pace.

The two stars complete an orbit around their common center of mass approximately every four days!

But the story of Spica may be even more fascinating than astronomers once imagined.

Earlier in 2026, new findings were reported suggesting that Spica is not simply a binary system after all, but part of a triple-star system.

That means this brilliant point of light in the constellation Virgo may conceal three stellar companions participating in an intricate gravitational dance.

What appears to our eyes as a peaceful gathering of the Moon, Venus, and a distant star is actually a meeting of objects separated by vastly different distances and operating on dramatically different cosmic scales.

The Moon is our nearest celestial neighbor. Venus is a nearby planet within our own solar system. Spica, meanwhile, lies hundreds of light-years beyond them.

Yet from our vantage point on Earth, they briefly share the same celestial stage.

🌀 THE WONDER BENEATH THE STARS

There is something extraordinary about a conjunction. Objects separated by unimaginable distances can appear close enough to touch, reminding us that the night sky is both a window into space and a matter of perspective.

And Spica offers an additional reminder: even the brightest points of light may conceal entire worlds of complexity. What looks like one star may actually be several, bound together by gravity and moving through an intricate celestial dance.

Tonight's photograph captures more than a beautiful arrangement above the Polish mountains. It captures the remarkable contrast between appearance and reality in our universe.

Sometimes, the greatest wonders are hiding in plain sight.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔭 TOMORROW'S PICTURE: WHAT'S NEXT?

🌠 Keep looking up. The universe never runs out of wonders.

Interlune was pleased to welcome NASA’s Johnson Space Center Deputy Director Stephen A. Koerner to our Seattle headquarters to demonstrate progress on several of these critical capabilities.
Highlights included hardware for Interlune's Prospect Moon mission, which will identify gases in lunar soil (regolith) and determine how to extract them. We’ll be ready to integrate with a lander in September 2027 and are looking for a ride.
Meanwhile, we're building out the Interlune Research Lab (IRL) in Houston, where we’re implanting lunar regolith simulants with helium and hydrogen.
NASA’s Johnson Space Center, the Texas Space Commission—which is helping fund IRL—and the broader Texas space ecosystem are essential to America's space ambitions. Their commitment also offers a powerful model for expanding support for the space industry in Washington state.

text:
REVELATION BEFORE 70 AD: NERO, THE DESTRUCTION OF JERUSALEM, THE MILLENNIUM, AND THE REIGN OF THE SAINTS

(Catholic/Orthodox contextual improvement, in my view anyway)

The traditional dating of Revelation places its composition near the end of Emperor Domitian's reign, around AD 95–96. However, a substantial body of biblical, historical, and textual evidence supports an earlier date, before the destruction of Jerusalem and the Second Temple in AD 70.

The early-date position is not a modern invention. It has been defended by historical commentators and modern scholars, including John A. T. Robinson and Kenneth Gentry.

The question deserves serious examination: Was Revelation written to warn first-century Christians about events that were about to unfold, particularly the persecution associated with Nero and the approaching destruction of Jerusalem?

And if many of these prophecies were fulfilled in the first century, what does that mean for our understanding of Christ's kingdom, the millennium, the heavenly assembly, and the intercession of the saints?

1. THE BEAST'S NUMBER: 666 WAS A CODE FOR NERO CAESAR

Revelation 13:18 states:

"Here is wisdom. Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man: His number is 666."

The original Greek specifically instructs the reader to calculate the number.

The proposed solution is Nero Caesar.

When Nero Caesar is transliterated into Hebrew as נרון קסר, its numerical value is 666.

Nun = 50
Resh = 200
Waw = 6
Final Nun = 50
Qoph = 100
Samekh = 60
Resh = 200

Total: 666.

This identification becomes even more interesting because some ancient manuscripts read 616 instead of 666.

When the Hebrew spelling is adjusted to reflect the Latinized form of Nero's name, omitting the final nun, the result is 616.

Both numbers can therefore point to Nero Caesar.

Why would John communicate the emperor's identity through a numerical riddle rather than simply writing his name?

One plausible explanation is protection.

Revelation was circulated among vulnerable Christian congregations under Roman authority. Explicitly identifying the emperor as the beast could have endangered the author, the couriers delivering the letter, and the churches receiving it.

John's Greek instruction to calculate the number allowed informed readers to recognize the accusation without an explicit written identification of the emperor.

The possibility that this coded language protected John and the messengers carrying the letter is a historical inference, not something John directly explains. Nevertheless, the Nero identification is a serious explanation of the textual evidence.

2. THE SYRIAC TRADITION: JOHN WAS BANISHED TO PATMOS BY NERO

An important piece of external historical evidence comes from the Syriac tradition.

A Syriac heading associated with a version of Revelation identifies Nero Caesar as the emperor who banished John to Patmos.

Moses Stuart, in his 1845 commentary on Revelation, quoted the Syriac title:

"The Revelation which was made to John the Evangelist by God in the Island Patmos, into which he was banished by Nero the Cæsar."

This is significant because it preserves an alternative historical tradition concerning John's exile.

It is important to be precise: Revelation was not included in the earliest Peshitta New Testament. The Syriac Apocalypse circulated in later Syriac textual traditions, including the Philoxenian and Harklean traditions. The surviving heading is therefore not a first-century document.

Nevertheless, it demonstrates that a Syriac Christian tradition associated John's exile with Nero rather than Domitian.

This testimony deserves consideration alongside the traditional interpretation of Irenaeus.

3. THE TEMPLE WAS STILL STANDING: REVELATION 11

Revelation 11:1–2 states:

"Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there."

John is instructed to measure the sanctuary while leaving the outer court to the Gentiles.

The early-date argument is straightforward: this language fits naturally into a historical setting in which the Jerusalem Temple still existed.

The Second Temple was destroyed by Roman forces in AD 70.

If Revelation was written around AD 68–69, this passage fits the historical circumstances immediately preceding Jerusalem's destruction.

Those who defend the later date generally understand the Temple symbolically or argue that John is using an earlier Temple tradition.

Those interpretations are possible, but the pre-70 interpretation deserves serious consideration.

4. THE SEVEN CHURCHES WERE REAL CONGREGATIONS

Revelation 1–3 addresses seven actual churches in Asia Minor:

Ephesus
Smyrna
Pergamum
Thyatira
Sardis
Philadelphia
Laodicea

These were real congregations with identifiable circumstances, spiritual struggles, persecution, and opposition.

John was addressing Christians living in a particular historical environment.

The book must therefore first be understood in relation to its original audience rather than automatically interpreted as a prediction about distant generations.

5. JESUS SAID THESE EVENTS WOULD HAPPEN SOON

One of the strongest connections is between Revelation and the words of Jesus in the Gospels.

Revelation 1:1:

"The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants things which must shortly take place."

Revelation 1:3:

"The time is near."

These are not vague expressions. John explicitly tells his original readers that the events being revealed were approaching.

Compare these statements with Jesus:

Matthew 16:27–28: Some standing with Jesus would not taste death before seeing the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.

Matthew 23:36: The judgment described by Jesus would come upon that generation.

Matthew 24:34: "This generation will by no means pass away till all these things take place."

Matthew 26:64: Jesus tells the high priest that he will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds.

These statements deserve to be understood in their original historical context.

Why should Revelation's repeated declarations that its events were near automatically be extended thousands of years into the future?

6. THE SEVEN KINGS: REVELATION 17

Revelation 17:9–11 describes seven kings.

Five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come and will remain only a short time.

Early-date interpreters connect this sequence to the Roman emperors.

One proposed reckoning identifies Nero as the fifth emperor, followed by Galba as the sixth, who reigned briefly from AD 68 to 69.

This would place the writing of Revelation during the period immediately following Nero's death and before Jerusalem's destruction.

The precise imperial counting method is debated, but the proposed chronology is historically coherent.

Importantly, the Nero interpretation does not require Revelation to have been written while Nero was still alive. Nero could be the beast represented in the vision while John writes shortly after his death.

7. JOSEPHUS: THE LAMB IN THE TEMPLE AND THE CHARIOTS IN THE SKY

The Jewish historian Flavius Josephus documented the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 in The Jewish War.

In Book 6, Chapter 5, Section 3, Josephus records extraordinary reported signs preceding the catastrophe.

One of the most unusual reports concerns a lamb being born from a sacrificial animal in the Temple.

In William Whiston's translation, Josephus writes:

"At the same festival also, a heifer, as she was led by the high priest to be sacrificed, brought forth a lamb in the midst of the temple."

Josephus also records the eastern gate of the inner Temple court opening by itself:

"Moreover, the eastern gate of the inner [court of the] temple, which was of brass, and vastly heavy, and had been with difficulty shut by twenty men..."

He then describes another extraordinary reported event:

"For, before sunsetting, chariots and troops of soldiers in their armor were seen running about among the clouds, and surrounding of cities."

Finally, he records the reported voice heard by those in the Temple:

"They said that, in the first place, they felt a quaking, and heard a great noise, and after that they heard a sound as of a great multitude, saying, 'Let us remove hence.'"

These are Josephus' descriptions of reported supernatural portents preceding Jerusalem's destruction.

They are striking when read alongside Jesus' words about the Temple, heavenly signs, judgment, and the coming of the Son of Man.

Jesus spoke of wars, famines, tribulation, and signs in the heavens. Josephus recorded extraordinary reports associated with the final days of the Second Temple.

These accounts provide important historical context for understanding the apocalyptic language of the first century. They should be treated as ancient historical testimony, not as independently verified supernatural events.

8. IRENAEUS, POLYCARP, AND THE LATER TESTIMONY

The principal early testimony supporting the traditional Domitianic dating comes from Irenaeus, writing in the second century.

Irenaeus personally knew Polycarp as a boy. In a letter to Florinus, preserved by Eusebius in Ecclesiastical History 5.20, Irenaeus recalls hearing Polycarp speak about his association with the apostle John and others who had seen Jesus.

This is an important historical connection. However, the chronology matters.

Irenaeus did not write Against Heresies until approximately AD 180, many decades after the events of the apostolic generation. His statement in Against Heresies 5.30.3 is traditionally understood as placing the Revelation near the end of Domitian's reign.

Consequently, this is retrospective testimony, not a contemporary first-century record of the date of Revelation's composition.

Furthermore, Irenaeus does not explicitly state that Polycarp personally told him Revelation was written under Domitian. His childhood recollections establish a connection to Polycarp, but that connection should not be expanded beyond what the surviving text actually says.

The grammatical interpretation of Irenaeus' statement has also been debated. The traditional interpretation refers to the vision being seen toward the end of Domitian's reign, while alternative readings have been proposed.

The Domitianic date remains the majority scholarly position, and Irenaeus must be taken seriously. Nevertheless, his testimony is not beyond examination, and it should be weighed alongside Revelation's internal chronology, the Nero identification of 666 and 616, the Temple imagery of Revelation 11, and the alternative Syriac tradition associating John's exile with Nero.

Historical testimony deserves careful consideration, not unquestioning acceptance or dismissal.

9. JOHN 21: DID JESUS SUGGEST THAT JOHN MIGHT REMAIN UNTIL HIS COMING?

John 21:20–23 contains a particularly interesting exchange.

After Jesus tells Peter about the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God, Peter asks about the beloved disciple.

Jesus answers:

"If I will that he remain till I come, what is that to you? You follow Me."
John 21:22
This statement deserves consideration alongside Revelation's declarations that the events being revealed must shortly take place and that the time is near.

Could John have remained alive to witness Christ's coming in judgment upon Jerusalem in AD 70?

That is a possible preterist interpretation.

However, the Gospel immediately clarifies that Jesus did not promise John would never die:

"Yet Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but, 'If I will that he remain till I come, what is that to you?'"
John 21:23

The passage does not establish that John lived until AD 70, nor does it definitively identify the coming as the judgment of Jerusalem.
There is also an important historical tradition to consider. Irenaeus associates John's later life with the reign of Trajan, suggesting that John survived well beyond AD 70.

Nevertheless, Jesus' words invite consideration of what He meant by His coming and how that language relates to the first-century generation.

10. THE DESTRUCTION OF JERUSALEM AS COVENANT JUDGMENT

Jesus' statements in Matthew 23–24 and Luke 21 can be understood within the context of Israel's covenant history and the impending destruction of Jerusalem.

Consider:

Matthew 23:36: Judgment upon that generation.

Matthew 24:1–2: The destruction of the Temple.

Matthew 24:34: The events would occur before that generation passed away.

Luke 21:20–24: Jerusalem surrounded by armies and its subsequent devastation.

Jerusalem fell to the Romans in AD 70.

This provides a coherent historical framework for understanding much of Jesus' apocalyptic language.

It also raises an important theological distinction: historical covenant judgment is not necessarily the same thing as the eternal condemnation of individual souls.

The destruction of a city does not establish the eternal destiny of everyone who lived there.

11. THE MILLENNIUM AND THE TRANSITION OUT OF THE OLD COVENANT

What if Revelation's millennium is not primarily a distant future event, but a description of Christ's reign and the heavenly victory of His saints?

Revelation 20:4 states:

"And they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years."

In a preterist framework, the millennium is understood in connection with Christ's victory, the establishment of His kingdom, and the transition out of the Old Covenant order.

The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 becomes a decisive historical event in that transition.

This interpretation sees the judgment of the old covenant world as part of the fulfillment of Jesus' warnings and the public vindication of His kingdom.

The exact beginning and nature of the millennium remain debated among Christians. AD 70 is a proposed historical framework, not an established consensus.

Nevertheless, this interpretation raises an important question: if Christ reigns now, what is the condition and activity of those who have died in Him?

12. THE CLOUD OF WITNESSES AND THE HEAVENLY ASSEMBLY

Hebrews 12:1 states:

"Therefore we also, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which so easily ensnares us."

The imagery follows Hebrews 11, which recounts the faithful who came before us.

They are presented as witnesses whose lives testify to God's faithfulness.

The passage does not explicitly say that they observe every event on earth, but it places living Christians in continuity with the departed faithful.

Even more striking is Hebrews 12:22–24:

"But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to an innumerable company of angels."

The passage continues:

"To the general assembly and church of the firstborn who are registered in heaven."

And:

"To the spirits of just men made perfect."

Notice the language: you have come.

The author describes the heavenly assembly as a present spiritual reality for Christians, not merely a future destination.

The Church on earth is connected to the heavenly Jerusalem. The departed righteous are not outside the life of Christ.

13. THE SAINTS REIGN, WORSHIP, AND PARTICIPATE IN HEAVENLY PRAYER

Several passages in Revelation describe an active heavenly assembly.

Revelation 20:4:

"And they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years."

Revelation 5:8:

"Golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints."

Revelation 6:9–10:

The departed martyrs cry out to God, asking how long until judgment and the vindication of their blood.

Revelation 8:3–4:

An angel offers incense with the prayers of the saints before God.

These passages portray heaven as a place of worship, participation, prayer, and communion.

The saints are not depicted as having ceased to exist or becoming irrelevant to the Church.

They are alive in Christ.

This provides a substantial biblical foundation for the historic Christian doctrine of the communion of saints.

14. THE INTERCESSION OF SAINTS

If the saints are alive in Christ, if they participate in His heavenly reign, and if Scripture depicts the heavenly assembly in connection with the prayers of the faithful, then the intercession of saints becomes much easier to understand.

Consider the wider biblical picture:

Hebrews 12:1: The cloud of witnesses.

Hebrews 12:22–24: The heavenly assembly and the spirits of the righteous made perfect.

Luke 20:38: God is not the God of the dead but of the living.
Revelation 5:8: Heavenly elders holding bowls identified with the prayers of the saints.
Revelation 6:9–10: Departed martyrs speaking to God.
Revelation 8:3–4: The prayers of the saints ascending before God.
The explicit practice of asking departed saints to pray for us is not stated in a single one of these passages. However, together they establish a biblical picture of the departed faithful as alive in Christ and participating in heavenly worship.
The historic Christian understanding of the communion of saints is not that Christians worship the departed or place them alongside God.

Rather, the saints participate in the one life of Christ, and any intercession they offer is dependent upon His unique mediation.

Death does not destroy the unity of Christ's body.

The Church is one body, not two disconnected communities.

15. THE MYSTERY OF JOHN'S REMAINS

Early Christian tradition associates John with Ephesus, where he is said to have lived and ministered for many years.

Polycrates of Ephesus, writing near the end of the second century, identifies John as one who rested at Ephesus.

The traditional burial place is associated with the site of the Basilica of St. John in Ephesus.

There is no independently verified physical identification of John's bodily remains.

This should not be confused with the Gospel's statement that Jesus promised John would remain until He came. John 21 explicitly corrects the rumor that Jesus had guaranteed the apostle would never die.

The historical question concerns the surviving evidence and traditions about his burial, not proof that he never died.

16. THE DORMITION AND ASSUMPTION OF MARY

The Dormition and Assumption of Mary are also important when considering the relationship between the earthly and heavenly Church.

Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions affirm Mary's extraordinary departure from earthly life, commonly called the Dormition in Eastern Christianity.

Catholic teaching declares that Mary was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory. Eastern Orthodox tradition celebrates her Dormition and glorification, though the theological formulations are not identical in every respect.

The traditional accounts describe Mary dying in the presence of the apostles, being buried, and subsequently being found absent from the tomb. Some accounts associate the discovery with the apostle Thomas.

The absence of universally accepted bodily relics of Mary is often discussed in connection with this tradition, although the absence of verified relics is not itself historical proof of the Assumption.

Could Mary's Dormition and Assumption have occurred around AD 70?

It cannot be ruled out as a theological possibility, because Scripture does not give us Mary's death date.

However, no reliable historical evidence establishes AD 70 as the year of her Assumption. The earliest surviving detailed Dormition narratives appear centuries after the apostolic period, and early Christian writers did not preserve one universally agreed chronology.

The question is therefore open historically, even though the bodily glorification of Mary is affirmed in Catholic and Orthodox tradition.

There is a meaningful theological connection here: the saints are alive in Christ, the heavenly assembly is real, and the ultimate destiny of the faithful is not disembodied existence forever, but resurrection and glorification.

Mary's Assumption is understood within this larger Christian hope.

17. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE DOCTRINE OF HELL

The dating of Revelation is not merely an academic debate.

It affects how Christians understand biblical prophecy, Gehenna, judgment, the coming of the Son of Man, and the destruction of Jerusalem.

If many of Jesus' warnings concerned first-century covenant judgment, Christians should be careful about automatically interpreting every warning as a description of everlasting conscious torment.

This does not independently prove universal salvation, but it challenges the assumption that every apocalyptic judgment passage must describe the eternal fate of unbelievers.

There is also a substantial biblical foundation for hoping in God's ultimate reconciliation of creation.

Romans 11:32:

"For God has committed them all to disobedience, that He might have mercy on all."

1 Corinthians 15:22:

"For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ all shall be made alive."

Colossians 1:20 describes God reconciling all things to Himself through Christ.

The historical judgment of Jerusalem, the reign of Christ, the communion of saints, and the hope of universal reconciliation deserve to be examined together.

CONCLUSION

The evidence and theological connections deserve serious consideration:

Nero Caesar corresponds to 666, with the 616 variant also fitting an alternative spelling.

The Syriac tradition identifies Nero as the emperor who banished John to Patmos.

Revelation 11 describes the Temple in language compatible with its existence before AD 70.
Seven actual churches received messages relevant to their historical circumstances.
Revelation repeatedly declares that its events must shortly take place and that the time is near.
The seven kings in Revelation 17 have been interpreted as Roman emperors in a chronology compatible with an earlier date.
Josephus records extraordinary reported signs preceding Jerusalem's destruction, including the lamb in the Temple and chariots appearing among the clouds.
Irenaeus personally heard Polycarp as a boy, but wrote his surviving testimony about Revelation's dating decades later, around AD 180. His connection to Polycarp does not establish that Polycarp personally supplied the Domitianic dating.
Jesus' words in John 21:22–23 raise questions about His coming and John's lifetime.
Hebrews describes a present heavenly assembly of angels and the spirits of the righteous made perfect.
Revelation portrays the saints reigning with Christ and participating in heavenly worship and prayer.
The communion of saints provides a biblical and historical framework for understanding intercession.
The Dormition and Assumption of Mary express the Christian hope of bodily glorification, although their precise historical chronology remains uncertain.
None of these arguments individually settles every historical or theological question. Together, however, they invite a broader reading of the New Testament in its original historical and covenantal context.
The central question remains:

Are we reading Revelation and the words of Jesus in the historical context of their original audience, or are we continually moving their fulfillment into the distant future despite their repeated declarations that the time was near?

And beyond the dating debate:

If Christ reigns, if the saints are alive in Him, if the heavenly assembly participates in worship and prayer, and if death cannot separate us from the love of God, should we understand the Church as a communion extending beyond the grave?

The evidence deserves a fair hearing.

And the character of God, His justice, His mercy, and His ultimate purpose for creation deserve equally serious examination.

Today's Anegudde Shri Vinayaka Alankara from Kumbhasi, Kundapura💐

Brahmi Shri Durgaparameshwari Devi at Kamalashile near Kundapura

Shri Brahmi Durgaparameshwari Temple (also known as the Kamalashile Temple) is located in the serene village of Kamalashile, Udupi district, Karnataka. Situated about 35 km from Kundapura and 61 km from Udupi, the Devasthan is located peacefully along the banks of the Kubja River, surrounded by the lush green forests of the Western Ghats.

The main deity is Devi Durga, worshipped in the form of a lotus-shaped stone Linga representing the divine union of Mahakali, Mahalakshmi, and Mahasaraswathi.

Nearby lies the ancient Suparsha Cave, where rishis once meditated. Devotees often visit the cave to witness the convergence of the three goddesses and the point of origin for the Naga Teertha (Kubja River). 

The temple is famous for its delicious and extensive midday Annadahasoha (free meals offered to all devotees). 

Traditional wooden and tiled architecture typical of Tulunadu architecture blends beautifully into the dense surrounding nature here.

#Anegudde #Kundapura #Kamalashile #Karnataka

MISSOURI, THIS IS WHAT WE WARNED YOU ABOUT.

We warned that Amendment 6 would make sweeping changes to Missouri’s Constitution and laws harder to reverse. Now, just days after its passage, 10 new initiative petitions targeting the 2028 election have been submitted to the Secretary of State.

And what’s being proposed should concern every Missourian.

Here’s a breakdown of what these proposals would do:

🚩001 – Redefining Marriage & Gender Rights: Removes Missouri’s constitutional definition of marriage as between a man and a woman, establishes constitutional protections for gender identity and sexual orientation, and allows minors to seek trans surgery, therapy, or counseling with parental or guardian consent.

🚩002 – Proxy Voting in the Legislature: Allows citizens to assign their legislative votes to individual lawmakers, giving some legislators potentially thousands of votes while others have far fewer. This would fundamentally change how representation works in the General Assembly.

🚩003 – Overhauling Missouri’s Legislature: Repeals multiple constitutional provisions, eliminates legislative primaries, introduces statewide elections for legislators, and radically restructures how representation works in Missouri.

🚩004 – Electronic Initiative Petition Signatures: Allows initiative petitions to be signed electronically rather than requiring traditional paper signatures, raising serious questions about verification, security, and FRAUD.

🚩005 – Stripping the Governor’s Authority: Takes away the Governor’s independent power to issue pardons, commutations, and reprieves, and replaces the line-item veto with recommendations subject to legislative approval.

🚩006 – Ranked-Choice Voting: Introduces ranked-choice voting in Missouri elections with more than two candidates for a single office, replacing our traditional voting system with multiple rounds of vote counting and candidate elimination.

🚩007 – Eliminating Primary Elections: Abolishes primaries for congressional and state legislative races and moves to statewide elections using party lists, stripping voters of their traditional ability to choose their party’s nominees.

🚩008 – Government-Run Healthcare: Creates a state-administered healthcare cooperative funded through income-based membership payments, dramatically expanding government’s involvement in healthcare.

🚩009 – New Taxes for Green Energy: Imposes a new tax on long-term capital gains and qualified dividends to fund a government-administered renewable energy program.

🚩010 – Government-Built Housing: Establishes a state-run housing program financed through government bonds, offering homes at cost with no down payment and no interest over 30–40 years.

Make no mistake: These aren’t minor policy adjustments. These proposals would fundamentally reshape Missouri’s government, elections, and economy.

We warned about the consequences of Amendment 6, and now we’re seeing exactly why those warnings mattered.

Missouri’s Constitution is not a playground for radical political experiments. The fight to protect our state and our representative form of government is far from over. 🇺🇸

text:
The Islamic Slave trade.    Jefferson and the Barbary Pirates
The Barbary states (the North African Ottoman regencies of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli, plus independent Morocco) ran a long-standing system of state-sponsored corsairing. They seized merchant ships, enslaved crews, and demanded tribute payments from European powers (and later the United States) for “protection” from further attacks. After independence, American ships lost the protection of the Royal Navy and became targets. In the mid-1780s, Algerian corsairs seized American vessels and crews, creating a crisis for the new republic.
As U.S. minister to France, Jefferson worked with John Adams (minister to Britain) on the problem. In March 1786 in London they met the Tripolitan ambassador Abd al-Rahman (Abdrahaman). When they asked by what right Tripoli attacked nations that had done it no injury, the ambassador replied that it was founded on the laws of their Prophet, written in the Koran: nations that had not acknowledged their authority were sinners; it was their right and duty to make war on them wherever found, enslave prisoners, and that any Muslim slain in such battle was assured of Paradise. He described the incentives for corsairs (extra slaves for the first boarder) and their aggressive tactics.
Jefferson consistently rejected the European practice of paying tribute. He viewed it as dishonorable, ineffective (it only invited higher demands), and more expensive over time than building a navy and using force. He advocated naval action and tried to organize a coalition of affected powers. In a July 1786 letter to Adams he wrote that he had early thought it best “to effect a peace thro’ the medium of war.” As Secretary of State under Washington he continued to argue the same line, though Congress and the weak early federal government limited options. The U.S. paid substantial tribute and ransom in the 1790s under the Washington and Adams administrations.
As President, Jefferson put his long-held preference into practice. In 1801 the pasha of Tripoli demanded more money and, when refused, declared war in the traditional manner by chopping down the flagpole at the U.S. consulate. Jefferson dispatched a naval squadron. The First Barbary War (1801–1805) followed: naval blockades, the famous raid in which Stephen Decatur burned the captured USS Philadelphia in Tripoli harbor, and a land expedition that included U.S. Marines (the origin of “to the shores of Tripoli” in the Marines’ Hymn). A 1805 treaty ended hostilities with Tripoli; it involved a ransom for American prisoners but stopped the ongoing tribute relationship with that state on the prior terms. Fighting and tribute issues with other Barbary states continued until the Second Barbary War under Madison (1815).
Jefferson’s earlier ownership of Sale’s Quran and his later encounters with the religious justification offered by the Barbary ambassador are related but distinct. He bought the book for study as a law student; the piracy crisis and the ambassador’s explicit appeal to the Quran came later. He treated the Barbary threat primarily as a practical and commercial problem of predation that required a naval response rather than continued payments, while remaining committed to religious liberty at home (including for Muslims).

text:
According to GROK, here is why this story matters to the US. —
It is significant for the United States primarily as a clear illustration of systemic problems in Somali official travel, document integrity, and migration patterns that intersect with U.S. immigration, asylum, security, and aid policies.

This fits a documented pattern of abuse of Somali diplomatic/service passports and official delegations:

•Cases of officials or associates using diplomatic passports for unauthorized entry and asylum claims (including a 2024–2025 Ireland case involving a Somali working in diplomatic services).

•Reports of passports, accreditation letters, and delegation spots being sold for thousands of dollars to facilitate travel to Europe or beyond.

•Prior incidents of delegation members or “officials” disappearing after arrival in Europe, plus discarded Somali diplomatic/service passports found at the U.S.-Mexico border.

•European countries have tightened or suspended certain visa processes for Somali passport holders in response to non-return and fraud concerns.

These practices erode the reliability of Somali official documents and government attestations.

Direct Relevance to the U.S.

The U.S. has resettled well over 100,000 Somali refugees over the decades, with a large concentration in Minnesota (Minneapolis area). This story matters for several interlocking reasons:

•Immigration and asylum integrity: Weak or corrupt issuance of official travel documents and the use of state delegations as cover make vetting harder. The U.S. system relies on foreign documents, government references, and claims of persecution or official status. Patterns of this type raise the risk of fraudulent asylum claims, family reunification based on questionable records, and chain migration. There have already been U.S. cases of Somali asylum fraud (including one involving familial ties to ISIS-Somalia) and large-scale welfare/fraud schemes in Minnesota involving networks from the community.

•Security and counterterrorism: Somalia remains a base for al-Shabaab (al-Qaeda affiliate). Corrupt control of passports and official channels increases the difficulty of screening for individuals with extremist ties or other risks. The U.S. maintains counterterrorism cooperation and a military footprint related to Somalia; unreliable partner institutions complicate that.

•Aid and governance: The U.S. provides substantial assistance to the Somali federal government. Ministerial-level involvement (or allegations thereof) in selling access to Western travel undercuts the very governance and anti-corruption goals that aid is meant to support.

•Policy context: In the current U.S. environment, this feeds into ongoing debates over refugee admissions from high-risk countries, post-admission re-vetting (e.g., efforts focused on Minnesota refugees), temporary protected status, and scrutiny of Somali official travel or diplomatic privileges. Europe’s responses (tighter short-stay rules, suspension of certain visas) offer a practical precedent for heightened U.S. caution on official Somali documents and delegations.

In short, while this specific incident occurred in Kosovo and is not a direct U.S. entry case, it exemplifies the kind of official-channel abuse that undermines confidence in Somali documents, increases fraud and security risks in Western immigration systems (including the American one), and highlights governance failures in a country that is both a major source of U.S. refugee admissions and a counterterrorism partner.
