text:
.@DanaBashCNN: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been a frequent flier in President Trump's orbit. Here are the president and Jensen Huang in late September at the White House. A few days earlier, Huang sat at the president's head table at a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping. In May, there was a last minute Air Force One ride to Beijing and this from a U.S.-Saudi investment forum last year. And this is just a small sampling. The president and Huang are, at least were, close. But now reports of two affairs, most alarmingly with an alleged Chinese spy, and Huang's resignation this morning from his multi-trillion dollar company are raising serious questions about the relationship between Nvidia and the Trump administration. Now why does this matter? Well until today, Jensen Huang was essentially controlling the chips powering the entire AI arms race and had extraordinary access to the president, which means the scandal could have a major impact on many things. National security, global politics, the world economy, and of course the politics of the Trump White House. CNN's Alayna Treene is at the White House. Alayna, the president, as we mentioned, the two of them have been very close. The president, just shortly before coming on air, put out on social media that he is endorsing Tim Cook to lead Nvidia. Here's what the president wrote, "Now that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place. Tim Cook of Apple. A legend replaces a legend." Now this is not Dana White being press secretary, this is a far more realistic and serious proposal. What are you hearing from the White House?

.@alaynatreene: There's a lot to say about this. Just to touch on that response from the president, which is the first White House response, I should say, in regard to Jensen Huang resigning effective immediately from Nvidia amid this entire scandal. One, Tim Cook, like Jensen Huang, very close to the president. I'd argue Huang is actually closer to the president than Cook is, but I think that's why that name came to mind. We should also note that Tim Cook is still very much involved in Apple, even though he resigned from his role as CEO a couple of months ago recently. I think it's unlikely Tim Cook would actually take him up on this offer. But to get into more of just why this is so important from a White House perspective, why I'm the one actually talking to you about this, Dana, is because of how close the president was to Jensen Huang. There are a few people in Silicon Valley that have a closer tie or direct line to Trump than Huang. There are many times when I've been in the White House having meetings, seeing Huang in his signature leather black jacket, going into the Oval Office to meet with the president. We know that he often calls the president, Trump often calls him. He once did so publicly, you know, dialed him up at a press conference or some sort of meeting recently. And so that's why I think there's a lot of questions about this, because, of course, we know that this relationship to Huang had the potential to really shape this administration's policy, particularly when it comes to the future of artificial intelligence, but also the sale of AI chips, Nvidia's most advanced chips to China and the export controls around that. A lot of controversial decisions that in conversations, Dana, that had been going on behind the scenes about whether or not that could continue. And that's why there's so many questions about this. I also want to bring up to you something you mentioned as well about Huang flying with the president. The last time Trump went to China, he's actually going a couple of days, but his last trip to Beijing was back in May. During that trip, he had a layover, the president in Alaska before carrying on. He summoned essentially Huang to Alaska to finish that leg of the journey to go to Beijing. And that was when actually we were told the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, had given the president an intelligence briefing informing him of this, you know, that the fact that Huang was suspected of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. So a lot to get into about who knew what, when and all of the national security implications of it. Yeah, and we were all—everybody was asking why at that point back in May, why wasn't Jensen Huang going on the trip? It didn't make a lot of sense, and the president, you know, it seems didn't know until he knew before he invited him on that trip. Lots of questions about their relationship, but also really big questions about how the White House, how the national security arm of the White House handled the knowledge or allegations of the spy who was involved here.

Dana Bash: Thank you so much, Alayna, I really appreciate it. Phil Mattingly, you are—you've done amazing work on this. I was just listening to your podcast, which I think everybody should listen to to understand why this matters so much. We are where we are right now. He has resigned. But there are so many questions, including what Alayna was just talking about at the end there, which is the chips and whether or not the United States should be sort of—should have all of its eggs in that basket. And there is now a tussle inside, or was almost physically, apparently, a tussle inside the Trump cabinet over this. Shockingly involving Scott Bessent, which seems to be the consistent through line of any potential tussle in the administration.

Phil Mattingly: To what Alayna was just detailing, I think what people need to understand right now is this is the first chapter, and it is not about one CEO or one company or a fall from grace. It is about to completely engulf Washington, as it's already in the process of engulfing Washington. And the reason why threads very closely to what you and Alayna were laying out in a relationship that did not exist prior to inauguration, their first meeting was January 31st in the Oval Office of 2025. Over the course of just 18, 19 months, more than at least 15 meetings that I could pin down between reporting and public identification between the two in the Oval Office, in Riyadh, at Windsor Castle, in Mar-a-Lago, regular phone calls, oftentimes late at night. Alayna was talking about how the president called in when Jensen was on the—at the All In summit, a big kind of tech summit. He also called in to an all hands meeting at NVIDIA on an earnings day just to congratulate him on earnings. So it's extremely close, like no other relationship with any other CEO. And I think the elements as to why are really important to understand, because it's transactional in a way that underscores NVIDIA's singular importance, not just to the U.S. economy, but to the global economy. Trump was always very aware of that, but also the leverage that NVIDIA's chips provided the administration in the negotiations with China, which Howard Lutnick, who's very deeply involved in this, utilized in a way that I think was very unprecedented for export controls in general. But also the degree to which because of that, Huang, you can literally trace meeting face to face with the president and a decision within hours or within the next day that directly affects NVIDIA's bottom line or NVIDIA's products or NVIDIA's business operations in the exact way that Jensen was lobbying for. And so I've counted at least four meetings and several rulemakings. You can go deep into export policy, which I'm going to save all of you from that at this moment. But the degree to which their priorities and their policy desires matched up with what actions were taken because of that relationship is going to be a central point of investigation going forward. In addition to, and I don't want to lose sight of why we're even talking about this, why he fell from grace because of an affair with, as you said in your podcast, it's not about the sex, it's about who it was with, an alleged Chinese spy. And that is going to be something that no question is going to be reported on and investigated. But back to the issues going on inside the cabinet about Howard Lutnick, the Commerce Secretary, and the Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent. Francesca, you cover the White House and I want to get you on this, but first I want to read a little bit of CNN's reporting on this. Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his department's reluctance to label NVIDIA customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat in a situation room confrontation last week. Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, also were briefed months ago about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who the intelligence community suspected of being a Chinese spy. People familiar with the matter said. But despite these warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list. Megaspeed being, as it sort of suggests in this reporting that I just read, the company of Alice Huang, who's the alleged Chinese spy, who was still, even though the suspicion was already there inside the Trump administration, Howard Lutnick kept the U.S. relationship going with that company. But this also does go back to the president, though, and how much the president did or didn't want this to happen.

Francesca: This is now what you see Hakeem Jeffries, who we expect to be Speaker of the House, saying that who knew what, when, you know, is something that they're going to be investigating heavily. I mean, members of Congress asking for classified briefings on this, promising probes on this in the next Congress. And I don't think you're overstating the relationship between the former Nvidia CEO and the president of the United States at all. When I interviewed him last July, the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, he told me that he had come to the White House, that he had spoken to President Trump. This was leading into one of his trips to China. He told me that every time that he was in Washington, D.C., he tried to sit down with the president of the United States and read him in and have the president read him in on what was going on with China. And then he went to China immediately after that. So that's just one example, I think, of what that relationship was like.

.@PamelaBrownCNN: Let's bring in Democratic Congressman Seth Moulton from Massachusetts. He's a veteran who serves on the House Armed Services and Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the U.S. and the Chinese Communist Party. Congressman, thanks for being here with us. Let's start with this big news about Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia. I mean, this is massive. What is your reaction?

.@sethmoulton: I mean, it's huge. And there are a lot of questions that this raises because obviously we are in a very serious strategic competition with China and both Jensen and President Trump have been doing things over the last several months, selling a lot of chips to China that arguably are very much in Beijing's interests and against the interests of the United States of America, against the intent of Congress that has tried to restrict the sale of these chips. So we don't know, for example, whether Jensen knew that this woman, his mistress, was a Chinese spy. We do know that Trump knew that, though, and he chose to do nothing.

Pamela Brown: So that's where the questions should begin. Do you think the Commerce Department should have done more regarding the longstanding concerns of selling these chips from Nvidia to China? We know that President Trump is standing by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, but how are you seeing this?

Seth Moulton: I'm seeing it that the president has a lot of investments in Nvidia and wants them to sell a lot of chips. And I recognize that I'm making an assumption there that Trump is someone who cares a lot about his personal wealth, maybe even more than our national security. And you may not agree with that assumption. You maybe you've spent the last 10 years in a coma. But the reality here is that President Trump very often acts in his own financial interests. And I think we should be asking questions about that as well. When did the president purchase this stock? Did that influence his decisions to do nothing about stopping Nvidia from selling chips or even recognizing that ensnaring the CEO publicly in this scandal could result in a dramatic downfall of the stock? Frankly, we should be asking what members of Congress have been investing in Nvidia as well.

Pamela Brown: We know the president has made billions since going into office. He has responded to this by saying that he has nothing to do with the stock trades, that someone else does that for him, that his sons run the businesses and so forth. But we are learning that he was made aware of these concerns about this alleged affair with a Chinese spy and Huang on his trip to China that Huang eventually joined. Here's what President Trump said when asked about that trip on Monday.

Reporter: When you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties with the Chinese spy then, or --

Donald Trump: No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it. And Jensen totally denies that.

Pamela Brown: The New York Times reports it was the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who briefed Trump on that just before they arrived in China. What do you make of that?

Seth Moulton: I mean, Trump is both a liar and in his old age, he's quite forgetful. So I guess we don't know whether he just can't remember the briefing or whether he's lying about it. But both are quite plausible. And the bottom line is that when he was briefed, when he was briefed by his own secretary of state and national security adviser, he chose to do nothing. He chose to do nothing in the name of our national security against our most existential adversary. He chose to do nothing because I would assume it might affect his own personal wealth or stock dealings. We don't know exactly why, but we've got to find out. And it's time for members of Congress to be asking these tough questions.

Pamela Brown: Several House Republicans are pushing for Huang to testify as soon as next week. What questions would you want to ask him?

Seth Moulton: Well, first of all, I want to just fundamentally understand why he wants to support China so much, why he wants to sell the most advanced chips in the world to an adversary that's trying to beat us in an A.I. race, to an adversary that every time you look at the classified intelligence is doing very dangerous things against us and our allies and is increasingly relying on A.I. to do so. I mean, China, for example, remember, has embedded cyber tools, cyber offensive weapons in our own infrastructure. I mean, they have the ability to shut off our water supply in different cities across the United States. They're increasingly doing this with the aid of A.I. and they're developing advanced A.I. with the help of chips from the best A.I. chip maker in the world, Nvidia. So we need to really get to the bottom of what the connection between NVIDIA and China really is.

text:
A 19-year-old from a small town in Illinois got fucked on camera for $2,000 to $3,000 after answering a Craigslist ad that said "Hot Girls Wanted," a modeling gig with a free trip to Miami.

She never told her parents, but they found out. So did everyone in her town. "I knew that I couldn't come back here. Then I'm just a burnt out porn star."

She thought she would do one or two scenes and come back. "If I would have had something to think it through, I probably wouldn't have gone."

In the video below, Rachel Bernard tells it herself, from the $2,000 to $3,000 offer to the moment she realized she could not go home. Wait for what she says about the $80,000.

"You can get $2,000, $3,000 for going out there once. I was just going to go there, do one or two, and come back."

"It's not like you're actually making $80,000. You're really just surviving." The agent took 15%. Nightline said she lasted six months, did 85 videos, and went home with $2,000.

"No one is really meant to have sex that long, or that vigorously, or that intensely for that many days in a row, and with different people."

She found a camera. "That saved my life." She said she had thought she had no talents but taking off her clothes and having sex with people.

Asked if she would ever go back: "No. I'm 100% certain. There's no worse feeling than being used."

Was this a $2,000 to $3,000 trip she chose, or a trap that only ended after her parents and her whole town already knew?

text:
Steve Stoute came up with a $10 million check to stop an 18-year-old LeBron James from meeting Nike.
LeBron left it on the table. Stoute says Reebok's offer was the bigger one.

LeBron was a high school senior from the Spring Hill projects in Akron. He says the rent was about $17 a month.

Stoute was consulting for Reebok at the time.

In the video below, he explains the logic from the record business: give the money "right there, up front," so the kid doesn't even take the other meetings.

Reebok chairman Paul Fireman had the check ready when LeBron flew in.

They pitched. Fireman handed it over. Everyone stepped out of the room.

When they came back, the check was still on the table. LeBron wanted to hear Nike and Adidas first.

Stoute says he clapped. "It was my idea that didn't work."

"A young black man, 18 years old, walked away from $10 million, going back to the projects."

LeBron signed with Nike for about $90 million over seven years. In 2015 it became a lifetime deal reportedly worth over $1 billion.

Did LeBron beat Reebok's money trap, or did he leave the bigger offer on the table for a logo?

text:
OPINION: WEAPONIZATION?

Democrats Backing Amy Acton, Sherrod Brown Spent Over $1 Million Promoting the Site That Smeared Me

Columbia Journalism Review reports the ad money behind https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ — a “local news” site run by a former Brown staffer whose company is registered to a Chicago apartment.

Commentary by Jack Windsor 

Columbia Journalism Review reported Thursday that https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ content was promoted by more than $1 million in Facebook ads, bought by Democrat-aligned groups, pushing the site’s stories at Ohio voters before the Nov. 3 election. The site’s publisher, Dylan Poe, worked for Sherrod Brown’s 2018 Senate campaign. His company, NorthStar Civic Media LLC, is registered to a Chicago apartment.

Read the full CJR report here: https://t.co/pY6hubfhoW

I know this site. I fact-checked it on my weekday afternoon drive-time talk-radio show — The Windsor Report — in July. On Aug. 20, I reported more in depth about its ownership and place in the Ohio political propaganda ecosystem.

This is my first commentary on the CJR findings. More reports on what I call the Democrat operative fake news ecosystem in Ohio will follow.

I fact-checked this site again and again 

I covered https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ stories on my Bias Buster segment multiple times before the midterms. For example, on July 22, the site published a “fact check” of a super PAC ad about Amy Acton. Its opening sentence stated as fact something Acton’s 1994 medical license application — which was highlighted in the ad against Acton — does not show and the super PAC ad never said. Nine paragraphs down, the article admitted the claim came from the Acton campaign. The “fact check” never linked the ad, and its description of the ad matched the Acton campaign’s press release line for line.

But let’s be real — most people don’t read beyond the headline or first paragraph. So if the goal was to create and promote the idea that the ad said something it didn’t — mission accomplished.

That same month, I took apart a https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ “fact check” that said Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-OH) ads misled voters about illegal immigrants getting Medicaid. Again, the “fact check” was easily debunked. I found the same thing each time I examined the website’s work — half the story, one side of the story, published under the words “fact check” despite the content clearly being Democrat propaganda.

The Acton campaign and the Brown campaign put https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ in their campaign materials as though it were a legitimate news outlet. CJR calls sites like this “pink slime” — partisan-run websites dressed up as local news. It counted more than 60 in Ohio, run by operatives of both parties.

CJR reports the buyers of the https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ ads. The list includes the campaign of Governor-elect Amy Acton (D-OH) and WinSenate, a super PAC backing Senator-elect Sherrod Brown (D-OH). CJR put WinSenate’s share alone at $894,000 to $1.06 million. https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ spent about $1,300 promoting itself.
Poe denies his site is pink slime.

The “reporters”

https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ pages state content is “Generated by NorthStar AI” and “AI-generated, newsroom-reviewed.” I sent questions to the site’s “reporters.” I asked three times whether “Dave Miller” — listed as a reporter on the site — is a human being. No one answered that question. I offered to arrange a phone call to discuss a significant omission and false presentation in one of their reports, but “Dave” refused vehemently via email (which read like an AI bot generated it).

I concluded that the bylines are fictitious names, and that AI-generated stories run under them. That is my opinion, based on the site’s own labels and its silence. CJR found 75 names on the site’s author page when it searched on Nov. 10. It identified five as staff and could not verify four of the five. That page was down by Nov. 11. Poe told CJR his staff are real people.

The questions I asked Acton and Pepper

I asked the Acton campaign about https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ. I asked Lieutenant Governor-elect David Pepper (D-OH) specifically — on more than one occasion. I asked what relationship he and Acton have with the site. I asked why their campaign put the site in campaign materials after it was fact-checked multiple times for half-true content, one-sided stories, propaganda and falsities — and after it refused my own credible and customary requests to correct stories.

First the lawyers, then the hit pieces

In the spring, I received two cease-and-desist letters from Elias Law Group, the Acton campaign’s law firm. Marc Elias, the controversial Democrat election lawyer, founded it. In my opinion, the letters were meant to sideline me. I kept reporting.

Then https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ started publishing hit pieces about me. There are many. I am not an elected official. I am not a candidate. I am a reporter who asked questions about Amy Acton, David Pepper, Sherrod Brown and ultimately about https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ and other websites like it that deliver political propaganda to Ohioans.

The site that smeared me is the same site the Acton campaign paid to promote.

The calls and texts

It happened more than once. I’d report on the radio or post on social media. https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ would republish its smear pieces on me. Then I’d receive about a half-dozen robocalls. All were harassing. Some were threatening. One call said the caller was a reporter with https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ. Vulgar text messages were also sent.
I do not know who sent them. I suspect they are connected to https://t.co/9SNaEjHpsQ, and I state that as my suspicion, not as a proven fact. I called and wrote the outlet to inquire about my suspicions, but no one responded.

What comes next

Come January, five of Ohio’s six statewide executive offices belong to Democrats — governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary of state and treasurer.

Acton’s campaign lawyers sent me cease-and-desist letters. When that didn’t chill me, a Democrat operative website that Acton’s campaign paid Facebook to promote published hit pieces on me. I received threatening calls. Then texts. It all happened while Acton was a candidate. What happens to a reporter who asks these questions — and more — when her administration runs the state? What happens to you? Is this what weaponization looks like in Ohio?

Governor-elect Acton, Lieutenant Governor-elect Pepper, Mr. Poe — answer the questions. If you got a robocall or a text message like the ones I described, send it to jack.windsor@theohiopressnetwork.com.

text:
Jeffrey Bagley says he made $450,000 in 2017 running a sex trafficking ring in Ohio. Asked from prison if he was sorry for what happened, he said he was sorry he got caught.

In the video below, a BBC reporter interviews him in an Ohio prison, where he is serving 10 years.

He was convicted in April 2019 after a 17-month investigation. The reporter says he and another man trafficked dozens of women, using drugs to control them.

Bagley says it started with a job offer. He was working construction and getting paid in drugs, with a free house to live in. Then the other man asked if he wanted to change jobs. All he had to do was drive a woman to hotels and make sure she was safe.

"That's pretty much when it all started."

He says each woman brought in $1,000 to $1,500 a day. Within about a year it got big, close to three-quarters of a million dollars, quickly.

"2017 I made $450,000 myself. I would never make that anywhere else."

The reporter stops him there. It could have been your daughter, the reporter says, and you make it sound so transactional. Bagley says he understands the reaction, kind of, and that for so long it was just normal.

Then the question. Sorry you got caught, or sorry for what happened?

"I'm sorry I got caught."

text:
Guns N' Roses' reunion tour grossed $584.2 million, with Axl Rose and Slash back on one stage for the first time since 1993. Izzy Stradlin, Axl's old friend from Indiana who co-wrote Sweet Child o' Mine and Paradise City, was reportedly offered a five-figure fee per show to come out for a few songs.

He said no, because they "didn't want to split the loot equally."

In the video below, from 1992, months after he walked out at the band's peak, Izzy says touring was never the problem. Then he gives the real story: "I had a bus, they had a plane, and I beat 'em to the gig."

He and Axl started the band together, and Izzy wrote or co-wrote most of Appetite for Destruction, the best-selling debut album in US history. In 1991, by his account, the band put a new contract in front of him. "They were gonna cut my percentage of royalties down," he said later. That November he quit.

The case for Axl and Slash: Izzy left in the middle of a world tour, they finished it without him, and the songs he co-wrote still pay him when the band plays them. Slash says they just "couldn't seem to meet eye to eye."

If you walk away from a partnership, get in writing what you are owed if it ever comes back, because a reunion is new money and nobody has to save you a seat.

So did Izzy price himself out of a $584 million tour, or did Axl and Slash offer the man who co-wrote their biggest songs a session player's fee?

text:
FAQ: Is Robinhood (or Coinbase) “gambling”?
Q: Isn’t Robinhood for stocks and Coinbase for crypto—not gambling?
A: Generally, yes. Most stock and crypto trading is regulated as financial activity, not “gambling.”

Q: So why would a Louisiana AG lawsuit list Robinhood or Coinbase?
A: Some platforms also offer or connect users to products that a state may argue function like wagers (for example, certain event-based contracts, “prediction market” style products, or derivatives). A lawsuit usually targets the specific product/offering and how it’s marketed and made available in the state, not the entire platform.

Q: What’s the legal test Louisiana cares about?
A: States typically look at whether something is a wager (stake + chance/event outcome + payout) and whether the operator is properly licensed/authorized. (Exact definitions and exceptions are state-specific.)

Q: Does this lawsuit mean investing is illegal in Louisiana?
A: No. Securities investing through regulated brokers is legal. The dispute is about whether certain offerings are unlawful gambling under state law.

Q: How should the public talk about this without spreading misinformation?
A: Focus on verifiable facts:

What specific product is being challenged?
What statute/regulation is cited?
What remedy is requested (TRO/injunction/penalties)?
Avoid claiming intent (e.g., “they’re trying to keep [group] poor”) unless you can back it up with evidence.
Q: What should users do if they’re concerned?
A: Read the complaint/press release, check whether the product is available in Louisiana, and watch for court orders or platform notices. If you lost money or believe you were misled, keep receipts and consider talking to a licensed attorney.

Three Kansas offensive linemen. Four seasons. Three different paths to the next level.

Since their freshman year these three have often been compared with one another. They’ve competed in different programs and built their own identities, but each has spent the past four years helping his team move the ball.

@WarrickJaymes | @SC_MustangFB  | @UCMFootballTeam 
A four-year varsity player, Warrick helped anchor a Salina Central offensive line that produced a state championship in 2025. He started at right tackle during that championship season before moving to left tackle as a senior. Over the four seasons reflected here, the Mustangs accounted for 17,547 total yards, including 9,340 rushing and 8,207 passing.

@NolanH72 | @MaizeHSFootball | @SDCoyotesFB 
Nolan stepped into the varsity lineup as a freshman and developed into a versatile lineman capable of playing across the front. A Kansas powerlifting state champion, he brings strength and mobility to the position. Over the same four-season span, Maize accounted for 14,205 total yards, including 7,386 rushing and 6,819 passing.

@MaddoxMcG2027 | @NWGRIZZLYFB | @UCMFootballTeam 
Maddox has been part of a Wichita Northwest offense known for putting up yards on the ground. A physical interior lineman who takes pride in finishing blocks, he helped pave the way for 11,869 rushing yards over the four seasons reflected here. Northwest accounted for 18,212 total yards overall, including 6,343 passing.

What makes this comparison interesting?

These three have been compared since they were freshmen, but they haven’t played in identical offenses. Each has had to help his team succeed in its own way—opening lanes in the run game, protecting the quarterback and adapting to what the offense needs.

That raises a question for coaches and football fans: When you evaluate an offensive lineman, what stands out most—film, consistency, versatility, physical traits or team production?

The team numbers offer one part of the story. The film shows what each player did to help make those numbers possible.

Three players who have been compared for years are now headed to the next level: Nolan to South Dakota, and Warrick and Maddox to Central Missouri.

Congratulations to all three on the work they’ve put in and what they’ve helped their teams accomplish. Looking forward to seeing what comes next. 🏈

text:
February 2012. The Atlantic Council publishes a paper called "Seeking National Responsibility for Cyber Attacks," and if you read it now knowing what came after, it has the uncomfortable quality of a document that was right about everything and largely ignored anyway.

The core problem the paper was trying to solve: there was no agreed framework for deciding when a cyber attack was actually a state act. Physical attacks have centuries of doctrine behind them. Cyber had almost none. And state actors, it turns out, are very good at exploiting gaps like that.

The Atlantic Council's answer was a three-tier model, and the architecture is worth understanding in detail because it became the template for most serious attribution debates that followed.

At the top: "state-ordered" attacks. The government, as a matter of explicit policy, directs third-party actors, proxies, criminal groups, contracted hackers, to conduct operations on its behalf. The state is the author. The proxy is the instrument. The deniability is thin but deliberately maintained. This is the category that matters most because it represents the most calculated use of the attribution gap, and by 2012 Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea were all running operations that fit cleanly into it.

The middle tier covered states providing material support or training to actors who then operated with some degree of independence. The state isn't issuing specific operational orders, but it's building the capability and pointing it in a direction. The legal and policy questions here are harder because the causal chain is longer, but the strategic logic from the sponsor's perspective is similar: strategic benefit, reduced fingerprints.

The bottom tier, and the most contentious: states that simply tolerate known cyber criminals operating from their territory and decline to prosecute them. Russia has lived in this category for decades, running a kind of implicit arrangement where criminal groups with obvious technical sophistication operate openly, don't touch domestic targets, and find themselves unbothered by law enforcement. The paper was asking: does deliberate failure to act constitute a form of state responsibility? The answer it suggested was yes, at some threshold, and that remains contested to this day.

What made the paper genuinely useful wasn't just the taxonomy. It was the explicit argument that the international community needed consensus norms around state cyber responsibility analogous to the norms governing state sponsorship of terrorism. That analogy is instructive. The terrorism sponsorship doctrine took decades to develop and is still imperfect, but it gave states a shared vocabulary and a set of consequences that could attach to behavior. Without something similar for cyber, you got exactly what the paper predicted: systematic exploitation of the attribution gap, with state actors conducting or enabling damaging operations while evading the diplomatic and legal consequences that would follow if the same damage had been caused by a missile or a soldier.

The Congressional Research Service compilation "Cybersecurity: Selected Cyberattacks, 2012-2025" treats 2012 as a period of significant escalation across all four of the main state-sponsored threat actors. That's not coincidence or noise. The operational tempo was increasing in part because the cost of getting caught remained low. Attribution was hard, consensus on consequences was nonexistent, and the gap between what states could do in cyberspace and what could actually be done about it was wide enough to drive operations of considerable scale through.

The FBIIC was developing parallel thinking on state responsibility at the same time, which tells you something about the moment. Multiple institutions, working separately, were arriving at similar conclusions about a problem that the policy world had been slow to treat seriously.

There's a particular irony in the proxy model that the Atlantic Council's framework identified. The use of criminal groups, hackers-for-hire, and nationalist volunteers creates a situation where the sponsoring state gets strategic effect while the operational actors face essentially none of the deterrence that might constrain a uniformed military unit or an intelligence officer operating under state authority. The proxies often don't care about international law because they have no standing in it. The sponsoring state can claim ignorance or deny control. Everyone involved understands the arrangement perfectly well, and the fiction of non-attribution serves all of them.

The paper's recommendation, that something like a terrorism-sponsorship norm framework needed to be built for cyber, was the right call. The problem is that building those norms requires the states most invested in exploiting the gap to participate in closing it, and they haven't had much incentive to do so. Russia and China in particular have preferred to push alternative frameworks in international forums, ones that emphasize sovereignty and non-interference in ways that happen to protect their own operational freedom while doing little about the specific problem of state-sponsored attacks on other countries' infrastructure.

Twelve years on from the Atlantic Council paper, the tiered attribution model it proposed is essentially the standard analytical vocabulary. When analysts and governments talk about whether an attack was state-ordered, state-supported, or state-tolerated, they're working in the architecture that paper sketched out. The norms question is less settled. There has been real progress, the UN Group of Governmental Experts processes produced some agreed principles, the Tallinn Manual provided legal analysis, various states have started publicly attributing attacks with more specificity and consequence. But the fundamental exploitation of the attribution gap that the paper warned about is still ongoing and in many respects more sophisticated than it was in 2012.

The documented cases that accumulated through 2012 and the years after showed something the paper had anticipated but perhaps underestimated: the gap wasn't just being exploited opportunistically. It was being exploited systematically, as a matter of strategic doctrine, by states that had concluded cyber operations offered a way to achieve geopolitical objectives at costs that remained, for a long time, acceptably low.

That calculus has shifted somewhat. Public attribution has become more common and more credible. Sanctions and indictments have attached real costs to specific individuals and entities. Some proxy groups have found their infrastructure disrupted or their members arrested in third countries. But the basic structural problem the Atlantic Council identified in February 2012, that the gap between what states can do in cyberspace and what can be done about it creates persistent incentives for exploitation, hasn't been closed. It's been narrowed in places, formalized in others, and contested constantly, but not closed.

The paper deserves credit for seeing clearly what was coming and for providing a framework that actually held up under pressure. Attribution doctrine in 2025 still looks recognizably like what a careful reader of that 2012 paper would have expected, which is either a compliment to the analysts who wrote it or a commentary on how slowly the policy world moves. Probably both.

text:
A government promises better services without asking citizens to pay the full cost today. It borrows the difference.

The services are visible now. The bill is spread across future budgets.

Borrowing can be sensible. A country facing a crisis may need to protect people and support the economy. A long-lived infrastructure project can benefit future generations as well as today's taxpayers. The question is not whether public debt is always bad. It is what happens when borrowing becomes the routine way to avoid choices that the political system does not want to make.

First, distinguish a deficit from a debt. A deficit is the gap over a period when public spending exceeds revenue. Debt is the accumulated stock of outstanding obligations, measured according to a particular definition. A country can have a deficit while its debt ratio falls under some conditions; debt also changes for reasons beyond the deficit alone.

France offers a concrete example of the scale of the debate. INSEE reported (https://t.co/mGlUqIOXTP) a general government deficit of 5.1% of GDP for 2025. In a separate release, it reported Maastricht public debt at 119.0% of GDP at the end of the second quarter of 2026 (https://t.co/9DMHLTxsbM). These are different measures for different periods. The debt figure is gross debt under the Maastricht definition; it is not a household credit-card balance or a complete measure of the state's assets.

Those figures do not tell us, on their own, whether every euro was spent well, which policy caused the deficit or what adjustment should come next. They do tell us that the gap between public commitments and resources deserves an honest explanation.

Consider a hypothetical government with three options. It can raise revenue, reduce or change spending, or borrow. Each choice has costs. Higher taxes can affect households and businesses. Spending cuts can damage services people rely on. Borrowing creates interest obligations and requires future refinancing.

The political appeal of borrowing is that it can delay part of the conflict. A government can support a program today while leaving future governments to decide how to finance the accumulated obligations. Citizens receive a benefit now; the cost is less visible because it appears across later budgets.

That incentive does not mean every deficit is an electoral trick. A recession can reduce tax revenue and increase demand for assistance without a government choosing to expand a program. A war, pandemic or natural disaster can require exceptional spending. Borrowing during a shock may be less harmful than withdrawing support when people need it most.

The problem is treating an exceptional tool as an explanation for a permanent mismatch. If spending and revenue repeatedly diverge, someone should explain why, which commitments are being financed and how the government expects to manage the obligations over time.

Interest matters because it competes with other uses of public money. A government that pays more to service its debt has less room, all else equal, for other priorities unless it raises revenue or borrows more. The effect of higher rates is not necessarily immediate: governments refinance debt over time, and the cost depends on maturity, existing rates and market conditions.

The IMF has examined (https://t.co/cbnyoclLof) how higher rates can put more pressure on public finances, especially when debt is already high. That is a risk, not a prediction that any one country will face a particular crisis on a particular date.

There is also a question of what the borrowed money buys. Financing maintenance that prevents a major failure is different from repeatedly covering a program whose costs are poorly understood. Building a useful asset is different from funding a project chosen mainly because it looks impressive at an announcement.

Those categories are not always easy to separate. Current spending can have lasting value: paying teachers, maintaining hospitals or supporting research can benefit a society for years. An infrastructure project can be wasteful. The test is the expected benefit, the evidence and the full cost—not whether the spending is called “investment.”

Citizens should be able to see more than a total debt figure. What are the government's annual revenues and expenses? How much is spent on interest? What commitments have been made for the future? Which programs are producing results, and which have not been evaluated?

A government should also explain the trade-offs in its plan. If it proposes to reduce a deficit, which taxes or services will change? If it expects growth to improve the ratio of debt to GDP, what assumptions support that expectation? If it borrows for a project, what will be built, maintained and evaluated?

A single household analogy can clarify that interest and repayment matter. It can also mislead if it suggests a state operates exactly like a household. Governments have taxing power, issue debt under different conditions and influence the economy through their decisions. Those differences do not remove budget constraints; they make the analysis more complex.

The public debate often swings between two slogans: debt does not matter, or every borrowed euro is a disaster. Neither tells us whether a particular policy is justified or whether the institutions using debt are accountable for its results.

Borrowing can buy time and productive capacity. It can also buy political convenience by pushing a difficult choice into the future.

When debt becomes the fuel that keeps a system running, the essential question is what that system delivers in return—and who will be asked to pay when the bill becomes harder to postpone.

text:
A college freshman shot his classmate twice in the head while the boy begged for his life  then dragged the body into a ditch, covered it with dirt and a stick, and walked home down a dark country road. His reason: he wanted to know what it felt like to kill someone. He never spent a day in prison.

His name is Jerrod Murray. He and Generro Sanchez were both 18, both freshmen at East Central University in Oklahoma. Murray knocked on Generro’s dorm door and asked for a ride to Walmart  offered $20 for gas. Generro, who friends say always saw the good in everyone, said yes.

In the Walmart parking lot, Murray pulled out a stolen .40-caliber handgun and ordered Generro to drive north, out of town. On a dark country road, he fired. The first shot missed. The second hit Generro in the head. The truck drifted off the road and slammed into a tree.

Hours later, a deputy spotted a young man walking alone on the highway at 3 a.m. and drew his gun. Murray didn’t run. He said: “I am the guy you’re trying to find.”

In the interrogation room, he sits in a suit and tie and explains, without a flicker of emotion, how he chose his victim. Not someone he hated  someone he figured nobody would miss. Why Generro? “He would have had the least impact. He didn’t have many friends.” Any remorse? “No.” What should happen to him? “Death sentence, sir.”

He never got one. In 2015, a judge found Jerrod Murray not guilty by reason of insanity. Instead of prison, he was sent to a state mental health facility. The district attorney put it flatly: “Nobody has been accountable for this crime.” Generro’s mother said her son had dreams and Jerrod crushed them.

So here’s what splits people: should “insanity” ever be a defense for a killer who calmly planned his murder, picked the victim he thought no one would miss, and felt nothing  or did a cold, deliberate choice just get called a sickness?

🇷🇺|The Kremlin Meeting Was Not a Negotiation. It Was a Receipt for a War Washington Cannot Win.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived at the Kremlin on 12 November 2026 for talks with President Vladimir Putin. The Russian readout, carried by TASS, RIA Novosti, Kommersant, and Channel One, describes a meeting that lasted approximately two and a half hours. The Russian delegation included Yuri Ushakov, Vladimir Medinsky, and Kirill Dmitriev, the head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, who met the Americans at Vnukovo Airport and accompanied them to the Kremlin.

What Putin Actually Said

The Russian president's statements, as recorded by Kommersant and Channel One, are the operative record of the meeting.

On the war's end: Putin stated that Russia has only one line of demarcation with Ukraine the state border. Moscow is aware of the Ukrainian side raising the question of "grey zones," but for Russia, the border is the only line.

On foreign troops: Putin stated that foreign troops on Ukrainian territory will be a legitimate target for the Russian Armed Forces. Their presence threatens Russia's national security, and Moscow has opposed this scenario from the start.

On territories: Putin stated that in the territorial question, people matter more than territory. The territorial issue will be discussed, but the priority is the population living there.

On the humanitarian track: Putin proposed organizing a humanitarian mission in Konstantinovka, by analogy with the earlier operation in Aleshki. Russia controls Konstantinovka and is ready to ensure the mission's security. Russia needs five days to demine the area around the city. If Kyiv believes it controls the city, it must ensure the mission's security from its side. About 400-500 civilians remain in Konstantinovka, and Putin suggested inviting foreign media, including from the US.

On Europe: Putin stated that Russia has never been against dialogue with Europe. He would like the US to work with the Europeans so they decide whether they want peace or war. Trump has proposed agreeing on a security system in Europe, but the Europeans are refusing this proposal.

On Trump: Putin asked Witkoff to convey gratitude to Donald Trump for organizing contacts between Russia and Ukraine, and gratitude to Melania Trump for her participation in resolving the humanitarian issue around Aleshki.

What Witkoff and Kushner Said

Witkoff stated that the upcoming prisoner exchange between Russia and Ukraine indicates progress in the settlement. He stated that the Europeans did not participate in the Abu Dhabi talks but were informed of the contacts. He said he would convey information about the Moscow contacts to Vladimir Zelensky.

Kushner stated that the US has begun discussing the architecture of security on the continent with the Europeans. The Americans see that Europe wants to participate in the negotiations and end the conflict. Trump asked to convey to Putin that it is very important to complete the conflict in Ukraine as quickly as possible.

The Chinese Read: The "Major Disagreements" the Kremlin Meeting Did Not Resolve

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that the Abu Dhabi trilateral talks produced an agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange, but that "major disagreements" remain on Ukraine's security guarantees and the future security architecture of Europe.

Xinhua reported that Kushner stated in Abu Dhabi that the Russia-Ukraine talks had agreed to the largest prisoner release to date, with the specific number to be finalized on 12 November.

The Chinese readout confirms the structure of the meeting: the humanitarian track produced a deliverable, the prisoner exchange while the security architecture remains unresolved. Putin's proposal for a humanitarian mission in Konstantinovka is the second humanitarian deliverable that the Kremlin is offering. It is a test of whether the Ukrainian side will cooperate on a civilian operation while the political talks remain deadlocked.

The Russian Position That Washington Cannot Answer

The Russian readout contains a structural demand that the US cannot meet without abandoning its own position.

The state border is the only line. Putin's statement rules out the "grey zones" and the frozen-contact-line models that the US and Ukraine have floated. Russia is saying the territorial question will be settled on the basis of the border, not on the basis of a ceasefire line.

Foreign troops are a legitimate target. This is the direct answer to the European proposal for a "reassurance force" or a "coalition of the willing" deployed to Ukraine. Putin is stating that any such force will be engaged by the Russian military, which means the US and Europe cannot offer Ukraine a security guarantee that involves troops on the ground without accepting a direct confrontation with Russia.

Europe must choose peace or war. Putin's formulation places the responsibility for the continuation of the war on the Europeans, not on Russia. The US is asked to deliver the European decision. That is the opposite of the Western narrative, which places the responsibility for the war on Russia.

The Contrast: What Washington Brings and What Russia Brings

Washington brings: Witkoff, a real estate developer with no diplomatic credential. Kushner, whose Affinity Partners holds $2 billion from the Saudi PIF plus money from Lunate and Qatari entities. The US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, signed 30 April 2025, giving the US a 50 per cent share of revenue from newly issued Ukrainian mineral, oil, and gas extraction licences. The frozen Russian assets at Euroclear roughly €210 billion with the windfall profits taxed at 99.7 per cent.

Russia brings: a humanitarian mission in Konstantinovka, with five days of demining, 400-500 civilians to be protected, and an invitation to foreign media including US journalists. A prisoner exchange that the Russian side is facilitating. A state border that Russia says is the only line. A demand that Europe choose peace or war.

One side is dividing the assets. The other side is organizing a humanitarian corridor and inviting the other side's journalists to film it.

The Bill

The meeting: Putin, Witkoff, Kushner at the Kremlin, 12 November 2026, approximately two and a half hours. The Russian delegation: Ushakov, Medinsky, Dmitriev.

Putin's position: the state border is the only line. Foreign troops are a legitimate target. People matter more than territory. A humanitarian mission in Konstantinovka with five days of demining and 400-500 civilians. Europe must choose peace or war. Gratitude to Trump and Melania Trump.

Witkoff and Kushner: the prisoner exchange is progress. The Europeans were informed but did not participate in Abu Dhabi. Information will be conveyed to Zelensky. The US has begun discussing European security architecture with the Europeans. Trump wants the conflict completed as quickly as possible.

The Chinese read: a large-scale prisoner exchange agreed, with "major disagreements" on security guarantees and Europe's future security architecture.

The contrast: Washington brings a 50 per cent minerals fund and €210 billion in frozen assets. Russia brings a humanitarian corridor, a prisoner exchange, and an invitation to US journalists to film the demining.

The bill is being paid in a meeting where one side is dividing the assets and the other side is organizing a corridor, and the receipt is a Kremlin readout that mentions "eternal peace" while the Western readout mentions "progress" and "security architecture."

text:
In April 1966, U.S. Army Private First Class Clark Richie was photographed pressing a letter against his face while serving in Vietnam, taking in the familiar scent of perfume sent by his girlfriend in Jay, Oklahoma. Captured by Associated Press photographer John Nance, the touching moment revealed a deeply personal side of the war. Thousands of miles from home and surrounded by the dangers of combat, a simple scented letter offered a brief connection to love, familiarity, and the life he had left behind.

Throughout the Vietnam War, handwritten letters served as an emotional lifeline for American soldiers stationed overseas. Before instant messaging and video calls, troops often waited weeks to hear from family, friends, and loved ones. Every delivery brought the possibility of photographs, personal stories, and comforting reminders of home. This photograph remains a powerful symbol of the human experience of war, showing how something as ordinary as a letter could momentarily erase the distance between a soldier and the person he longed to see again.

text:
Judith Slaying Holofernes (1612–1613), an iconic Baroque oil painting by the Italian artist Artemisia Gentileschi, currently housed in the Museo di Capodimonte in Naples, Italy (with a later version from c. 1620 residing in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence)...

Based on the deuterocanonical Book of Judith from the Old Testament, the scene depicts the Israelite widow Judith and her maidservant Abra assassinating the Assyrian general Holofernes to save her besieged city.

Heavily influenced by Caravaggio’s use of chiaroscuro (dramatic contrasts of light and dark), Gentileschi portrays the physical struggle with gritty realism, showing the coordinated effort required to overpower the general.

Art historians often note how Gentileschi’s visceral, powerful depictions of female triumph and vengeance mirror her own life—including her public trial after being sexually assaulted by Agostino Tassi, a colleague of her father Orazio.

. . . 

The story of Judith comes from the deuterocanonical Book of Judith in the Bible... 

The Assyrian general Holofernes, serving King Nebuchadnezzar, led a massive army to conquer Judea and besieged the Jewish city of Bethulia. Holofernes cut off the city's water supply and food sources, pushing the desperate townspeople to the brink of surrender.

Judith, a pious, wealthy, and courageous Jewish widow, lost patience with the leaders' lack of faith. She dressed in her finest clothes, left the city with her loyal maidservant Abra, and walked straight into the Assyrian camp. Judith claimed she wanted to help the Assyrians win and offered false intelligence, quickly charming Holofernes and winning his trust.

Holofernes invited Judith into his private tent for a celebratory feast, drinking heavily to impress her until he passed out into a drunken stupor. Seizing his own sword, Judith prayed for strength, severed Holofernes's head, and handed it to Abra, who placed it in a food sack. 

The two women slipped out of the camp undetected and returned to Bethulia with the severed head. Displaying the general's head on the city walls, the leaderless Assyrian army panicked and was completely routed by the Israelites.

text:
On 6 May 2025 WeightWatchers, the company that spent 62 years teaching women to count their dinner, filed for bankruptcy in a court in Delaware to get rid of $1.15 billion of debt.

Sixty-two years of points. You'd think they'd be better at sums.

It landed in Britain in 1967. Church halls. Community centres. Weeknight weigh-ins in front of a room full of strangers, shoes off, earrings off, holding your breath like that makes you lighter. Since 2007 the NHS has been referring patients to commercial slimming clubs, so some of us were sent there by the bloody surgery.

And here's the bit that should make every woman who ever stood on those scales spit her low-fat yoghurt across the room. Their own former finance director, Richard Samber, who had the job from 1968 to 1993, explained it on the BBC in 2013: "It's successful because the other 84% have to come back and do it again. That's where your business comes from."

The company denied that's the model, obviously. Course it did.

But an Oxford academic who went through the company's own five-year figures said only about 16% of its best members were still at their goal weight. The rest came back. And paid again.

So what does a business built on women being hungry do once it's been through the bankruptcy court? Finds a new way to charge women for being hungry. On 8 September 2025 it launched WeightWatchers for Menopause in America, with a celebrity spokeswoman, a "tailored version" of the points, and prescriptions on offer, GLP-1 jabs included.

You couldn't make this shit up. They didn't have to. It's in their own press release.

Me, I don't count a bloody thing. Meat, fish, eggs, butter and fat when I'm hungry, and I stop when I'm not. No snacks. No points. No weigh-in. No fee.

The women never failed the diet. Failing was the subscription.

text:
$VLO $MPC $PSX $DK $CLMT CITGO PETROLEUM Q3 2026: A RECORD QUARTER, A QUIET GUIDE CUT, AND A SALE THAT NOW LOOKS CHEAP

Citgo Petroleum reported the best quarter in its history on November 12, 2026, and quietly cut its full-year guide below a private guide circulated to investors in October. The print also sharpens the fight over the court-ordered sale of the company: the approved cash bid now sits below one year of guided earnings.

THE PRINT

• Q3 2026 net income was $2,199 million, the best quarterly earnings in company history. EBITDA was $3,008 million and Adjusted EBITDA $2,958 million (the $50 million difference is a LIFO inventory permanent dip item). The bridge to EBITDA is exact: $2,199 million of net income, less $18 million of net interest income, plus $657 million of tax expense and $170 million of depreciation and amortization, equals $3,008 million. Source: Citgo's Q3 2026 release, PR Newswire, 2026-11-12.
• Q3 net income is 2.35 times Q2 2026's $936 million. Year-ago Q3 2025 net income was $167 million and EBITDA $363 million, so the quarter is about 13 times the year-ago profit.
• Nine months 2026: net income $3,292 million, EBITDA $4,757 million, Adjusted EBITDA $4,713 million. Year-to-date Adjusted EBITDA of $4.7 billion already exceeds the company's previous full-year record, set in 2022.
• The full quarterly net income path: 1Q25 -$82M, 2Q25 $100M, 3Q25 $167M, 4Q25 $268M, 1Q26 $157M, 2Q26 $936M, 3Q26 $2,199M. The 2025 quarters sum to $453M against the reported full-year $452M (a $1M rounding difference in the company's own tables); the 2026 quarters sum exactly to the reported nine-month figure.

OPERATIONS: THE RECORDS ARE REAL, AND ONE BLOOMBERG WORDING IS IMPRECISE

• Total refinery throughput was 904,000 bpd, up 10 percent on Q2's 820,000 bpd. The crude-only rate was a quarterly record 855,000 bpd, which is 103 percent of rated crude capacity. Bloomberg wrote that the plants "processed nearly 900,000 barrels of crude each day": the 904,000 figure is total throughput including other feedstocks and blendstocks, and it is just over, not nearly, 900,000. The crude figure is 855,000 bpd.
• Distillate production set a combined record of 365,000 bpd, led by a Lake Charles distillate record of 208,000 bpd. Corpus Christi set a quarterly crude rate record of 176,000 bpd. Marketing volume was 411,000 bpd.
• Rated capacity: Citgo's own profile gives Lake Charles 479,000 bpd, Lemont 183,000 bpd, Corpus Christi 167,000 bpd, totaling exactly the 829,000 bpd the release uses (the step-up from 807,000 bpd was documented in the Q3 2025 release). The EIA Refinery Capacity Report (January 1, 2026, calendar-day atmospheric basis) gives 471,200 + 188,023 + 165,000 = 824,223 bpd. The difference is basis and timing, not error; the company's rated figure is the denominator behind the 103 percent.
• Per-refinery throughput for Q3 2026 is not disclosed in the release. A specialist newsletter citing state data puts Corpus Christi at a record roughly 177,000 bpd, Lake Charles around 510,000 bpd through August, and Lemont at about 190,000 bpd. Single source.

WHERE THE MONEY CAME FROM: LAKE CHARLES CARRIED THE QUARTER

• Management-estimated refinery EBITDA, Q3 2026: Lake Charles $1,873M, Corpus Christi $721M, Lemont $568M, total refining $3,162M. Non-refining was negative $51M (Product Supply negative $133M against Terminals and Pipelines $61M, Marketing $13M, Lubricants $8M), corporate negative $103M, and the pieces tie exactly to consolidated EBITDA of $3,008M.
• Against Q2's split (Lake Charles $780M, Corpus Christi $324M, Lemont $267M), Lake Charles alone supplied about 61 percent of the quarter-over-quarter refining EBITDA increase ($1,093M of $1,791M), and the two Gulf Coast plants together supplied about 83 percent ($1,490M of $1,791M). On a nine-month view Lake Charles is $3,244M of the $5,171M total refining EBITDA, about 63 percent. This is a Gulf Coast distillate print: record crude rates and record distillate output sold into the distillate-led margin spike.
• The release cites no crack benchmark and no capture rate. The only margin figure in the company's recent releases is an average refining gross margin of $11.48 per barrel for full-year 2025, and that figure is available only through a PDVSA ad hoc board summary of the release, not the release text itself. Single source. Market context from trade coverage: benchmark US crack spreads averaged about $63 per barrel in Q3 2026 against about $50 in Q2 and about $26 a year earlier, and US Gulf Coast margins hit an all-time high of about $72 per barrel in September on a Dallas Fed estimate.
• Reuters adds that Citgo has ramped up purchases of Venezuelan crude this year. Single source.

CASH, DEBT, AND SPENDING

• The company built $2.0 billion of cash in Q3 and ended September 30 with $4.9 billion of liquidity including full availability under the $500M receivables securitization facility (derived cash about $4.4 billion; the release states liquidity, not a standalone cash balance). Q2 liquidity was $2.9 billion, so the $2.0 billion step ties.
• The Q3 release discloses no debt balance, no repayment, and no dividend. The standing debt picture: at December 31, 2025 gross debt had been cut $1.825 billion during 2025 to a negative net debt position of about $795 million (cash above debt), and Fitch (August 3, 2026) treats the $1.1 billion 8.375 percent senior secured notes due January 15, 2029 as the only outstanding notes, covered by the cash balance.
• Q3 spending was light against the print: $50 million of turnarounds and catalyst, $128 million of capital projects. Full-year 2026 capex plus turnaround and catalyst is projected at $856 million, a second small trim after Q2 cut the forecast from $985 million to $867 million. The $128 million includes the Corpus Christi crude fractionation and yield improvement project, expected to be mechanically complete in December 2026 with startup in early January 2027.

GUIDANCE: THE LADDER, AND THE RECONCILIATION

Full-year 2026 EBITDA guidance, in order:

• May 2026, with Q1 results: $3.2B to $3.6B (year-end cash $3.5B to $3.9B).
• August 13, 2026, with Q2 results: about $5.8B (year-end cash about $5.7B), based on late-July forward curves.
• October 16, 2026, circulated privately to investors and reported by Bloomberg on October 19: $7.7B to $8.0B, with cash of about $5.6B at October 15 and a preliminary nine-month EBITDA range of $4.5B to $4.8B. Every non-Bloomberg account of this document traces to the single Bloomberg story, so it counts as one origin. What the document formally was (noteholder presentation or informal update) is not specified in any source found.
• November 12, 2026, official with Q3 results: $7.2B to $7.5B (year-end cash $6.7B to $7.0B), explicitly based on prices and forward curves as of early November, assuming no material working capital change.

Reconciliation of the private October guide against the official guide:

• Same measure. Both are labeled full-year 2026 EBITDA, and the October document's preliminary nine-month range of $4.5B to $4.8B brackets the reported nine-month EBITDA of $4,757M. The reported nine-month figure is from the release; the October range itself rests on the single Bloomberg story.
• The official guide is $0.5B lower at both ends, and the entire gap sits in implied Q4: $2,443M to $2,743M implied by the official guide against $2,943M to $3,243M implied by the October document (both less the same actual nine-month $4,757M). The official side of that arithmetic is release-verified; the October side carries the weaker, single-origin sourcing. On an Adjusted EBITDA base ($4,713M) the official implied Q4 is $2,487M to $2,787M; the release labels the guide "EBITDA" while headlining the adjusted year-to-date figure, a $44M labeling wrinkle worth noting wherever implied Q4 is used.
• The step-down is explained on the company's own stated basis: the official guide is marked to early-November curves, the private one to mid-October, nearer the margin peak. The price path is consistent (the EIA weekly retail diesel benchmark peaked at $6.529 on September 21, 2026 and was $6.127 by November 9). Attributing the full $0.5B to the curve move is an inference.
• One tension does not resolve: the October document's $5.6B of cash at October 15 sits above the September 30 liquidity of $4.9B (derived cash about $4.4B). Either cash built about $1.2B in the first half of October, or the private document's "cash" was a broader liquidity-style measure. No source found settles it.

THE SALE: NOTHING HAS MOVED, AND THE PRINT SHARPENS THE FIGHT WITHOUT CHANGING ANY TERM

• What is being sold: the shares of PDV Holding, Inc., Citgo's Delaware parent, in the Crystallex v. Venezuela enforcement proceedings in the District of Delaware. Judge Stark approved Amber Energy's bid on November 25, 2025 and signed the sale order on November 29, 2025 (Document 2556, read directly). Cash consideration is $5.892 billion of judgments extinguished, plus a Transaction Support Agreement providing about $2.125 billion for holders of the PDVSA 2020 bonds, for a total package of roughly $8.0 billion. The $5.9 billion headline is the cash bid for the shares only.
• Appeal: Venezuela, PDVSA, PDVH and Citgo appealed on December 1, 2025. The Third Circuit heard argument on October 21, 2026 (judges Restrepo, Porter, Matey) on conflict-of-interest, procedural and valuation grounds; PDVSA's counsel argued the bid sits about $7 billion below the court adviser's Evercore valuation and about $12 billion below Venezuela's expert figure. The court had not ruled as of November 6, 2026, and no stay is in place. The court also refused to hold the appeal in abeyance for repayment talks, and the United States told the court on October 13, 2026 that it had no views to express at that time. The allegations are contested and are not findings.
• Closing gates: the sale can close seven days after OFAC issues a specific license. No license has been granted (Reuters, 2026-11-12). Amber's own Third Circuit filing states its financing arrangements expire in April 2027 with, in its words, a vanishingly small chance of further extension. The expiry is Amber's representation in advocacy.
• The collateral side track is a different clock: on October 27, 2026 the Second Circuit upheld the validity of the PDVSA 2020 bonds (about $2.859 billion, 8.5 percent) and their pledge of 50.1 percent of Citgo Holding, and OFAC's GL 5AA (November 4, 2026) then moved the bond collateral authorization date to December 18, 2026. That is not a sale closing date. Separately, GL 52C (September 14, 2026) refuses to authorize changes to the governance of PDVH, Citgo Holding or Citgo Petroleum.
• The Q3 release contains no mention of the sale, the appeal, or OFAC.
• The comparison the appellants are already making in court: Venezuela's October 1, 2026 abeyance motion argued that even the August guide of $5.8B made expected 2026 earnings "essentially the same as Amber's headline $5.9 billion bid." The official guide of $7.2B to $7.5B now exceeds the $5.892B cash consideration, the guided year-end cash of $6.7B to $7.0B also exceeds it, and the full roughly $8.0B package is about 1.11 times one peak year of guided EBITDA at the low end of the guide and 1.07 times at the high end. This strengthens the appellants' optical argument; it changes no legal ground (the appeal is process, conflicts and procedure) and no price mechanism was found in any source.
• Buyer plans on record: in April 2026 Reuters reported Amber CEO Greg Goff promising $11 billion of investment if the sale closes, including about $1 billion to add 125,000 bpd at Corpus Christi, about $500 million of coking at Lemont, and about $250 million of premium gasoline capacity at Lake Charles. Single source (Reuters, read in syndication).
• Fitch flags the closing risks underneath: change-of-control provisions in the 2029 notes could force a refinancing, plus OFAC timing and new-owner policy.

WHAT X ADDED, AND WHAT IT DID NOT

• The print traces cleanly: Citgo's release post (2120868941950075114, 13:18:54Z), Bloomberg's business post, then Reuters correspondent Marianna Párraga's thread (head post 2120914057113080165, 16:18:10Z) adding the year-ago $167M comparison, the $4.9B quarter-end liquidity, and the live posture: appeals decision pending after the October hearing, Treasury has not greenlit Amber's offer, and rebid arguments based on increased valuation "gaining traction" (parties unnamed). Tom Kloza's first post on the print carried the release's $3B best-ever adjusted EBITDA, $4.7B year-to-date EBITDA, and 904,000 bpd total input (2120901493012283549). Capture caveat: the Kloza post and the Párraga thread posts were captured through a mirror fallback after the X API single-post route timed out, so their text is checked against the mirror capture and the underlying release and wire figures, not against a direct API read. The rebid-traction line is a correspondent's characterization, single source.
• The deal-risk narrative on X is thin: a second Bloomberg item (bond traders betting the windfall imperils the $5.9B deal) reached X only in Chinese and Turkish amplification. No creditor, bidder, or Elliott or Amber account speaks in its own voice anywhere in the sweeps; OPIS official, Sparta and Argus accounts are silent on the print.
• A "$15 to $20B equity value" figure circulates from one account with no citation and near-zero reach. Single source, unsupported.
• One amplification error caught: a Spanish-language account understated net income a thousandfold ("2,2 millones"). Noted so it is never repeated.

CONTEXT CHECKS ON THE BLOOMBERG ARTICLE'S FRAMING

• Diesel above $6: AAA's national average on November 12, 2026 was $6.0977 per gallon; the EIA survey for November 9 was $6.127. The two peak prints are different series and are not in conflict: the AAA daily record was $6.5276 on September 22, 2026, and the EIA weekly benchmark topped at $6.529 on September 21, 2026.
• "About 60 percent more than when the war began": a 60 percent rise to about $6.10 implies a baseline near $3.81, inside the observed pre-war range (AAA-based reporting puts diesel near $3.73 to $3.75 in November 2025). The exact late-February 2026 war-start baseline was not pulled at a primary source.
• Big Oil's "$50 billion plus of windfall profits": the five largest Western majors' combined Q3 2026 net income exceeded $50 billion (ExxonMobil $15.4B, Chevron $9.9B, Shell $12.1B, TotalEnergies $8.3B, plus BP). It is one quarter's combined net income, not a cumulative war total, and "windfall" is the article's framing.

THE READ

• This is peak realized capture, confirmed at the primary source, from the complex best positioned for it: Gulf Coast weighted, distillate long, running at 103 percent of rated crude capacity with record distillate output. It validates the refining margin story; it says nothing by itself about 2027.
• The guide tells the forward story. Earlier this season the break conditions for the peak-products thesis were 2027 consensus revisions upward through print season, and any walk-back of the private guide before the print as the key negative tell. The tell fired in a mild form: the official guide stepped $0.5B below the private October guide, entirely in implied Q4, on a stated curve re-mark rather than an operating miss (nine-month EBITDA landed in the top half of the private range). Read it as the curve rolling over from the September peak, not as the company missing; but it is the first guide move of the season that points down, and it comes from the purest distillate capture story in the complex.
• The sale is a legal and licensing process running on its own clocks (Third Circuit ruling, OFAC license, April 2027 financing expiry, December 18, 2026 collateral date), none of which the print moves. What the print moves is the politics and the appellate optics: a court-approved $5.9B cash bid for a company now guiding to $7.2B to $7.5B of EBITDA and $6.7B to $7.0B of year-end cash is the appellants' exhibit, and a second Bloomberg story already has bond traders pricing deal risk. If the Third Circuit rules for the appellants or OFAC stays silent into the spring, the financing expiry becomes the hard deadline that forces either an extension fight or a rebid argument with this print as its evidence.

THE OTHER SIDE

• Opposing read on the guide: the step-down is trivially small against a $1.4B to $1.7B raise over August, the Q4 implied range still annualizes near a $10B run rate, and marking a guide to the current curve is what every refiner does. Conceded on size; the tell was directional, and direction is what changed.
• Opposing read on the sale: Stark's order survived a full fairness fight once, the appeal's grounds are process rather than price, appellate courts do not re-run auctions on earnings prints, and the United States has said nothing against closing. All consistent with the above; the claim is only that the optics and the rebid constituency strengthened, not that the outcome changed.
• What would disprove the "limbo" read: a Third Circuit affirmance or an OFAC specific license, either of which starts a seven-day closing clock.
• What would disprove the "peak capture, curve rolling" read: a Q4 print at or above the October document's implied Q4 range ($2.9B to $3.2B), which would show the step-down was conservatism rather than curve.

OPEN QUESTIONS

• The October document's formal character (noteholder presentation, offering document, or informal investor update) and its $5.6B October 15 "cash" definition, which sits about $1.2B above the derived September 30 cash. Neither resolved.
• No public Q3 2026 noteholder report with September 30 balance-sheet detail could be obtained; Citgo is not an SEC reporting company. Q3 debt balances, any repayment, and any dividend remain as-reported absences, not established facts.
• Per-refinery Q3 throughput is undisclosed; the state-data figures in circulation are single-source.
• No open-access Argus or OPIS item on the print surfaced; both are subscription products.
• Whether the Third Circuit rules before year-end, and whether OFAC acts on the sale license before the April 2027 financing expiry, are the two live clocks.

SOURCES

Primary: Citgo Q3 2026 release (PR Newswire, 2026-11-12); Citgo Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 and full-year releases for 2025 and Q1, Q2 2026; Citgo company profile; Delaware sale order, Document 2556 (2025-11-29); Amber Energy Third Circuit filing, Document 297 (2026-10-08); Venezuela abeyance motion (2026-10-01); OFAC FAQ 595 and OFAC action notice (2026-11-04); AAA fuel prices (2026-11-12); EIA refinery capacity data; Fitch Ratings action (2026-08-03). Wires and press: Bloomberg (the Q3 article, plus its October 19, 2026 investor-document story as the single origin of that document's contents); Reuters (2026-11-12 print story; 2026-10-21 appeals coverage; 2025-11-29 sale authorization, read in syndication); Oil and Gas Journal (2026-08-13); Hydrocarbon Processing; FleetOwner (EIA diesel data, 2026-11-11); RBN Energy (2025-12-04). Specialists, flagged where used: Venezuela Restructuring Desk tracker (updated 2026-11-06); Chartroom Venezuela dashboard; Plainview Energy (2026-11-09).
