text:
Part 3 of 3 | $NVDA @NVIDIA #NVIDIA #AI #Shareholders #CorporateGovernance

WHAT SHAREHOLDERS CAN DO NOW

First, demand a full accounting, not a public-relations statement. Request that independent counsel investigate not only Jensen but the board, its committees, security personnel, reporting systems and prior disclosures. Demand independent oversight of any director whose own decisions are being examined. Ask for voluntary departures from committee leadership where conflicts exist.

Second, contact the board. NVIDIA identifies shareholdermeeting@nvidia.com as the address for written communications to directors. Investors can also press major institutional holders—Vanguard, BlackRock, State Street, pension funds and active managers—to explain what evidence they require before voting to reelect any incumbent.

Third, use shareholder inspection rights where warranted. Delaware General Corporation Law Section 220 allows properly qualified shareholders to seek specific books and records for a proper purpose, subject to procedural and legal limits. Credible evidence can be reported to the SEC and the relevant export-control and law-enforcement authorities. A securities class action has already begun; director fiduciary-duty litigation is a separate possibility if facts support it.

Fourth, use the 2027 proxy deadlines, because waiting until the annual meeting itself may be too late. NVIDIA lists January 12, 2027 as the deadline for eligible Rule 14a-8 proposals. The ordinary window for director nominations is February 24 through March 26, 2027, subject to date-change rules. A qualified shareholder or group of up to 20 owning 3% for three years may use proxy access for a limited number of nominees; a separate contested election route exists under applicable notice and proxy rules. People serious about replacing directors should organize well before these dates.

Fifth, consider a special meeting. NVIDIA's bylaws provide a route for qualifying holders of at least 15% of shares, continuously held for at least one year, to request one. That does not automatically remove anyone. Removal without cause requires a two-thirds vote of all outstanding voting power under the current charter; removal for legal cause is a different, fact-dependent process. A normal contested annual election follows a different voting standard. Anyone promising an instant clean sweep through a simple majority is leaving out the legal obstacles.

Sixth, vote director by director. In an uncontested NVIDIA election, an incumbent receiving more AGAINST than FOR votes must offer a resignation, although the board decides whether to accept it and must explain that decision. In a properly contested election, the nominees receiving the most votes win. Shareholders are not limited to venting anger on social media. They can help nominate a qualified alternative slate, support proxy campaigns and replace incumbents through the election process.

Finally, revisit the supermajority provisions. In 2025 an overwhelming proportion of votes cast supported eliminating those rules, yet the binding amendment failed because it did not meet the required threshold of two-thirds of all outstanding shares. In 2026 shareholders again backed a nonbinding simple-majority proposal. The board should explain why the existing barriers continue to serve shareholders.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT

Next earnings will tell us about demand and margins, not whether the board did its job. CUDA, engineers, customers and roadmaps did not disappear. The AI investment thesis and the governance failure must be evaluated separately.

But shareholder trust is a fundamental too. A company critical to U.S. AI leadership cannot afford a governance structure in which directors learn material risks from newspaper reporters, if that is what happened. Nor can it afford a board that receives credible warnings and looks away, if that is what investigators find.

I expect pressure for major board changes to grow, especially if reports about internal awareness, the handling of witnesses, Megaspeed, or national-security warnings are substantiated. It is possible that some directors acted properly. It is possible others were misled. Those facts need to be separated, not buried.

But nobody should confuse the absence of a completed investigation with a requirement to reelect the same people.

A serious board would publish the investigation's scope, preserve the records, establish independence from the directors under review, address the missing expertise and provide a credible succession and compliance plan. And any director who cannot justify the oversight he or she provided should leave.

Jensen has resigned. The directors now have to answer for their own performance.

What did each of you know? When? What action did you take? And why should shareholders vote for you again in 2027?

To @elonmusk, President @realDonaldTrump, Secretary @PeteHegseth, and the individuals within America's technological and national security institutions who heard my appeal:

You have my sincere gratitude.

Earlier today, I publicly challenged what appeared to be continuing restrictions on my expression here on X, following an enforcement decision that the platform itself had overturned.

Within hours, my visibility began recovering.

To those who took notice and helped resolve this matter, thank you. I regard this outcome as something considerably more important than a correction to an algorithm.

It is a demonstration of the very principle I was defending.

Consider the extraordinary contrast.

I am an American citizen in Massachusetts, openly corresponding with senior Iranian officials in Persian, challenging their geopolitical arguments, supporting the mission of my country's armed forces, and simultaneously demanding accountability from the institutions of my own government.

When I believed the platform carrying these arguments had treated me unjustly, I challenged that institution publicly as well.

And here I remain, free to continue the conversation.

In Iran, citizens who challenge powerful institutions have faced detention by security forces, coercive interrogations, unfair trials, and, in documented cases, execution before the public.

The difference is not that America possesses flawless institutions. Clearly, it does not.

The difference is that American freedom provides the opportunity to challenge those institutions, expose their errors, demand accountability, and seek correction without surrendering one's liberty.

That distinction matters more than any proclamation of national superiority.

It is demonstrated through conduct.

I support the United States military in its responsibility to defend our country, protect American lives, and uphold our legitimate security interests. That support includes the obligation to examine its decisions critically. Accountability is not an obstacle to national strength; it is among the foundations of its legitimacy.

The same principle should apply universally, including to the Iranian institutions and officials with whom I have been communicating.

My purpose has never been merely to win an argument with Tehran. It is to use history, strategic reasoning, and the extraordinary possibilities of human intelligence working alongside artificial intelligence to help identify a path away from further destruction.

Military power may establish the conditions for negotiation. It cannot, by itself, produce the mutual understanding upon which lasting peace depends.

To my American audience, I offer this experience as a reason for renewed confidence in the freedoms we possess—and continued vigilance in preserving them.

To my Iranian audience, I offer it not as an insult, but as an invitation to consider what becomes possible when criticism is permitted to correct power rather than punished for confronting it.

And to everyone who helped restore this dialogue, I offer my thanks once again.

Now let us make meaningful use of that freedom—not merely to defend our respective positions, but to discover whether reason can accomplish what further bloodshed cannot.

A month before his trial, he says, the district attorney offered him a deal. Admit to a conspiracy, do seven years, walk out.

He said no. He walked out with three life sentences instead.

His name is Caius Veiovis. He has horns surgically implanted in his forehead, “666” tattooed between them, and ears cut to a point. He was born with the last name Gutfinski. He changed it in prison.

In the video below is the moment the jury found him guilty, and what he said to them. Then watch him at his sentencing, when he finally gets to speak.

In August 2011, three men disappeared from an apartment in Pittsfield, Massachusetts. David Glasser, Edward Frampton and Robert Chadwell. Ten days later, police found their bodies buried on a property in a nearby town.

Prosecutors said Glasser was about to testify against a man named Adam Lee Hall. The other two were killed because they were there.

Hall was convicted. So was a second man. Veiovis was the third. There was no DNA and no murder weapon. The case was built on witnesses.

When the verdicts were read, he turned to the jury: “I’ll see you all in hell. Every one of you.”

At sentencing, he told the judge he had spent three years in isolation and refused to talk to police.

“I’d rather spend the rest of my life in prison and be able to face myself in the mirror at the end of the day than make that kind of deal.”

“If anybody thinks I’m going to hang my head today and beg for mercy...”

“Justice was not served. I’m an innocent man.”

The judge gave him life without parole, three times over.

He put the devil on his own face. Was Caius Veiovis convicted for what he did, or for what he looked like?

Romania Willing to Cover Part of the Costs for Stationing US Troops on Its Territory

Bucharest has submitted a cost-sharing plan to Washington and is counting on an expansion of the American military contingent, President Nicușor Dan stated in an interview with the Financial Times.

"We want more American troops and more lethal capabilities," Dan said. Currently, 1,172 US military personnel are stationed in Romania, down from around 1,700 previously.

According to the FT, Romania is considering a financial contribution comparable to Poland's offer to pay $15,000 per year for each stationed American service member. Bucharest has not yet disclosed the exact figure of its proposal.

Dan explained that strengthening the contingent is necessary due to the threat from Russia, Russian drones crashing on Romanian territory, and attacks on vessels in the Black Sea. It has not been reported whether Washington has agreed to deploy additional units.

Earlier, we reported on a drone attack targeting a Turkish vessel carrying Ukrainian grain off the coast of Romania. According to Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the strike was carried out by Russian drones, killing the captain.

text:
From Jensen Huang’s Resignation to the True Nature of American Politics: Why Silicon Valley Must Grow the Horizontal Pupils of a Sheep 🐑🐺

Jensen Huang is out at NVIDIA. The headlines are obsessed with the scandal. They are missing the larger story.

For 33 years, Jensen Huang helped build NVIDIA into one of America's most consequential technology companies. He helped place extraordinary computing power at the center of the AI revolution.

Now he has resigned, amid personal scandal and national security scrutiny.

But his departure raises a much larger question about the political environment surrounding American technological leadership.

You can build the future of civilization and still become vulnerable to the battles of those who govern it.

Look at what is being done to Jensen Huang and to American tech leaders today.

This is not governance. It is a bipartisan masterclass in political extortion.

The Masterpiece of Bipartisan Schizophrenia

Feed current U.S. tech policy into any high-end AI cluster, and the machine would crash from an unrecoverable logic paradox.

Listen to Washington:

"America must win the AI race!"

"China must not surpass the United States!"

"Don't export our most advanced GPUs to China!"

And then, from another corner of the same political system:

"Stop building new AI data centers!"

"Slow down AI development!"

"Protect America from the dangers of artificial intelligence!"

Wait a minute.

On Monday, Washington weaponizes "national security."

Congressional grandstanders drag tech CEOs into hearings and scream that selling commercial GPUs abroad is practically treason.

"You're arming the adversary! You're handing over the keys to the future!"

Tech leaders are forced to surgically lobotomize their own chips to comply with arbitrary export rules, then beg for permission to conduct basic commerce.

On Tuesday, the same political machine strangles domestic innovation.

The moment companies try to build infrastructure at home, the political class panics.

Suddenly, AI data centers are an "existential threat to the power grid." Environmental lobbies scream about carbon footprints. Alarmist factions demand a moratorium on model training. Regulators introduce stifling bills to cripple algorithmic development in the name of "safety."

Do you see the grotesque hypocrisy yet?

Sell compute abroad, and you are "arming the enemy."

Build compute at home, and you are "destroying the planet."

So what, precisely, is an American tech giant supposed to do with the world's most advanced semiconductors?

Bury them in the Potomac to appease the gods of Capitol Hill?

Washington roars that America must win the AI race—on the strict condition that nobody is actually permitted to run.

It Was Never About National Security. It Is About Power.

The political class does not care about semiconductor architectures, FLOPs, or global competitiveness.

Most politicians grandstanding at tech hearings could not tell a GPU from a microwave without a twenty-something staffer whispering in their ear.

This has nothing to do with safeguarding democracy and everything to do with the perpetual consolidation of power.

Tech as a foreign scapegoat:

Banning exports is the easiest way for politicians to look "tough on China" on television without solving a single structural crisis at home. It is theatrical red meat for election cycles.

Tech as a domestic shakedown:

Demonizing AI and stalling infrastructure permits is the fastest way to extract campaign donations, enforce regulatory capture, and keep tech companies subservient to the state.

By controlling the choke points of infrastructure, politicians force tech titans to bow down, kiss the ring, and keep the campaign donations flowing.

Whenever power shifts on Capitol Hill, the score-settling begins.

Tech pioneers suddenly find themselves in a partisan crossfire where every commercial transaction is retroactively labeled a conspiracy and every corporate footprint is deemed a violation.

The punishment arrives first; the rationale is selected later.

When the political wolves come hunting, they don't look for logic. They look for a scalp.

And when faced with an unchecked political machine that will brand you a traitor just to win a Sunday news cycle, what choice does an executive have?

You either become the ultimate sacrifice, or you scramble for cover while the wolves feast on the carcass of American innovation.

Borrow a Man's Head to Calm the Troops

There is a chilling Chinese expression for this:

借人头一用，以安军心 — "Borrow a man's head to calm the troops."

When a regime is factionalized, anxious, and bankrupt of real strategy, it does not solve the underlying crisis.

Instead, it selects a prominent head, mounts it on a spike, and claims order has been restored.

Jensen Huang—the architect of America's computing dominance—became too visible, too autonomous, and ultimately, too convenient a sacrifice.

I am not claiming some secret committee orchestrated Huang's departure; that would require evidence.

But I am asking whether Washington has become so comfortable with political spectacle that it confuses the downfall of one executive with the resolution of far larger problems.

Huang's personal conduct is his own. His achievements do not exempt him from the law.

But neither should his personal controversies become substitutes for serious national policy.

Let Washington choke on this truth:

Removing one man does not resolve America's semiconductor strategy.
Destroying a reputation does not build a single data center.
A congressional sound bite does not manufacture a single GPU.
And a political victory is not a technological victory.

America's technological leadership was built by people willing to take enormous risks, invest decades of their lives, and pursue discoveries that once seemed impossible.

Whatever the evidence ultimately supports, Huang's personal mistakes should not erase his technological achievements, and his departure should not become an excuse to avoid examining Washington's larger policy contradictions.

A nation cannot credibly demand technological supremacy while treating technological leadership as an expendable piece in its political chess game.

If America wants to lead the AI century, its political institutions must answer a fundamental question:

Are their decisions guided by a coherent vision for the country's future?

Or is the future increasingly becoming collateral damage in the struggle for political power?

That is the contradiction worth debating.

Wake Up, Silicon Valley

The lesson of this era is brutal and final:

Technological supremacy does not grant political immunity.

Biologists tell us prey animals—sheep, goats, and deer—evolved horizontal, slit-shaped pupils for a singular reason: survival.

When a lamb lowers its head to graze, its eyes automatically rotate to maintain a panoramic view of the horizon.

It can never afford to blind itself in pure focus.

Because in the wild, the wolves are always circling.

And to America's technology leaders, perhaps nature offers one final piece of advice.

It is time to evolve the horizontal pupils of the sheep.

Keep watching the technological frontier.

But never forget to watch the political horizon.

Keep one eye on your code, but keep the other 300 degrees locked on Washington, D.C.

Because the wolves running the state will not hesitate to sacrifice the entire technological future of this nation just to keep their grip on the throne.

The sheep may have lost its place at the head of the flock.

But the wolves still have some explaining to do.

Silicon Valley, grow those horizontal pupils.

The wolves haven't gone vegetarian.

They've just learned to call dinner "national security." 🐑🐺

text:
I maintain that Trump won't make any move other than a major escalation. This has been clear since the outset of Epic Fury. It's a matter of when, not if.

Expect weeks of heavy bombing against Iranian energy installations and critical infrastructure, alongside SEAD/DEAD and an attempt to cripple Iran's offensive missile and drone capabilities. Then ground forces seize the Iranian islands around the Strait of Hormuz and Kharg, with Israel potentially supplying a large chunk of the troops. Kharg is only ~16 miles off the mainland, within range of Iranian missiles, drones, and coastal rockets. They'd need to cripple those capabilities before putting troops there.

I think any offensive plan is foolish and wouldn't give Trump enough leverage to force Iran to capitulate. Almost nothing would make Iran surrender, and the US won't accept defeat while Trump is in power either. That creates an escalation ratchet reminiscent of Vietnam.

Many are under the silly assumption that Trump can simply "pull out." He can't, not without major concessions. That would mean the US retreating from the Middle East with its tail between its legs, Iran emerging vastly stronger, controlling the Strait of Hormuz, and building a nuclear arsenal, as it now must to deter the US and Israel. It would be the greatest military failure in history, a glaring admission that the war had left the US far worse off than before. The odds of Trump accepting that are effectively zero, especially given his character. It's a game of roulette where even cutting your losses means conceding defeat. The conflict is already past the singularity.

The US has no other feasible military option left. Trump could keep bombing civilian infrastructure, but that's pretty much been tried, and Iran would retaliate asymmetrically by hitting civilian infrastructure and oil installations across the Gulf. I'd be very surprised if CENTCOM commanders pushed for infrastructure bombing alone; surely they understand Iran's nearly unlimited tolerance. It should've been clear before Epic Fury began that a "luxury war" fought from the air with powerful bombs wouldn't achieve the stated objectives or produce tangible gains. So I expect that bombing to set up an operation with boots on the ground.

I also wouldn't be surprised to see terrorist attacks in the coming months, either organized or backed by Iran's IRGC or carried out by lone actors. Israel narrowly avoided a 9/11-style attack during the September 30 flydubai hijacking attempt. A successful attack of that scale would catalyze major escalation.

WTI at $85/bbl is very mispriced. The same irrational optimism sent it to ~$67/bbl after the MOU was signed, barely above prewar levels. The war is FAR from over. Given the scale of the potential supply disruption, oil above $200/bbl seems quite likely.

The market is putting too much weight on diplomacy. The pressures driving escalation dominate, yet the market keeps biting on the noise. There is simply no path for diplomacy.

Seizing Kharg was on the table back in March. The US hit military targets on the island during Epic Fury, but Trump chickened out on taking it. Too many fuses have burned down since. The war is even more unpopular, the SPR is at its lowest level since 1982, munitions and interceptor stockpiles are dwindling, and the longer this drags on, the more obvious the defeat becomes. The Trump admin has a fire under its ass.

The idea that "economic strangulation" will force Iran to surrender is absurd. I'd be surprised if the Trump administration actually believes that, though given its stupidity so far, I wouldn't rule it out. I expect Trump is losing patience as he realizes he can't bully Iran into handing him a victory. He'll test the hard limits of US military power again.

Netanyahu may lose power soon, now that Eisenkot has the mandate to form a government. If Trump wants to act while Bibi is still caretaker PM, he can't keep waiting indefinitely. One thing I'm sure of is that Netanyahu is pushing Trump hard for a major escalation, including heavy strikes and a ground operation. I think it's likely he's already offered Trump Israeli ground troops.

With 2 years left and Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress in January, Trump is paranoid about his legacy. That pressure is making him increasingly desperate.

2 CSGs are already in CENTCOM: USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. USS Theodore Roosevelt is on the way. USS Makin Island (LHD-8) is due around the end of November, replacing or overlapping with USS Boxer. It's a more advanced amphibious assault ship that would support a landing.

You don't move all these assets just to "keep options open." Asset movements don't lie. Trump and "US officials" do. Trump's messaging is sloppy deception. Taking the opposite of what he says often points to his real intentions.

I strongly suspect this starts between late November and early February. Before Thanksgiving wouldn't surprise me.

text:
Iran War Update, Nov 12 (Day 257): “We don’t need a deal with Iran.” President Trump made that clear today, and America’s pressure campaign keeps going at full strength.

On Truth Social Thursday, Trump wrote that the days of needing a deal “have long since passed,” adding, “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” He also pulled VP Vance off possible Iran talks and back to domestic anti-fraud work. On Veterans Day he said America has won and it’s “just a question of when we want to end it.” The White House says the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s economy is collapsing, and the naval blockade and the expanded land-and-sea blockade, Operation Iron Gate, will continue at full strength.

Tehran is grasping. At the COP31 climate summit, Iran’s president demanded compensation for “environmental damage” from U.S. and Israeli strikes. Iran offered to shorten a ceasefire rollout from seven days to two, but it kept every core demand: lift the blockade, unfreeze its assets, and keep its enriched uranium. Secretary Rubio calls those terms unacceptable. Even Iran’s president admits the country is stuck in “neither war nor peace.”

The regime is still lashing out. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened U.S. bases from the Middle East to Europe. Treasury Secretary Bessent was moved to a military base after Iranian threats. Saudi air defenses shot down Iran-backed Houthi ballistic missiles fired at western Saudi Arabia, and debris fell in the Mecca region. A tanker was hit by a projectile off the UAE’s Ras Al-Khaimah and its crew was evacuated. Iran says two more tankers caught fire after hitting mines on a route Tehran hasn’t approved. The U.S. Navy has escorted tankers through the safer southern route.

Neither side has launched large-scale strikes since summer, and oil prices have eased as Washington makes clear that economic pressure, not new bombing, is the plan for now. Israel’s defense minister says he, Netanyahu and the military chief agree on Iran policy and are ready to act if needed. Pressure works. America holds the cards.

text:
Imagine this scenario: Elon Musk calls Jensen Huang this weekend and offers him a blank check and a new chip company. 

Then every Nvidia engineer who would rather follow the founder than the board walks out behind him. 

California doesn’t enforce noncompete agreements, so nothing in Santa Clara can stop them.

Now Nvidia has a real competitor, and the guy heading it up is the guy who made Nvidia. 

Musk already runs xAI’s Colossus supercomputer in Memphis on Nvidia chips, and he has spent years trying to build his own chips at Tesla. What he has never had is the man who turned CUDA into the language AI is written in. Put the biggest buyer and the best builder in one company, and Nvidia’s best customer becomes its most dangerous competitor overnight.

Then we get the X Processor. Nvidia’s board would keep the logo, the campus and the ticker symbol. Jensen would take the one thing that ever made them worth anything. After all, a board can fire a founder, but it can’t fire the people who would follow him out the door.

text:
Trust Me, Bro (Enterprise Edition)

Like clockwork: within 48 hours of a major AI model drop, someone on tech Twitter suddenly becomes the main character of global AI geopolitics.

You know the genre by now. It's written in the weary, burdened tone of a reluctant industry insider: A massive, unnamed lab secretly slid into my DMs begging for help to do something shady. I heroically turned them down, lectured them on ethics, and told them to go train on public domain books instead.

Never mind that these labs employ thousands of PhDs and spend billions on compute—apparently, their secret weapon is cold-DMing an account with "Tech Expert" in the bio for basic R&D advice. There are never any names. No screenshots. No timestamps. Just pure, unfiltered vibes—and within hours, half a million views.

Stepping back from any single post, the fascinating part isn't that people tell tall tales on the internet. That's a tradition older than dial-up. What's remarkable is how the modern AI timeline has evolved into a friction-free ecosystem for unverifiable storytelling.

1.The Half-Life of a Walkback

In an algorithmic feed, attention operates on a steep discount curve. A sensational claim that flatters our existing biases—about rival labs cutting corners, secret breakthroughs, or impending tech collapses—acts like rocket fuel. People hit repost before their skepticism even boots up.

Fifteen hours later, once actual engineers start poking holes in the plot, the inevitable quote-tweet "clarification" arrives. By then, the original post has already retired comfortably with 700,000 impressions, while the walkback gets seen by twelve people and a bot.

In that quiet follow-up, the blockbuster scoop magically mutates: the brand-new model becomes "an older release"; the direct outreach from a lab becomes "a guy who knows a guy"; the sweeping industry diagnosis becomes "just my personal opinion." The story shrinks, the engagement stays banked, and the cycle resets.

2.Bulletproof "Unfalsifiability"

The best part of these narratives is how cleanly they are engineered to dodge the burden of proof. You can't name the source because of "legal liability" (a thrillingly vague phrase when nobody has been named). You can't show a single message because the whole thing went through a middleman, so nothing official exists. If people keep asking questions, you simply channel a White House press secretary and announce that you are "closing this topic for good."

There is an inverse law of internet credibility at work here: the fewer receipts an author has, the longer their closing paragraph about how much "honesty and transparency" mean to them. Virtue signaling isn't used as a standard to be met; it's used as a smoke bomb to exit the stage.

3.The Hype-Cycle Authority Vacuum

Why does this work so reliably? Because AI is moving faster than almost anyone can comfortably metabolize. That speed creates a massive authority vacuum.

When the ground shifts every week, audiences are desperate for someone who sounds like they're sitting in the room where it happens. Put a shiny title in your bio, adopt a tone of quiet certainty, and drop a few "you heard it here first" predictions—and half the timeline will be panic-downloading open-source weights into a digital bunker before lunch.

We spend a lot of energy worrying about AI flooding the internet with synthetic text and deepfakes. Yet some of the most effective misinformation in tech still requires zero GPUs—just a Notes app, a vague appeal to insider access, and an audience willing to mistake confidence for credibility.

In a feed built to reward velocity, the most radical habit left is simply pausing before you amplify, and asking what in a story can actually be verified. And if the only evidence on offer is a monologue about the author's integrity, enjoy the fanfiction for what it is.

text: Fresh winter air is not the enemy of a horse's health; stale, sealed-up air is. A barn can stay draught-free and dust-managed without being shut tight, but it takes deliberate daily habits rather than a single autumn fix. The 2026 winter checklist below covers airflow, moisture, ammonia, bedding and dust control so horses breathe cleaner air while the building still protects them from wind and precipitation.Table of ContentsWhy does a closed-up barn cause more problems than cold air?How can I tell if my barn's air quality has gone bad?Which barn openings should stay open when it is cold outside?How does ventilation actually work in a horse barn?What temperature should a winter barn be kept at?How do moisture, manure and bedding affect winter air quality?How do I cut dust without shutting off the fresh air?What should go on a 2026 winter barn checklist?Key TakeawaysReferencesWhy does a closed-up barn cause more problems than cold air?A closed-up barn causes more problems than cold air because sealing the building traps ammonia fumes and dust, both of which irritate a horse's lungs. According to EQUUS Magazine, a shut-tight barn allows those irritants to collect in the air horses breathe. Horses with a history of respiratory disease, such as heaves, are especially vulnerable to stuffy https://t.co/AiPnmsTpd1 night in a poorly ventilated barn can trigger a respiratory episode in a heaves-prone horse that takes weeks of care to settle. The same source notes that a horse with a thick winter coat can comfortably tolerate temperatures well below freezing. The core principle is to ventilate for air quality, not for warmth. A barn that feels cosy to a human may be doing real harm to the animals inside https://t.co/fqppsAgAEV can I tell if my barn's air quality has gone bad?You can tell your barn's air quality has gone bad with two simple field tests: smell for ammonia and watch for dust particles hanging in shafts of sunlight. Any hint of ammonia smell means ventilation has gone seriously awry, according to EQUUS Magazine. Ammonia is not a normal barn smell; it is a warning sign that urine and wet bedding are off-gassing into the air.A low-tech draught check involves holding a length of toilet paper at arm's length. If the paper blows sideways, there is a draught to address. The temperature test is equally straightforward: indoor air more than 10 degrees above the outside temperature signals over-closing. EQUUS Magazine reports that a barn running more than 10 degrees warmer than outside has likely been sealed too tightly for healthy air exchange.Which barn openings should stay open when it is cold outside?If it is not windy, raining or snowing, leave all barn doors and windows open regardless of temperature. That guidance comes directly from EQUUS Magazine, and it applies even when the mercury drops well below freezing. Cold air moving through the barn is not a health risk for a horse with a winter coat; stagnant air is.When wind and precipitation are a concern, close only the openings needed to block them, typically windows and doors on the windward side. Closing even a few openings can sharply reduce air quality as particulates build up. The difference between a targeted draught fix and sealing the whole building matters. Block the weather, not the https://t.co/KVfIKR7Lo4 does ventilation actually work in a horse barn?Ventilation in a horse barn works through either natural or mechanical means, and both have a specific winter job list. Natural ventilation relies on warm air rising through thermal buoyancy, using wind forces to push exhausted air out of the building. Mechanical ventilation involves fans with planned intake and exhaust areas, according to Horse Health Products.Winter ventilation is needed to remove moisture, ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, dust and airborne pathogens. Barns built to mimic modern residential construction have become more air-tight and tend to hold stale air inside. That residential-style tightness works against horse health. A barn needs planned air exchange, not the sealed envelope of a family home.What temperature should a winter barn be kept at?A winter barn should be kept at no more than 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above the outside temperature as a working guideline. Horse Health Products lists that range as the practical target for interior barn temperature. The practical sign of over-closing is indoor air more than 10 degrees warmer than outside, which EQUUS Magazine identifies as a signal to open more doors and windows.A thick winter coat means the horse does not need a heated barn. Warmth inside a barn is a comfort goal for humans, not a health requirement for horses. Keeping the building too warm also accelerates ammonia release from soiled bedding, which compounds the air quality https://t.co/1RFDrQiMzF do moisture, manure and bedding affect winter air quality?Moisture, manure and bedding affect winter air quality because wet bedding is where ammonia fumes come from. Manure and wet bedding should be removed on a consistent basis, usually at least twice per day, according to Horse Health Products. Skipping a morning muck-out in winter has a bigger air quality penalty than skipping one in summer. Think of Urea organic Nitrogen the fuel for microbes in bedding material. if you combine oxygenated bedding material with Urea and the right moisture balance you get microbial activity on a scale of several trillion ammonia producing composters. Insulation can be used to minimise condensation inside the barn. Condensation drips onto bedding and walls, feeding the damp conditions that release ammonia and harbour pathogens. Keeping the barn clean includes removing dust, spider webs, old hay and bedding from corners and walls. Moisture control and ammonia control are the same job in a winter https://t.co/vuv1PIiwMk do I cut dust without shutting off the fresh air?You cut dust without shutting off fresh air by separating the two problems: fresh air is desirable, airborne dust is not. The goal is to keep air moving while reducing the particulate load at its source. Clean bedding, regular mucking out and clearing cobwebs from corners all reduce dust without closing a single window. EQUUS Magazine and Horse Health Products both frame dust control as a cleaning and airflow task rather than a sealing task.A dry salt aerosol approach is one option for creating a cleaner indoor microclimate. The Ultisalt™ platform uses Dry Salt Aerosol Therapy, known as DSAT, to distribute a fine treatment salt mist through a barn space. Equine Salt Therapy offers Licensed Business Opportunities and Master Licenses for Equine, Poultry, Swine and Companion Animals, sold by territory under US Patent 11,497,593 and CA 3019046, with pricing from $110,000 to $1,000,000. The platform is one tool among several barn-management habits, not a cure-all, and it does not replace the daily work of mucking out and ventilating. Treatments strat at $100 per horse. What should go on a 2026 winter barn checklist?A 2026 winter barn checklist should include these daily and seasonal items: open what the weather allows, smell for ammonia daily, watch for dust in sunlight, strip wet bedding twice daily, clean corners and cobwebs, insulate against condensation, and check the indoor-versus-outdoor temperature gap. The checklist applies to horse owners, trainers, breeders and rehabilitation yards alike. EQUUS Magazine and Horse Health Products both emphasise that ventilation is a daily habit, not a one-off autumn job.The temperature gap check takes seconds: if the barn is more than 10 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than outside, open more openings. The ammonia check takes a single breath at the door. The dust check takes one look at a shaft of sunlight. None of these habits requires equipment, and all of them protect the respiratory health of horses through the coldest months of the year.Key TakeawaysA shut-tight barn lets ammonia fumes and dust collect, and both irritate a horse's lungs.A single night in a stuffy barn can trigger a respiratory episode in a heaves-prone horse that takes weeks of care to settle.A horse with a thick winter coat can comfortably tolerate temperatures well below freezing.If it is not windy, raining or snowing, leave all barn doors and windows open regardless of temperature.Any hint of ammonia smell means ventilation has gone seriously awry.Indoor barn temperature should sit no more than 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above the outside temperature.Manure and wet bedding should be removed at least twice per day to control moisture and fumes.ReferencesDon't make your barn too cozy — EQUUS Magazine, 2019-07-25Keep your barn well ventilated this winter — EQUUS Magazine, 2024-09-30Something's in the Air: Winter Barn Ventilation — Horse Health Products, 2014-08-31

The fatal flaw of mainstream economics is that it tries to turn human action into mathematical mechanics. But people don't obey equations. They learn, adapt and change their minds.

That's why Ludwig von Mises believed economics requires a fundamentally different method.  Praxeology, developed by Mises and refined by Murray Rothbard, begins with one undeniable axiom: human beings act purposefully to achieve ends using scarce means. From this single truth, all valid economic propositions are derived through logical deduction rather than observation or experimentation.

This method stands in direct opposition to mainstream economics, which treats human action as if it were mechanical and predictable like particles in physics. By relying on historical data, regressions and ever-more-complex models, it produces correlations and predictions that are constantly overturned. Praxeology rejects this because human action is not governed by constant quantitative relationships. People learn, change their minds, and respond to incentives in ways that cannot be captured by mechanical laws.

What praxeology provides instead are apodictically certain truths: the law of marginal utility, the impossibility of economic calculation under socialism, the distorting effects of central banking, and the spontaneous coordination of free markets. It places the acting individual at the centre of analysis and demonstrates why only voluntary exchange and private property can allocate resources efficiently.

In an age dominated by econometric modelling and technocratic “nudges,” praxeology offers a fundamentally different approach: the clearest and most consistent defence of reason and economic liberty.

text:
RELIGION IS A CHOICE, BUT EVERY CHOICE HAS CONSEQUENCES.

You are free to believe in whatever you want, worship whoever you choose, and follow whichever spiritual path gives you meaning. But freedom of religion does not mean freedom from the consequences of your beliefs and actions.

The Freedom to Believe

I have always believed that religion should be a matter of personal conviction, not coercion.

If you want to be a Christian, be a Christian. If you want to be a Muslim, be a Muslim. If you want to practise traditional African religion, that is entirely your decision. If you choose not to believe in the existence of God, that is also your right.

Nobody should be forced into a religion simply because they were born into a particular family, community, tribe, or geographical location.

Your parents may have introduced you to their faith, but ultimately, your beliefs should become your own conscious decision.

However, there is something I believe we do not discuss enough when talking about religious freedom:

You have the freedom to choose your beliefs, but you also have the responsibility to examine what those beliefs demand of you.

Every religion has teachings, expectations, moral boundaries, and spiritual claims. Some practices encourage compassion, self-discipline, and service to humanity. Others, particularly when interpreted through extremism, fear, or manipulation, can lead people into destructive decisions.

And that is where my concern begins.

1. When Religion Becomes a Justification for Taking Human Life

Let me begin with one of the most disturbing manifestations of religious extremism: the belief that killing another human being can be justified as an act of devotion to God.

There are extremist individuals and groups who invoke the Islamic concept of jihad to justify violence against people they consider unbelievers.

They believe that their actions are religious obligations or that committing violence in the name of their faith will earn them divine rewards.

But we must make an important distinction: jihad has different meanings within Islamic teaching, and the overwhelming majority of Muslims do not believe that murdering non-Muslims is an acceptable expression of their faith.

My argument is directed at those who choose violent interpretations and use religion to justify murder.

Because whatever spiritual explanation you attach to your actions, society has laws.

If you deliberately take an innocent person's life, you cannot simply escape responsibility by declaring that you acted in the name of God.

You may believe that you are fulfilling a divine assignment, but the law can still hold you accountable for murder.

That is the reality of living in a society governed by laws rather than the personal religious convictions of individuals.

Imagine a world where everyone could commit a crime and escape prosecution simply by claiming that their religion permitted it.

What would happen to justice?

What would happen to human dignity?

What would happen to the right to life?

Religious freedom cannot become a licence to destroy the freedom and existence of another human being.

Your right to practise your religion ends where your actions violate another person's fundamental rights.

If your interpretation of religion requires you to murder innocent people, then you must also understand that the criminal justice system can hold you accountable.

You cannot demand the protection of society while denying that same protection to others.

2. Traditional Worship, Ancestral Obligations, and the Fear of Spiritual Consequences

Africa has an incredibly rich spiritual and cultural history.

Long before Christianity and Islam became widespread across the continent, our ancestors practised various forms of traditional religion.

Some communities maintained sacred groves, revered rivers, honoured ancestors, or worshipped deities associated with natural forces.

For some practitioners, these traditions remain deeply meaningful expressions of identity, spirituality, and cultural continuity.

And I respect their right to practise them.

However, there is an aspect of certain traditional religious beliefs that I find troubling.

In some families and communities, people believe that ancestral deities or spiritual obligations can bring misfortune upon descendants who abandon established worship practices.

There are stories of families who believe they must continue performing particular rites because failure to do so could invite spiritual punishment.

Some fear sickness, poverty, unexplained hardship, or even death if the next generation refuses to continue the tradition.

Now, whether these supernatural claims are true is a matter of belief, not something we should automatically treat as established fact.

But the fear itself can have very real consequences.

Imagine being born into a family where you are told that you cannot freely choose your religion because an ancestral deity will punish you.

Imagine wanting to become a Christian, Muslim, or atheist but being threatened with spiritual consequences for making that decision.

Is that still freedom of religion?

A belief system that people cannot freely question or leave without fear of punishment raises serious questions about personal liberty.

I am not suggesting that every traditional African religion operates this way. Traditional spiritual practices are diverse, and many practitioners do not impose such threats.

My concern is with any practice that uses fear to control the decisions of future generations.

If a religion is meaningful to you, practise it.

But should your children automatically inherit obligations they never personally accepted?

Should your grandchildren be forced to continue rituals simply because their ancestors participated in them?

I believe every generation deserves the opportunity to examine its beliefs and decide what spiritual path it wants to follow.

Tradition deserves understanding, but tradition should never become an excuse for coercion.

3. The Pursuit of Money Through Rituals

Another disturbing issue, particularly within some African societies, is the pursuit of wealth through supposed spiritual shortcuts.

We have heard stories of individuals who consult spiritual practitioners because they believe certain rituals can produce money, influence, or extraordinary financial success.

Some are promised wealth in exchange for sacrifices, obedience to particular spiritual instructions, or participation in secret ceremonies.

It is important to distinguish ordinary religious rituals from fraudulent schemes and criminal acts carried out in the name of wealth.

There is no reliable scientific evidence that performing supernatural rituals can generate money.

However, the pursuit of so-called ritual wealth can have devastating real-world consequences.

People can lose their savings to fraudsters.

Families can be manipulated through fear.

Individuals may abandon productive work in pursuit of unrealistic promises.

And in the most disturbing criminal cases, people have committed violence believing it would somehow produce wealth.

But money obtained through fraud, exploitation, or criminal violence is not a blessing.

It is a liability.

Imagine seeking financial freedom only to lose your freedom through imprisonment.

Imagine pursuing wealth so desperately that you destroy another person's life and your own future in the process.

What exactly have you gained?

Not every promise of supernatural prosperity is worth pursuing, especially when it demands that you surrender your conscience, dignity, or humanity.

We must stop romanticising shortcuts to wealth that depend on exploiting people or breaking the law.

There is dignity in building something through legitimate effort.

There is value in patience.

And there is wisdom in recognising that not every opportunity presented as a spiritual breakthrough is genuine.

4. Why I Consider Being a Christian a Privilege

Now, let me speak from my personal conviction.

I am a Christian, and I consider my faith a privilege.

Not because I believe Christians are inherently better human beings than Muslims, traditionalists, atheists, or anyone else.

Not because Christianity makes me incapable of wrongdoing.

And certainly not because identifying as a Christian automatically makes someone morally upright.

I consider Christianity a privilege because of how I understand the relationship between God, grace, forgiveness, and salvation.

At the centre of my faith is the belief that salvation is a gift made possible through Jesus Christ.

I do not believe I can purchase God's love through money.

I do not believe that I need to harm another human being to prove my loyalty to God.

And I do not believe that I must live in constant terror of spiritual punishment every time I make a human mistake.

Christianity teaches me that I am imperfect, that I will sometimes fall short, and that God's grace offers forgiveness and the opportunity for transformation.

That is incredibly meaningful to me.

The Bible says in Ephesians 2:8–9 that salvation comes by grace through faith, rather than being earned through human works.

For me, that is liberating.

I do not have to pretend to be perfect before approaching God.

When I make mistakes, I can repent, seek forgiveness, make amends where necessary, and work toward becoming better.

Of course, this does not mean Christianity offers a licence to behave recklessly.

Grace is not permission to commit evil, and forgiveness does not automatically erase the earthly consequences of our actions.

A Christian who steals can still be prosecuted.

A Christian who murders can still face criminal punishment.

A Christian who defrauds others cannot escape responsibility simply by attending church or praying for forgiveness.

In fact, I believe genuine Christianity should encourage greater personal responsibility, not less.

My confidence in God's grace is not an excuse to disregard the law or mistreat other people.

It is a reason to strive for a more compassionate and responsible life.

And when I speak about not living in fear of death, I am referring to my Christian hope of eternal life, not a belief that Christians are exempt from suffering, mortality, or the consequences of wrongdoing.

That distinction matters.

5. Your Religion Does Not Place You Above the Law

One of the biggest problems in society is the tendency to confuse religious conviction with moral or legal immunity.

People sometimes believe that once an action has been endorsed by a religious authority, it automatically becomes acceptable.

But religious conviction and civic responsibility are not the same thing.

A pastor cannot justify financial fraud by calling it a divine instruction.

An imam cannot justify the murder of innocent people by claiming religious authority.

A traditional priest cannot legitimately subject another person to violence or coercion under the guise of spiritual obligation.

And an atheist cannot justify harming others simply because they reject religious moral frameworks.

There must be standards of justice that protect everyone, regardless of belief.

In a pluralistic society, the law should protect the freedom to worship, the freedom not to worship, and the fundamental rights of every citizen.

That includes the right to change one's religion.

It also includes the right to reject the religion of one's parents.

And it includes the right to live without being intimidated, assaulted, or discriminated against because of religious identity.

Nigeria, for example, recognises freedom of thought, conscience, and religion under Section 38 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended.

But freedom of religion does not exempt anyone from laws protecting human life and public safety.

Religious tolerance should never require society to tolerate criminal violence.

6. Every Belief System Deserves Critical Examination

I believe we should be courageous enough to question the ideas we inherit.

Not necessarily because those ideas are wrong, but because understanding why we believe something is better than following it blindly.

If you are a Christian, ask yourself whether your actions genuinely reflect the teachings of Christ.

If you are a Muslim, examine whether your understanding of Islam promotes justice, mercy, and peaceful coexistence.

If you practise traditional religion, consider whether your customs respect the freedom and dignity of those who may choose a different path.

If you do not believe in God, reflect on the moral principles that guide your treatment of other human beings.

Nobody should be exempt from introspection.

Religion becomes dangerous when questioning is treated as rebellion, compassion is replaced with hostility, and obedience is demanded without moral reflection.

An inherited belief is not automatically a personal conviction.

And a strongly held conviction is not automatically a justification for an action.

The maturity of our beliefs should be reflected in how we treat people who disagree with us.

A person's humanity should never depend on whether they worship the same God, practise the same rituals, or accept the same religious teachings as we do.

7. Freedom of Choice Does Not Mean Freedom From Consequences

This is the central message I want everyone to understand.

Life gives us choices, but choices can produce consequences.

If your religious practice involves financial fraud, you may face prosecution.

If it involves violence against innocent people, you may face serious criminal penalties.

If it involves threatening family members who choose a different faith, you may destroy relationships and violate their rights.

If it encourages intolerance, you may contribute to a society where communities become divided by fear and suspicion.

But consequences are not always negative.

A belief system that inspires kindness, honesty, generosity, self-discipline, and peaceful coexistence can also produce positive outcomes.

Likewise, a person with no religious affiliation can live a principled and compassionate life.

The important question is not simply, What religion do you practise?

It is also, What kind of person is that religion helping you become?

I do not believe society should judge every member of a religious community by the actions of extremists, criminals, or manipulative leaders.

Every faith tradition contains individuals with different interpretations, motivations, and behaviours.

We must judge harmful actions fairly rather than assigning collective guilt.

And we must remember that claimed spiritual consequences are different from demonstrable legal, social, financial, and personal consequences.

We may disagree about what happens in the spiritual realm.

But we can still agree that human life deserves protection and that no person should be forced to surrender their freedom of conscience.

8. My Faith Is My Choice. Yours Should Be Yours.

I am not writing this to force Christianity on anyone.

I am writing because I believe religion is too important to be followed without reflection.

I have chosen Christianity because I believe in Jesus Christ, the power of grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the hope of eternal life.

That is my conviction.

You may find meaning in Islam.

You may find spiritual identity in traditional African religion.

You may belong to another faith entirely.

You may choose not to practise religion at all.

We do not have to agree on theology to agree on the value of human life.

We do not have to worship together to coexist peacefully.

And we do not have to abandon our convictions to respect another person's freedom.

However, whatever you believe, I encourage you to understand what your faith asks of you, consider the effects of your practices, and take responsibility for your decisions.

Do not commit atrocities in the expectation of a heavenly reward.

Do not violate another person's dignity because someone promised you supernatural prosperity.

Do not use ancestral customs to imprison the conscience of your descendants.

And do not hide behind religious identity when your actions harm others.

Final Thoughts: Choose Your Faith, But Own Your Actions

At the end of the day, religion is deeply personal, but our actions affect the society around us.

You are free to believe.

You are free to worship.

You are free to question.

You are free to change your mind.

But you are not entitled to harm others and escape responsibility simply because you claim a spiritual justification.

As a Christian, I find peace in the grace of Jesus Christ. I recognise my imperfections, seek forgiveness when I fall short, and understand that faith must be accompanied by responsibility.

I do not expect everyone to share that conviction.

What I expect is that we respect one another's right to choose.

Believe what you want. Worship whom you choose. Follow the spiritual path you sincerely accept. But understand the demands of your beliefs, examine their consequences, and never forget your responsibility to humanity.

Because while religion may shape what you believe happens after death, your actions determine much of the impact you have on people while you are alive.

And that impact matters.

Religion should be a matter of conviction, not coercion. Faith should inspire responsibility, not provide immunity from it.

A question for you: If you had been born into an entirely different religious family, do you think you would still practise the religion you believe in today?

A useful conversation in the right group of 200 people can do more for your business than a generic post shown to 20,000 people who don't care.

That's why niche communities are worth your time. LinkedIn groups, Reddit threads, Slack groups, Discord servers, industry forums. The places where your buyers ask real questions.

Read each community’s rules, including its limits on promotion. Participate because you can contribute something useful.

Spend a few weeks learning how the group works. Answer questions. Share examples. Point people to good resources, even when they aren't yours.

If every comment you leave leads back to your offer, members will notice. Once that trust is gone, it's hard to win back.

Pay attention while you're in there, too. The questions people ask are some of the best content ideas you'll ever find, and they come written in the exact words your customers use.

text:
...Losing a child is a tragedy no parent deserves, regardless of their position, wealth, or past mistakes.

But as I stood there watching him grieve, my mind returned to Angwan Rimi.

I remembered Hauwa.

I remembered the hospital with the freshly painted gate.

I remembered the husband who had knelt down in gratitude for ₦50,000.

And I found myself thinking about the difference between the two families.

One father had access to the best medical facilities his money could afford, yet still lost his daughter.

Another father had watched his wife and unborn child die while searching for basic emergency care.

Both men experienced grief.

But only one had been denied the opportunity to give his family a reasonable chance of survival because essential medical services were unavailable.

And that was what made the comparison so disturbing.

Honourable Danjuma could afford to spend millions trying to save his daughter.

Hauwa's husband couldn't even afford to transport his wife to another hospital without borrowing a vehicle.

The Honourable had access to specialists.

Hauwa had two overworked nurses trying to manage a medical emergency with inadequate equipment.

The Honourable could contemplate an air ambulance.

Hauwa's husband had to beg a neighbour for a car.

Yet the hospital in Hauwa's community had supposedly received public funding for rehabilitation years earlier.

I wondered whether the Honourable ever thought about that.

Whether he remembered the hospital project.

Whether he knew how many women had suffered because that facility remained poorly equipped.

Whether he ever considered that the money allocated to hospitals was not merely a figure in a government budget.

It represented beds.

Medicines.

Laboratories.

Blood banks.

Ambulances.

And sometimes, the difference between a mother returning home with her newborn baby and a husband returning home with two corpses.

Aisha was eventually buried.

The funeral attracted powerful people from across the country.

Governors sent condolences.

Senators visited.

Religious leaders offered prayers.

His colleagues described him as a compassionate man who had dedicated his life to serving humanity.

And perhaps, in his own understanding of compassion, he genuinely believed that description.

After all, he had helped people.

He had paid school fees.

He had sponsored pilgrimages.

He had donated food.

But I have often wondered whether those charitable gestures were enough to compensate for the public responsibilities left unfulfilled during his administration.

Can a man donate ₦5 million to a church and consider himself generous when a hospital under his watch remains without essential equipment?

Can he distribute hundreds of bags of rice and call himself a friend of the poor while the same people are forced to beg for money to treat illnesses that functional public hospitals should be able to manage?

And what happens when such a man genuinely believes he has done nothing wrong?

That is the part I find most difficult to understand.

Because guilt requires a person to recognise that something is wrong.

But what if a man has spent so many years benefiting from a broken system that he no longer sees anything wrong with it?

What if he has convinced himself that government money belongs to whoever controls the government?

What if the applause of his supporters has become louder than the questions his conscience should be asking?

Honourable Danjuma eventually returned to politics.

He continued attending public functions...

text:
Sometimes I wonder why Thomas Tuchel insists on playing Declan Rice and Elliott Anderson together. Both players have quite similar profiles, and I honestly think it should be a case of one starting ahead of the other rather than trying to squeeze both into the same midfield.

The problem with playing them together is that you end up sacrificing creativity. You have two midfielders who are more comfortable doing the defensive work, winning duels, covering ground and progressing the ball, but you need someone who can offer that extra bit of imagination in the final third.

Personally, I'd much rather see a midfield three of Rice, Bellingham and Eze/Josh King.

Rice sits at the base as the DM, Bellingham operates as the left-sided 8, driving forward and arriving in the box, while Josh operates as the 10, finding pockets of space and creating chances.

That midfield offers a much better balance between defensive security, ball progression and creativity.

text:
There is something darkly comedic about watching someone try to disprove "Abrahamic polemics" by practicing the most stereotypical 19th-century missionary habit imaginable: ripping verse 1 out of a Sanskrit ritual manual, slapping a colonial mistranslation onto it, and praying nobody reads verse 4(of the same mantra) 

Open the actual Sanskrit text of Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.1 instead of whatever anti-India Discord server you scraped that quote from. The specific passage you are referring to isn't a cosmic power-ranger tier list; it is the liturgical instruction for the Dīkṣaṇīya Iṣṭi (initiation rite), explaining why a single 11-potsherd rice-cake (puroḍāśa) offered jointly to Agni and Viṣṇu covers the entire Vedic pantheon.

Look at what happens when you read three sentences further than your attention span allowed:

• verse 1: Agnir vai devānām avamo Viṣṇuḥ paramas, tadantareṇa sarvā anyā devatā. (Agni is indeed the avama of the gods, and Viṣṇu is the parama; between them stand all the other deities.)

• verse 2 & 3: Āgnāvaiṣṇavam puroḷāśaṃ nirvapanti dīkṣaṇīyam ekādaśakapālaṃ. Sarvābhya evainaṃ tad devatābhyo 'nantarāyaṃ nirvapanti. (Therefore, they offer the initiation cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu; by doing so, they offer it to all the deities seamlessly, without leaving any out.)

• verse 4: Agnir vai sarvā devatā, Viṣṇuḥ sarvā devatā. (Agni indeed is ALL the deities; Viṣṇu is ALL the deities.)

• verse 5: Ete vai yajñasyāntye tanvau yad Agniś ca Viṣṇuś ca. (These two, Agni and Viṣṇu, are the two terminal bookends/bodies of the sacrifice itself.)

Reading "from Agni to Viṣṇu" as a deity power-ranking-system is like reading "from A to Z" and thinking the alphabet has a personal vendetta against the letter A. 

Confusing ritual Arthavāda (liturgical praise) with sectarian chest-thumping violates the most elementary rules of Mīmāṃsā and Pramāṇa. We learn that “A” is for “Apples” when we’re children in books and 24 years later if you’re unlucky enough to be sitting in a graduate physics class you’ll come to realization everything you learn in school was what you spend unlearning in grad school. 

They’re both in books, we learn them both don’t we? 

If your fingers were burnt by fire but there were a thousand Vedic verse telling you fire is cold, would you try to argue fire is cold or try to figure out what in your chain of interpretation was wrong (if you’re convinced the Vedas are true)? 

Do you think the ancient Vedic Hindus when told their village was on the Ganges they used to lose their heads wondering how houses float o neater instead of assuming that they meant the Lakṣaṇārtha, that it was on a riverbank?

text:
FHE: Love Your Enemies
About 20–30 minutes.

Opening (2 min)
Sing "Love One Another," then have someone say a prayer.

1. Jesus's higher law
- Matthew 5:43–45: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you... that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven."
- Luke 6:27–28: "Do good to them which hate you."
Talk about it: Why is it so much harder to love an enemy than a friend? Why do you think Jesus asks it of us anyway?

2. Jesus showed us how
- Luke 23:34: On the cross, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
- Acts 7:59–60: As Stephen was stoned, he prayed, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge."
Talk about it: What does it take to pray for someone who is hurting you?

3. Overcome evil with good
- Romans 12:20–21: "If thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink... Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
- Story: Alma 17:25–39 and Alma 18. Ammon goes among the Lamanites, who were enemies of his people, and offers to be the king's servant. He protects the king's flocks, and his service opens the king's heart to the gospel.
Talk about it: How did serving his enemies change everything for Ammon and King Lamoni?

4. Burying our weapons
- Story: Alma 24:17–19. The Anti-Nephi-Lehies buried their swords deep in the earth as a covenant with God, and they chose to suffer rather than fight.
- Mosiah 28:3: The sons of Mosiah "could not bear that any human soul should perish."
Talk about it: What "weapons" might we need to bury, like angry words, grudges, or unkind thoughts?

5. Loving enemies makes us free
- Matthew 5:9: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."
- Matthew 6:14–15: "If ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you."
Talk about it: How does holding a grudge hurt us more than the other person? How does forgiving bring peace?

For the kids (5 min): Bury the sword
Give each child a paper "sword" or a craft stick. Ask them to name something unkind we sometimes want to do when someone is mean to us, like hitting, yelling, or saying something mean back. Then let them "bury" their sword in a box of rice, sand, or a blanket. Tell them about the Anti-Nephi-Lehies, who buried their swords and promised God they would never fight again. Then think of one kind thing to do for someone who wasn't nice to us.

Family goal for the week
Pray by name for someone who has been unkind to us, and do one quiet act of kindness for them. Share at the end of the week how it changed the way we feel.

Closing
Bear your testimony that the Savior can soften hearts, ours and theirs, then close with a prayer.

text:
TUESDAY, 1:18 PM — OUTSIDE THE MEETING ROOM

The meeting had officially ended.

Than was packing his laptop when Kavin approached Dunk.

“Hey, are you free for lunch?”

Dunk looked up.

“Yeah, I think so.”

“Good. I know a place nearby.”

Kavin smiled.

“Come with me?”

Dunk hesitated briefly.

Then nodded.

“Sure.”

Joong, who was packing his laptop a few feet away, suddenly became very interested in the contents of his bag.

Nita stood beside him.

“Are you coming with us?”

Joong looked up.

“Where?”

“Lunch. I was thinking of asking Fai and Than too.”

“Maybe.”

Nita smiled.

“Come on. It’ll be fun.”

Joong glanced towards Dunk.

Kavin was already walking beside him.

Dunk turned briefly to say something to Fai.

Then he followed Kavin towards the stairs.

Joong looked back at Nita.

“Yeah. Sure.”

Nita’s smile widened.

“Great.”

And just like that, Joong had agreed to lunch with three people he barely knew because he couldn’t stand the thought of Dunk having lunch with Kavin.

A new personal record.

TUESDAY, 1:34 PM — UNIVERSITY CAFETERIA

Dunk was seated between Phuwin and Kavin.

Figo and Satang had joined them after spotting the group near the cafeteria.

Kavin had insisted on buying lunch for everyone.

Dunk had offered to pay for his own food.

Kavin had refused.

And now, Dunk was beginning to understand that the football captain was not particularly good at accepting no for an answer.

“You didn’t have to buy mine,” Dunk said.

“It’s fine.”

“I can pay you back.”

Kavin smiled.

“You can buy me something next time.”

Figo looked up from his food.

“Oh?”

Dunk kicked him under the table.

Kavin laughed.

“What?”

“Nothing,” Dunk answered quickly.

Satang looked at Figo.

Figo looked at Satang.

They both smiled.

Dunk wanted to disappear.

“So,” Kavin continued, “what are you doing this weekend?”

Dunk looked at him.

“Nothing much. Why?”

“There’s a night market near the stadium. I was thinking of going.”

Figo slowly put down his fork.

Satang stopped drinking.

Kavin smiled.

“Would you like to come with me?”

Dunk blinked.

“Oh.”

“Just the two of us.”

There it was.

The clarification.

Dunk glanced at Phuwin.

Phuwin was suddenly very interested in his rice.

Traitor.

“That’s nice of you,” Dunk began. “But I’m not sure about my schedule yet.”

“No problem. Just let me know.”

Kavin didn’t push further.

He simply smiled and returned to his food.

Figo waited until Kavin turned away.

Then he leaned towards Dunk.

“Just the two of us.”

Dunk closed his eyes.

“Please eat.”

“I’m eating.”

“Then eat quietly.”

TUESDAY, 1:46 PM — SAME CAFETERIA, DIFFERENT TABLE

Joong was not having a good lunch.

He was sitting with Nita, Fai, and Than.

Nita was telling them about a design exhibition she had visited during the semester break.

Fai was listening.

Than was asking questions.

Joong was staring at a table across the cafeteria.

More specifically, at Dunk.

Who was currently laughing at something Kavin had said.

Again.

“Joong?”

He turned.

Nita was looking at him.

“Sorry?”

“I asked if you’ve ever visited the art gallery downtown.”

“Oh. Yeah.”

“When?”

“A while ago.”

Nita smiled.

“We should go sometime. They have a new exhibition coming up.”

Joong nodded politely.

“Maybe.”

Nita leaned closer.

“I’d love to see your work too. You could show me some of your designs.”

“Sure.”

Across the cafeteria, Figo noticed them.

He followed Dunk’s gaze.

Then he looked at Joong.

Then back at Dunk.

Oh.

This was going to be interesting.

“Dunk,” Figo said casually.

“Hmm?”

“Look over there.”

Dunk didn’t want to.

He really didn’t.

But he looked anyway.

And there was Joong.

Sitting beside Nita.

She was smiling at him.

Leaning closer.

Joong was listening.
