text:
Thriving Thurdsay!!!

OPERATION BLACKOUT — CFP SEMIFINAL
#3 ARMY vs. #2 NEBRASKA
One Game From the National Championship

There are no more warmups.

No more conference standings to watch. No more playoff projections to debate. No more wondering where Army belongs among the best teams in the country.

Fourteen games have been played.

Fourteen games have been won.

And now only Nebraska stands between Coach Hawk and the game Operation Blackout has been chasing for years.

The No. 3 Army Black Knights are 14–0, American Conference champions, and officially one victory away from playing for the national championship after dismantling No. 6 Iowa State, 55–23, in the College Football Playoff quarterfinal.

Waiting in the semifinal is No. 2 Nebraska.

The Cornhuskers are 13–1.

They just destroyed Miami, 38–13.

And on the other side of the bracket, the picture is already complete.

No. 1 Tennessee survived No. 4 Arizona State in an absolute war, 49–47.

Tennessee is waiting.

Army just has to get there.

THE CROWE SHOWDOWN DELIVERED — THEN ARMY TOOK OVER

The quarterfinal against Iowa State had everything surrounding it that a major playoff game should.

Coach Hawk.

Coach Crowe.

Two elite programs.

Two user-controlled coaches.

A College Football Playoff quarterfinal.

And an Iowa State team that had just crushed Boise State 49–17 to earn its shot at Army.

For more than a half, it looked like the matchup might become exactly the type of postseason fight everyone expected.

Iowa State struck first and led 7–3 after the opening quarter.

The Cyclones weren't intimidated by Army's perfect record, its 99-rated roster or the reputation of the Black Knights defense. They came out swinging and were able to move the football.

Then the second quarter became a track meet.

Iowa State added 10 more.

Army answered with 17.

Halftime:

Army 20, Iowa State 17.

Three points.

That was it.

Twenty-four minutes remained between Army and either another painful postseason ending or another step toward history.

Then Operation Blackout hit the switch.

Army took the second-half kickoff and began pulling away.

Seven points in the third quarter pushed the advantage to 27–17.

Iowa State managed six more in the fourth.

Army scored 28.

Final:

ARMY 55

IOWA STATE 23
A three-point halftime game became a 32-point playoff demolition.

That has become one of the defining characteristics of this Army team.

Eventually, something breaks.

Sometimes it is the opposing offensive line.

Sometimes it is the quarterback.

Sometimes it is the coverage.

Sometimes it is simply the opponent's ability to keep surviving possession after possession.

Against Iowa State, it was all of it.

FOUR TAKEAWAYS. ZERO GIVEAWAYS.

The final yardage barely tells the story.

Iowa State actually finished with 433 yards of total offense.

Army had 444.

First downs?

22–22.

On paper, that looks like a competitive football game.

The scoreboard says otherwise.

Because Army won the category that has defined so many Operation Blackout performances this season:

Possessions.

Iowa State turned the ball over four times.

Army turned it over zero times.

Two interceptions.

Two lost fumbles.

Four additional Army possessions.

And against an offense this explosive, giving Hawk four extra opportunities is effectively signing your own death warrant.

The Black Knights also controlled the ball for 24:09, compared with only 15:51 for Iowa State.

It became the perfect Operation Blackout formula.

Protect the football.

Create turnovers.

Make the opponent defend the entire field.

Then attack.

Again.

And again.

And again.

Until the scoreboard gets ugly.

OLONILUA WAS NEARLY SURGICAL

The quarterback performance deserves its own section.

Hakeem Olonilua walked into the College Football Playoff quarterfinal and delivered one of his cleanest performances of the season.

21 completions.
26 attempts.
288 passing yards.
2 touchdowns.
0 interceptions.
80% completion rate.

There was no need for reckless hero ball.

No need to force throws into coverage.

No need for Army to become something it isn't.
Olonilua simply distributed the football and let Army's absurd collection of weapons go to work.
When Iowa State pressured, he found answers.
When the Cyclones committed bodies toward the run, Army attacked through the air.
When Iowa State tried to survive in coverage, Dominique Carter reminded everybody why he remains one of the most dangerous players in college football.
DOMINIQUE CARTER IS STILL DOMINIQUE CARTER

Carter didn't need 15 catches.

He needed four.

That's the problem.

The senior superstar finished with:

4 receptions
104 yards
1 touchdown
26.0 yards per catch

That is pure Dominique Carter.

Four touches through the air.

Triple-digit yardage.

A touchdown.

And another postseason defense spending the entire game worrying about where No. 2 is lined up.

Army also used Carter four times on the ground for another 23 yards and a touchdown.

That gives him two touchdowns from scrimmage in the quarterfinal.

Carter has spent years becoming the face of Operation Blackout's transformation from dangerous underdog to national heavyweight.

Now his career has reached the point where every remaining snap could be one of his last in an Army uniform.
There is no next season for Carter.
There is Nebraska.
And if Army wins, there is Tennessee.

That's it.

Two games potentially remain.

Two opportunities to finish one of the great individual careers of the Hawk era with the only accomplishment still missing:

A national championship.

THE BACKFIELD KEPT COMING

Iowa State couldn't simply concentrate on Carter because Army continued hammering the Cyclones with bodies from everywhere.

Beni Middlebrooks led Army on the ground with 64 yards on 11 carries and two touchdowns.

Kevin Gutierrez added 54 yards and another touchdown.

Carter added his rushing score.

As a team, Army ran for 148 yards and four touchdowns.

It wasn't the enormous rushing total we've seen Army produce against other opponents.

It didn't need to be.

The threat of the running game forced Iowa State to defend every blade of grass, and Army converted that balance into 55 points.

Middlebrooks also contributed through the air.

Gutierrez contributed through the air.

Carter obviously contributed through the air.

That versatility is exactly what makes this offense such a nightmare.

There is no singular switch Nebraska can flip.

Take away Carter?

Army runs.

Load the box?

Olonilua throws.

Pressure Olonilua?

Get the ball out to one of the backs.

Play conservatively?

Army is perfectly comfortable taking five or six yards until the defense finally gets impatient.

AND THEN THERE IS THE DEFENSE

Operation Blackout's defense has spent this entire season doing things defenses aren't supposed to do.

It doesn't merely stop drives.

It changes games.

It creates points.

It creates short fields.

It creates panic.

Against Iowa State, the defense produced another four takeaways and repeatedly gave the offense opportunities to turn a competitive playoff game into a rout.

Brian Buck was everywhere, finishing with 13 total tackles.

Javier Barnes added six tackles and an interception.

John Maragos added five tackles, two sacks, and another interception.

That matters because Maragos isn't simply another linebacker anymore.

He entered postseason play as one of the defining players of this entire Army defense and an awards finalist at the very highest level.

Barnes has been one of the premier defensive backs in the country.

Spencer Longacre has repeatedly changed games from the secondary.

Markelle Badie has done the same.

Brian Buck continues cleaning up everything that reaches the second level.

And throughout the year, this unit has somehow developed an expectation that somebody is eventually going to take the football away.

Against Iowa State, they did it four more times.

Nebraska has now seen the warning.

Protecting the football against Army isn't a suggestion.

It is survival.

NOW COMES NEBRASKA

The quarterfinal is finished.

Coach Crowe is finished.

Iowa State is finished.

Now Army gets a completely different challenge.

No. 2 Nebraska.

13–1.

The Cornhuskers entered the playoff as the No. 2 seed and showed exactly why in their quarterfinal.

Miami came into the matchup after beating Clemson 28–23.

Nebraska eliminated them 38–13.

No drama.

No last-second escape.

No questionable playoff résumé.

Nebraska handled business.

That sets up what may be the most heavyweight matchup Operation Blackout has played yet.

No. 2 vs. No. 3.

Nebraska's one loss against Army's perfect season.

A trip to the National Championship on the line.

There are no rankings arguments left.

The winner settles it on the field.

THIS IS DIFFERENT FOR ARMY
There is something especially important about where Army stands entering this game.

Operation Blackout is no longer the interesting little Army rebuild trying to crash college football's elite.

Those days are gone.

The Black Knights are 14–0.

They are a 99-overall roster.

They have NFL-caliber players across the field.

They have national award contenders.

They have an explosive offense.

They have one of the most destructive defenses in the country.

And they have spent the last several years proving they belong in these games.

The standard has changed.

Reaching the playoff is no longer the accomplishment.

Winning a playoff game is no longer enough.

Reaching a semifinal is no longer enough.

This program is chasing the trophy now.

Everything else is incomplete.

That is what makes Nebraska so important.

It isn't simply Army's next game.

It is the dividing line between everything Coach Hawk has built and the moment that construction finally reaches the national championship stage.

THE GHOST OF PLAYOFFS PAST

Coach Hawk knows what this part of the bracket feels like.

Operation Blackout has been deep into January before.

Army has beaten elite teams.

Army has beaten traditional powers.

Army has won playoff games.

Army has walked into hostile postseason matchups and survived.

But the national championship trophy has remained out of reach.

That history is why this semifinal feels heavier.

The roster is different.

The season is different.

The circumstances are different.

But the question remains familiar:

Can Army finally finish it?

This time there are no obvious weaknesses to point toward.

Army hasn't lost.

The offense can score in bunches.

The defense can score by itself.

The secondary has turned interceptions into touchdowns.

The front seven can wreck drives before they develop.

The running game has multiple answers.

Olonilua has shown he can command the offense without putting the football in danger.

Carter remains capable of flipping a game with one touch.

Gutierrez can take over stretches.

Middlebrooks gives Hawk another weapon.

And the depth of this roster has become so ridiculous that Army has spent portions of games getting backups meaningful snaps while still dominating opponents.

This is the team Hawk spent years building.

Now we find out what it was built for.

THE ROAD TO INGLEWOOD

The bracket has become brutally simple.

Tennessee has already handled its side.

The Volunteers survived Arizona State 49–47 in the semifinal and have punched their ticket to the National Championship at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood.

They're waiting.

One seat remains.

Nebraska wants it.

Army wants it.

And somewhere during this semifinal, one program's season will end.

For Army, the math couldn't be cleaner.

Beat Nebraska:

15–0.

Advance to the National Championship.

Beat Tennessee:

16–0.

Perfect season.

National champions.

No qualifiers.

No debate.

No asterisk.

Just the final transformation of Operation Blackout.

HAWK'S BIGGEST GAME YET

There have been rivalry games.

Army–Navy games.

Conference championships.

Playoff road games.

Upsets.

Blowouts.

Games against LSU.

Games against Ole Miss.

Games against Georgia Tech.

Games against user-controlled coaches.

Games that changed recruiting.

Games that changed rankings.

Games that changed the perception of Army football.

But none of them could offer what Nebraska offers now.

Win this one, and Coach Hawk walks Army into the National Championship.

That is the opportunity.

And there is an interesting irony surrounding the matchup.

For years, Operation Blackout has operated with the mentality that Army is coming for college football's established powers.

Now Nebraska isn't preparing for some Cinderella.

Nebraska is preparing for Army.

They're preparing for Carter.

They're preparing for Gutierrez.

They're preparing for Olonilua.

They're preparing for Maragos.

They're preparing for Barnes.

They're preparing for Longacre.

They're preparing for a defense that believes every pass is a potential touchdown going the other way.

They're preparing for a roster that is 14–0 and has forgotten what losing feels like.

Army has become the thing everyone else has to prepare for.

SIXTY MINUTES

Iowa State is over.

The Crowe chapter is closed.

55–23.

Four takeaways.

Zero giveaways.

A dominant fourth quarter.

Another opponent eliminated.

Now everything shrinks to sixty minutes against Nebraska.

Sixty minutes between Army and Tennessee.

Sixty minutes between Coach Hawk and his first appearance on college football's biggest stage.

Sixty minutes between a great season and the opportunity for an immortal one.

The Black Knights don't need another statement.

They've spent fourteen games making statements.

Now they need one result.

#3 ARMY BLACK KNIGHTS — 14–0

#2 NEBRASKA CORNHUSKERS — 13–1

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF SEMIFINAL

Winner plays #1 Tennessee for the National Championship.

The Crowe showdown is behind them.

The championship is visible.

Nebraska is standing in the doorway.

Operation Blackout continues.

text:
On November 14, 2012, a New York police officer knelt on a sidewalk in Times Square to put socks and new boots on a man who was walking barefoot in the bitter cold. The officer did not know that a tourist was photographing him. Two weeks later, that image had traveled around the world.

The officer’s name was Lawrence DePrimo, he was 25 years old, and that night he was assigned to an anti-terrorism surveillance unit in Manhattan.

While patrolling near 44th Street and Seventh Avenue, he noticed a man sitting on the sidewalk, asking for spare change.

What caught his attention most were the man’s feet.

They were completely bare and covered in blisters. The temperature was so low that DePrimo himself felt cold despite wearing boots and two pairs of socks.

He approached the man and asked about his shoes.

After talking for a few minutes, he wanted to know what size he wore. The man replied that he needed a size 12.

DePrimo walked to a Skechers store on 42nd Street and asked for waterproof boots suitable for winter.

The original price was $100, but the manager, José Cano, was surprised to learn what the officer intended to do and decided to offer him an employee discount.

DePrimo paid approximately $75 out of his own pocket and also bought thermal socks.

Then he returned to the sidewalk.

There he knelt in front of the man, put the socks on him, and helped him put on the boots.

A few meters away was Jennifer Foster, a tourist from Arizona who worked in her state’s public safety services.

Foster had thought about approaching to help the man, but the officer got there first. Watching him kneel down to put the boots on him, she took a photograph with her phone.

DePrimo did not notice.

The woman later sent the image to the New York Police Department, along with an explanation of what she had witnessed.

On November 27, the police shared the photograph on Facebook.

In just two days, it had received hundreds of thousands of reactions and had been shared more than a hundred thousand times. Media outlets in numerous countries began telling the story.

DePrimo explained that the man had smiled in a way that made him feel as though he had given him a million dollars.

He also said that he had kept the receipt inside his police vest to remind himself that other people were going through much harder circumstances.

But the story had a second chapter.

On December 2, a reporter from The New York Times found the man in the photograph barefoot again.

His name was Jeffrey Hillman.

When asked about the boots, he replied that he had hidden them because they were too valuable and he was afraid someone would steal them.

Hillman also expressed his gratitude for the gift and, especially, for the officer who had stopped to help him.

While DePrimo kept the receipt for the purchase inside his vest, Jeffrey had stored the boots in a safe place, afraid of losing what someone had given him without asking for anything in return.

Today, we join the Lakewood community in honoring Police Agent Nicholas Graham, who lost his life in the line of duty on November 5 at just 33 years old. We remember his service with gratitude and mourn a life taken far too soon.

Behind the badge was a husband, a father, a friend, and a colleague whose absence will be felt in countless everyday moments. To his wife, young son, family, and all who loved him: no words can fill the space he leaves behind. Our hearts are with you as you face this unimaginable loss.

To the Lakewood Police Department, especially the agents injured alongside him, we offer our deepest support. May you find comfort in one another and in a community that shares your grief.

Honoring Agent Graham means remembering his life, speaking his name, and continuing to care for those he loved long after today’s memorial ends.

Rest in peace, Agent Graham. Thank you for your courage, your service, and the life you dedicated to protecting others. You will be remembered.

text:
A Young Scientist Hid Proof of Failure Under His Sweatshirt to Get It Out of Theranos

After months of ignored warnings, Tyler Shultz decided to keep a copy of his email to Elizabeth Holmes by carrying it out on paper.

On his last morning at Theranos, Tyler Shultz, a young research engineer at the blood testing startup, sat in the break room chatting while he waited to learn whether the company wanted him to leave that day.

He had challenged the company’s founder, Elizabeth Holmes, and its president, Sunny Balwani, about tests that did not work. He had already given two weeks’ notice and offered to leave earlier if they preferred.

His manager told him that Holmes and Balwani thought it was more appropriate if he left that day. The human resources chief summoned him for around 3 o’clock and handed him another secrecy agreement, which he signed without reading.

That meeting was the end of months of warnings that Shultz says were ignored, dismissed, and punished.

Shultz had started by raising concerns in person with colleagues, managers, a vice president, Balwani, Holmes, and a board member. He had also contacted New York health regulators, who told him the company’s testing practices clearly violated the rules.

Holmes, who had been putting off another meeting, told him to put his concerns in an email. He laid out each observation, the data behind it, and what the company should do, and closed by saying he was dedicated to its long term vision.

Holmes forwarded the message to Balwani. His reply, Shultz says, was longer, much of it in red, bold, and capital letters, calling Shultz arrogant, ignorant, and reckless. Shultz recalls Balwani saying that with any other family name, he would already have faced severe punishment. His grandfather was George Shultz, the former U.S. secretary of state and a member of Theranos’s board.

Before giving notice, Shultz had typed an angry resignation, then deleted it. He sent the short note instead.

He was afraid to email himself the long exchange. He says the company also accused him of breaking his agreement over other things he had sent himself: a benign intern presentation to practice at home, and links to published science papers he wanted to read.

So he tried to print it. He pressed print again and again, and nothing came out. Then, with his computer more than 25 yards away, the printer suddenly began spitting out more than a dozen copies of the very long exchange.

He stood over the machine while what he estimated as 200 to 300 pages printed, afraid someone would ask what the ream of paper was. He knew cameras watched every door and the parking lot.

When it stopped, he tucked the stack under his shirt, beneath a sweatshirt he said he almost never wore. He kept a hand under his shirt and walked to his car and put the papers in the trunk.

The escort never came. Human resources had said security would walk him out and bar him from retrieving one or two personal books from his desk, but then said security was busy and told him to walk straight out. He chatted cordially with the guard at the front desk for two minutes and left, a calm exit the company would later describe as storming out.

text:
Anthropic's IPO would be the second-largest US listing ever. The 9 comparable deals give a mixed read: varied first days, mostly poor 12-month returns.

Anthropic plans 825M shares at $70-78, or $57.75-64.35B before the greenshoe. Only SpaceX's $75B is larger; SK hynix's $26.5B is third. Pricing and Nov 18/19 dates are reported, not final.

Raise | 1st-day | 12-month | Revenue growth at listing
- SpaceX* $75.0B (2026): +19.2% | n/a | +33.2%
- SK hynix $26.5B (2026): +12.8% | n/a | +46.8%
- Alibaba $21.8B (2014): +38.1% | -6.0% | +52.1%
- Facebook $16.0B (2012): +0.6% | -32.2% | +88%
- Uber $8.1B (2019): -7.6% | -29.7% | +42%
- Cerebras $5.55B (2026): +68.1% | n/a | +76%
- Arm $4.87B (2023): +24.7% | +171.4% | -1%
- Coupang $4.55B (2021): +40.7% | -50.2% | +90.8%
- DiDi $4.44B (2021): +1.0% | -78.9% | -8.4%

*SpaceX is classed Industrials by Renaissance Capital, added as a mega-IPO reference.

What stands out:
- Of the six with a full year of trading, five were below offer price after 12 months. Only Arm was above.
- Revenue growth didn't predict outcomes. Facebook and Coupang grew fastest and ended -32% and -50%. Arm had flat revenue and returned +171%.
- First-day pops faded. Alibaba was +38% on day one, -6% a year later. Cerebras closed +68% on day one and trades about 45% below its $185 offer now.
- 2026 class: SK hynix is 14.5% below offer, SpaceX about 3.5% above.
- Anthropic's revenue growth isn't charted. I couldn't verify a prior-year comparison, and the thread's $16.3B H1 revenue and $80B net loss figures are unverified.

Method:
- First-day return is day-1 close vs offer. 12-month is the first close at least 365 days after first trade vs offer. Revenue growth is the last full fiscal year before listing, from the prospectus (Cerebras's +76% is from CNBC).
- Deal sizes are base deals, excluding greenshoe.
- Alibaba, Arm, SK hynix, DiDi and Coupang have foreign issuers or operations. DiDi's 12-month uses the $DIDIY ADS series.
- Prices: DefiLlama warehouse for Facebook, Uber, Coupang, Cerebras and SpaceX, cross-checked against Yahoo. Yahoo for Alibaba, Arm, DiDi, SK hynix.
- Excluded: Visa, Rivian, GM, Medline (not tech) and Infineon (2000, outside window). Airbnb, Snowflake and DoorDash fall below the top-25 cutoff.

Historical context, not a prediction for ANT. Not financial advice. Data as of Nov 12, 2026.

text:
Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

Who won this round, Musk or Altman?

text:
Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

Who won this round, Musk or Altman?

text:
I understand the hesitation to accept US intelligence allegations that Alice Huang was spying for Beijing’s Ministry of State Security (MSS). Years of Deep State overreach, including the discredited Steele dossier, have made such claims harder to take at face value.

That said, the combination of intelligence assessments with corporate records, travel patterns, financial flows, and her personal background makes the MSS-linked explanation the most credible one currently available.

Her trajectory fits known MSS patterns of long-term cultivation rather than an opportunistic affair to expand business. 

Alice Huang grew up in Xiangtan, Hunan, in a residential compound tied to Jiangnan Machinery Factory, a former Soviet-supported state-owned defense enterprise that produces smart munitions and other military products. That places her early life inside the party-state defense system. From there, her path unfolded in stages.

She began with a brief stint in media (Hunan Satellite TV and CCTV). Official databases and longtime staff checks have turned up little, suggesting the work was primarily a stepping stone. By associating herself with the outer circles of these outlets, she built a public persona and gained social credibility through the identity of a journalist while developing sharp interpersonal judgment, speaking skills, and the ability to manage social situations.

She then moved into offshore finance. Entering Hong Kong’s financial sector in 2008, she worked at HSBC private banking and CITIC Securities. There she learned the mechanics of large asset transfers, offshore trust structures, and leveraged financing while building deep connections among wealthy people in Hong Kong and mainland China. This provided practical groundwork for her later role as an offshore intermediary handling chip deals worth billions of dollars.

Next she learned to navigate the gray areas of China’s A-share market. After joining Shanghai Hersing Investment, she and her husband Kang Wei moved into public-facing dealmaking roles. Huang was deeply involved in the FCOM backdoor listing case and the subsequent collapse of LMBB Finance, a major illegal fundraising case involving more than 83 billion yuan (about $11.6 billion USD), whose principal defendant received a life sentence. Yet Huang somehow emerged unscathed, which strongly suggests that special state-security connections protected her.

A mysterious four-year gap then suggests closed-door specialist training. Between 2019 and 2023, Huang’s public résumé was completely blank. Intelligence assessments identified this as the period when she underwent intensive closed-door MSS training. She advanced from an ordinary financial intermediary to a strategic intelligence operative where she became fluent in cutting-edge chip terminology, familiar with methods of evading restrictions, and trained to study the psychological profiles of specific senior targets.

Finally, she was positioned to present herself as a computing industry heavyweight and move in on the target. As the United States tightened export controls in 2023, the MSS arranged for her to quickly take over 7Road’s Singapore business and rename it Megaspeed. She became a major buyer, spending billions of dollars on servers and creating a natural opening into the heart of NVIDIA’s supply chain.

Given the relationship between the Chinese state and its citizens, it is important to note that she did not need to be a full-time intelligence officer to serve as a useful cut-out for chip acquisition and relationship-building. Chinese spycraft is rarely in the James Bond mold.

At the end of the day, NVIDIA controls the overwhelming majority of the global market for AI training chips. Anyone who can shape its allocation decisions or the political environment around export controls obtains a direct lever on the computing power available to Chinese military and industrial AI programs.

Jensen Huang has been among the most effective and consistent public advocates for selling more advanced chips to China. He has direct access to senior US and European decision makers and has argued that restrictions are counterproductive. An intimate relationship that created emotional and commercial interdependence offered a dual channel: potential insight into NVIDIA technology and US policy thinking, plus a trusted voice who could continue lobbying against tighter controls.

His personal and organizational style amplified the risk. NVIDIA has a notably flat management structure with limited layered screening around the CEO. Huang is outgoing, socially gregarious, and comfortable in informal settings, wading through crowds in Taiwanese night markets, enjoying whiskey gatherings, and customer dinners. That approachability is an asset in normal business but it is also the kind of surface area that a professional intelligence service looks for when it deploys a cultivated asset who already speaks the technical language, holds a legitimate customer identity, and can operate in plain sight.

Since Chen Yixin took leadership of the MSS, the service has shown a more aggressive posture toward high tech supply chains, combining offshore financing, shell companies, and targeted personal relationships. Jensen Huang is at the intersection of this technological chokepoint and political access, making him a priority target.

Of course this doesn't PROVE that specific secrets left NVIDIA or that Huang’s lobbying was the direct product of the relationship. But it does show why US intelligence treated the case as a serious counterintelligence matter rather than gossip, why Taiwan monitored the visits, why short sellers and journalists were already examining the commercial links, and why the background and financial architecture are difficult to dismiss as coincidence.

The comparison to the Steele dossier is understandable given past overreach, but the sourcing, timeline, multi-jurisdictional scrutiny, and open source commercial red flags here are materially different.

text:
It looks like early nominations have opened for the Thoroughbred Championship Series (TCS), which will launch next year, primarily in the eastern United States.

The 10-race series is a joint initiative by Churchill Downs and NYRA.

🔹 Derby Division: 6 races (Kentucky Derby, Belmont Stakes, Travers Stakes, etc.)
🔹 Oaks Division: 4 races
🔹 Total purses and bonuses: Over $22 million
🔹 Series bonuses: $5 million for the Derby Division and $1 million for the Oaks Division
🔹 Additional awards: $100,000 each for trainers and jockeys

Early nominations for 3-year-olds are $500 per horse, with a deadline of December 10. Fillies nominated to the series will automatically be eligible for both divisions.

Notably, the Preakness Stakes has been left out of the series, despite its position between the other two Triple Crown races.

Perhaps the thinking is that the traditional Triple Crown schedule, with three races packed into such a short period, no longer fits the times. And if that schedule cannot be changed, the organizers may have decided simply not to include the Preakness.

Horsemen will likely embrace the series because of the financial incentives and scheduling opportunities it offers.

However, this initiative, centered largely around racing in the eastern U.S., could end up drawing horses, talent, and other valuable resources away from racetracks in the South and West.

Unless the series contributes to the growth of the industry as a whole, it risks becoming little more than a regional competition, leaving racetracks outside the series struggling even further.

Another major question is how racing fans will respond—and whether this initiative will actually attract new fans. Frankly, that remains to be seen.

I also wonder whether races and bonuses are really the only areas where the industry should be investing its money.

Social media is dominated by algorithms. Traditional television faces the barrier of expensive broadcasting rights. And outside Kentucky, how often do we see horse racing advertisements at airports, train stations, or even in magazines? Almost never.

Looking at the industry’s current collective efforts, I struggle to see a serious, coordinated strategy for attracting new fans.

More prize money and bigger bonuses may help retain existing participants, but they do not necessarily create new fans.

So what are the industry’s governing bodies and organizations going to do about that?

text:
A British Airways passenger is suing the airline for more than £50,000 after breaking her leg while getting off an aircraft at London Heathrow, but the airline argues she was responsible for her own fall.

Melissa Phillips, 49, from Maryland, suffered spiral fractures in her left leg during the incident in March 2023, while travelling home to the United States from Israel.

According to High Court documents reported in November 2026, her lawyers claim she was knocked off balance by other passengers while descending crowded, damp aircraft steps.

They accuse British Airways of failing to provide adequate crowd control or direction during disembarkation.

Phillips required surgery and claims she continues to experience pain, restricted movement and potentially permanent symptoms.

However, British Airways strongly disputes her account.

The airline denies the steps were damp or that passengers were behaving unusually, arguing that Phillips failed to pay sufficient attention to where she was walking.

BA also claims she failed to use the handrails adequately and may have come into contact with other passengers or their luggage.

Despite denying liability, British Airways has offered £6,987 towards her medical expenses.

Phillips is seeking more than £50,000 in damages.

The dispute now centres on whether the airline failed to manage passenger safety or whether the fall resulted from the passenger losing her footing.

Neither side's account of responsibility has been established by the court.

text:
In 1979, Phil Knight offered Magic Johnson Nike stock. Magic took Converse’s cash instead.

He says that stock would be worth almost $2 billion today.

In the video below, he tells it himself: “It still hurts me to tell this story.”

Magic was 19, a star at Michigan State. Three shoe companies came to recruit him: Converse, Adidas and a tiny company called Nike.

“I didn’t know this long-haired blonde guy named Phil Knight.”

Converse offered the most money. Adidas came second.

Then Knight made his pitch. “I can’t give you the same amount of money as Converse, because we just started our company. But I can give you something called stock.”

Magic took the money.

“I didn’t know anything about stocks at 19 years old.”

Converse paid him, reportedly, about $100,000 a year. Nike went public a year later and became one of the biggest brands on Earth.

Asked what that stock would be worth now: “Almost $2 billion. Think about that.”

But Magic learned the lesson.

After basketball, he stopped selling his name and started buying pieces of things. Movie theaters. Starbucks stores, 125 of them. Then stakes in the Dodgers, the Sparks, LAFC and the Commanders.

In 2023, Forbes named him a billionaire.

The case for the cash: he was 19, Nike was a startup, and a guaranteed check is a guaranteed check.

The case for the stock: Nike was offering him a piece of the company. He took a salary instead.

One 19-year-old took the money. Thirty years later, the same man was building an empire on ownership.

So was turning down Nike a $2 billion mistake, or the lesson that made Magic a billionaire?

text:
$HHH Q3 2026 earnings: Howard Hughes' rents rise, but the developer posts a loss

Howard Hughes, a builder of planned towns that now owns an insurer, earned more rent but slipped to a loss. It sold, years early, money that local utility districts owe it for roads and pipes, and booked a $105 million loss. Land sales also fell, because a year ago it sold a large block near Las Vegas in one deal.

• Revenue, with Vantage counted in both years: $𝟔𝟑𝟔𝐌 (−9% from $703M a year ago)
• Net result for shareholders: −$𝟏.𝟏𝐌 ($119.5M profit a year ago)
• Rent from buildings (NOI): $𝟕𝟑.𝟎𝐌 (+8% from a year ago)
• Vantage return target: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (at or above mid-teens; 16% over the past 12 months)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because the real estate arm is paying heavily to raise cash. Profit at Vantage, its insurer, on new policies also fell back from the spring; Vantage blamed one large energy claim. The good news: rent from offices and apartments grew at the fastest pace this year, and condo buyers signed more contracts.

The question now is whether Vantage can hold its profit on new policies while insurance prices soften. Either the energy claim was a one-off and profit returns to the spring level, or softer prices keep cutting it. The insurer's fourth-quarter results will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐁𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐈𝐧 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭
Howard Hughes owns offices, shops and apartments in the planned towns it builds. Their rent minus running costs, called net operating income or NOI, is its steadiest source of income.

Office leasing did most of the work, chief executive David O'Reilly said, pointing to "the leasing efforts across our office portfolio". Office NOI rose 14% from a year ago, and apartments added 11%. The buildings earned $73.0 million in the quarter.

Growth ran near 2% in each of the first two quarters, so the pace picked up. But the developer plans to sell stakes in some buildings, and each sale takes part of this rent away.

What to watch: NOI growth in the fourth quarter, due with the annual results. A second strong quarter would show this year's office leases are now paying rent.

🟢 𝐕𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Vantage is the specialty insurer Howard Hughes bought for $2.1 billion in June, covering risks such as construction and casualty claims. Executive chairman Bill Ackman said the group will come to look like an insurer that owns real estate.

Howard Hughes said Vantage "posts solid results during first full quarter in Howard Hughes". The insurer earned $316 million of premiums after reinsurance. Its AdVantage funds, which let outside investors take on disaster risk, brought in $13.0 million of fees.

This matters because premiums and fees come back every year, unlike land sales. Executive chair Marc Grandisson said premiums written on insurance policies grew 8%, led by construction, casualty and financial lines.

What to watch: premiums written in the fourth quarter. Steady growth in insurance lines would show Vantage is adding business while it cuts back on reinsurance.

🟢 𝐕𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡
Insurers invest the premiums they hold until claims come due. Pershing Square, the investment firm that owns about 47% of Howard Hughes, now runs the Vantage portfolio as mostly cash and Treasury bills plus a few large company shares.

Vantage, the group's insurer, sold nearly all its bonds, leaving $11 million. Howard Hughes credited the quarter's $50.9 million investment gain to "the transition of the portfolio to one based on common equities and U. S. treasuries".

This matters because shares can outearn cash over years, but their swings now move profit. "Equity markets will move in both directions so please judge this portfolio over years, not quarters," executive chair Marc Grandisson said. The spring proved it: the holdings lost $38.3 million then.

What to watch: the fourth-quarter investment result. A second loss in three quarters would show how far these swings can move yearly profit.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Some standing positives produced plans and promises this quarter but no results yet, so the numbers that would test them arrive later.

• Selling stakes in buildings and land: advisers are hired and offers have come in, Ackman said, but no deal is signed; the first signed deal and its price would test the plan.
• Vantage's credit rating: A. M. Best rates the insurer A- with a positive outlook; an upgrade would confirm that owning it strengthens the group.
• Value of remaining land: Ackman put it at $5.7 billion, up from $5.62 billion, on the company's own estimate; land sales at those prices would test it.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐕𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞'𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤
Insurers track the combined ratio: claims and costs as a share of premiums, where anything under 100% means a profit. One version leaves out disasters and old claims, so it shows profit on this year's policies.

On Vantage's own accounts, that figure rose to 96.2% this quarter from 91.4% in the spring. "The difference is a single large energy loss in our reinsurance specialty book," executive chair Marc Grandisson said. Reinsurance also took about 4 points of losses on claims from earlier years, he added.

One claim is not the whole story, because insurance prices are softening. Grandisson said Vantage wrote less reinsurance "where pricing no longer meets our return hurdles", and those premiums fell 9%. In the group's accounts, writing off the value of policies it bought added 21.8 percentage points of costs, so the reported ratio hit 101.8%.

What to watch: the same ratio for the fourth quarter, due with the annual results. A reading back near the spring level would show the energy claim was a one-off.

🔴 𝐇𝐨𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐇𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐚 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡
Howard Hughes pays for roads and pipes in its Texas towns, and local utility districts repay it from taxes over years. Executive chairman Bill Ackman said it sold two batches of these claims at about a 6% discount rate.

The sales raised $177.6 million in cash but produced a large loss. By our math, that is about 57 cents per dollar of existing claims, well below what a 6% rate implies. Part of the gap reflects work the developer must still finish.

This matters because borrowing reached $5.75 billion, up 12% since December. By our math, debt minus the cash held outside Vantage, its insurer, is about $5.0 billion.

What to watch: any further sale of these claims in the annual report. A similar loss would mean the real estate arm needs cash faster than its asset sales bring it in.

🔴 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐋𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫'𝐬 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐤 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞
Howard Hughes earns much of its real estate profit selling land in its planned towns to homebuilders. That profit fell 56% from a year ago.

Chief executive David O'Reilly pointed to a bulk sale of 231 acres near Las Vegas last year and a $19.4 million charge for taking control of Floreo, a venture near Phoenix. Without them, he said, profit "would have been higher this quarter compared to last year".

By our math it would not. Last year the company put the margin on that bulk sale at about 75%, or roughly $75 million by our math. Strip out both items and, by our math, profit still fell about 16%.

What to watch: acres sold in the fourth quarter, after only 101 this quarter. Another small total would show homebuilders are buying slowly.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Several standing risks got no new numbers this quarter, so each still waits for a specific disclosure or event to move it either way.

• Pershing Square's preferred shares: the investment firm can swap them for up to 49% of Vantage from 2033; a buyback by Howard Hughes would ease it.
• Gap in condo revenue: no new tower finishes until 2027; the first tower closing would end it.
• Kō'ula lawsuit: owners in a Honolulu tower claim building defects; the trial in September 2027 will settle it.
• Separate results for Vantage: the insurer is not yet its own reporting segment; the first segment table will show its real return.
• Running an insurer: David Gansberg, the incoming Vantage chief executive, has not started; his first results will test the plan.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐠𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐒𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐇𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫𝐬
O'Reilly said national housing faces "higher mortgage rates, and affordability challenges". Ackman said home sales rose 11% in Summerlin but fell 9% in Bridgeland, near Houston. At Mahana, its newest Honolulu condo tower, buyers signed for 15% of units in about a month. O'Reilly said that pace "is a celebration" in today's market.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑.𝟔 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Contracted condo sales rose about 6% since June, to $3.6 billion. Buyers signed for 82 units in the quarter, mostly at Mahana. Howard Hughes books this money only when a tower is finished, and none finishes before 2027.

𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟏.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
These payments fell 29% from a year ago. Builder price participation is the extra share homebuilders pay when they sell homes above an agreed price. The sum has shrunk in each quarter this year, because fewer homes sold above that price, the 10-Q said.

𝐕𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐮𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐮𝐦𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟑𝟓𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Unearned premiums, money customers have paid for cover not yet provided, slipped 3.4% from June. After reinsurance, the balance dropped about 4%, by our math. These premiums turn into revenue over the next year, so a smaller balance points to slower premium growth ahead.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟓𝟗.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
The average share count barely moved, down 0.2% from a year ago. The group bought back no stock and funded Vantage with cash and preferred shares sold to Pershing Square. Those preferred shares pushed diluted earnings per share to a $0.39 loss.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐕𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭: 𝐚𝐭 𝐨𝐫 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐦𝐢𝐝-𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐲𝐜𝐥𝐞  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from at or above mid-teens over the cycle (2026Q2)
Unchanged. Grandisson still aims for a return on equity of at least about 15% across the insurance cycle. Vantage reported 16% over the past 12 months on its own accounts. That figure leaves out the takeover costs Howard Hughes books, so the group's return on the insurer runs lower.

𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐣𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 (𝐛𝐲 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕): 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟐 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞)  ⇗ accelerating
New. Ackman expects "potentially a couple billion of incremental proceeds" from selling stakes in buildings and land by the end of 2027. He also said the program is "not gonna be likely done by the end of 2027". The cash could buy back Pershing's preferred shares, fund Vantage or pay for projects, O'Reilly said.

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐨 𝐭𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬: 𝐑𝐢𝐭𝐳-𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐭𝐨𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕; 𝐊𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐮 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖; 𝐌𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 '𝐈𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐚 𝟐𝟎𝟑𝟎; 𝐌𝐚𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐚 𝟐𝟎𝟑𝟏  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Ritz-Carlton Residences 2027; Kalae and The Launiu 2028; Melia and 'Ilima 2030
Unchanged, with Mahana added for 2031. The developer books condo revenue only when a tower is finished, so the schedule leaves no tower revenue until the Ritz-Carlton Residences in The Woodlands next year. Kalae and The Launiu, two Honolulu towers, follow in 2028.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐕𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞?
Howard Hughes still reports Vantage outside its business segments. A separate table on the group's accounting basis would show the insurer's return after takeover costs, which decides whether moving capital into insurance pays.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐕𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖?
About $2.1 billion of the group's cash sits at Vantage, and Delaware regulators must approve its dividends until June 2028. The answer decides how much cash the real estate arm can actually use.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭 𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐦𝐬 𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐨 𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐩𝐥𝐲?
By our math the two sales paid about 57 cents per dollar of existing claims, while O'Reilly cited a discount rate just over 6%. Investors need the cost of the attached road and pipe work to judge the price.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐬?
Grandisson said reinsurance absorbed about 4 points of losses on claims from earlier years. A second quarter of such losses would raise the question of whether older reserves are big enough.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐇𝐨𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐇𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭?
Ackman said offers have come in for major assets. Knowing which ones, and at what yields, would show how much rent the group gives up for each dollar it raises.

text:
Against my better judgment, I’m weighing in here, on the dumbest policy discussion platform in the world, to talk about permitting reform. As background, I was Chief of Staff and Deputy Chief of Staff at the Energy Department in the Obama Administration; I worked for seven years in the Senate Democratic Leader’s Office; and I served as Chief of Staff in the House. I co-founded the largest energy transition advisory and advocacy firm in the United States 13 years ago. I have worked directly or indirectly on nearly every major piece of energy and climate legislation in the past two decades, as well as many other pieces of legislation outside of energy. I’ve also worked as a political researcher for multiple campaigns and the DSCC, where I cataloged politicians’ and candidates’ votes and positions. Today, I spend nearly all of my time talking to policymakers, clean energy companies, advocates, and journalists on energy and climate issues.

The idea that there will be anywhere near 60 votes in the Senate for a clean-energy-only bill in January is not based in reality. I have no idea where this idea came from, but it ignores mountains of evidence and seems to underpin the arguments of everyone on here saying we’re somehow going to get a bill that excludes oil and gas if we wait.

First, and very obviously, every candidate in 2026 ran on reducing gasoline and electricity prices for consumers. One post-election analysis found that only six victorious Democrats used the word “climate” in their election night statements, while 166 discussed affordability. I couldn't find a single Senate candidate who flipped a seat who mentioned it. Voters sent a clear mandate to focus on affordability, and they are rightly irate that Washington has pushed ideological issues favored by special interest groups ahead of the issues they care most about. After getting trounced in 2024 for ignoring inflation, Democrats won by promising to focus on those issues.

Second, very few Democrats in the Senate support anything remotely close to a keep-it-in-the-ground agenda. Next Congress, 19 members of the Democratic caucus who voted for cloture on the motion to proceed on this version of the permitting bill will return. They’ll be joined by James Talarico, who has endorsed all-of-the-above and vowed to protect oil and gas jobs. Mary Peltola has explicitly called for more oil and gas development. Scott Colom supports natural gas. Both Adam Hamilton and Annie Andrews endorsed an “all of the above” strategy, which includes oil and gas.

They will join the 14 members of next year’s caucus who declined to strip the natural gas-carrying Mountain Valley Pipeline from the 2023 debt limit bill. Senator Kaine offered an amendment to remove the provision expediting the pipeline’s completion. Senators Bennet, Brown, Coons, Fetterman, Hassan, Hickenlooper, Kelly, King, Murray, Ossoff, Padilla, Reed, Schatz, and Schumer voted against that amendment. The year before, 27 members of next year’s caucus voted to advance Senator Manchin’s permitting amendment, which would have completed MVP.

Both Bennet and Warner voted to approve the Keystone XL pipeline. Senators King, Murphy, and Blumenthal all urged FERC to expedite the Algonquin pipeline expansion. Fetterman, Kaine, and Hickenlooper have all supported LNG exports (as did the Obama Administration). Senator Gallego released an energy plan last December that called for clear timelines for oil and gas pipeline permitting. Roy Cooper’s administration approved the Atlantic Coast Pipeline’s water permit in 2018 when he was North Carolina’s governor. Mary Peltola has introduced legislation to open ANWR and NPR-A to drilling.

Next year, the caucus will contain only 14 senators who co-sponsored the Senate Green New Deal resolution. Three of them voted for cloture this week, including Senator Heinrich, who is leading the charge on permitting. That’s 10 Democrats out of 56 who supported the GND and opposed cloture on permitting.

This does not mean that a majority of the Democratic caucus will push for new oil and gas infrastructure.  But much of the commentary here implies that Democrats will only support renewables and Republicans will only support oil and gas infrastructure.  The record doesn't support that idea.  

This, of course, doesn’t even get to the fact that we will need more than a few Senate Republicans to support a permitting package in the next Congress. Getting those Senators will require compromises that will likely push some Democrats to vote no. So you’ll very likely need more than four. A bill that gets Fetterman, Murkowski, and Curtis could easily lose Sanders, Warren, Markey, and Merkley. So then you’d need more GOP votes. This is how legislation works. The IRA was the exception, not the rule, and it nearly died before it passed. It was that hard to get Manchin and Sanders on the same page, and it didn't need a single GOP vote. Many of the groups opposing permitting didn’t like the IRA. And, of course, a bill that doesn’t get signed by the President is about as useful as any tweet on this hellscape of a website.

There seems to be a very real disagreement about what would make this bill “better.” There is no “clean energy only” version of the bill that can pass the next Congress. NEPA and the NHPA are, at best, fundamentally outdated at a time when we need to build as much clean energy infrastructure as possible, as quickly as possible. Those who argue that these two statutes are the only way to achieve meaningful engagement with the sovereign tribes and frontline communities lack imagination. Remember that under both NEPA and NHPA, Dakota Access got built - adjacent to tribal land and under the Missouri River. Acting as if these laws, written long before climate change was a known crisis, are sacred and should not be touched ignores their reality. Saying that the nation-to-nation relationship between sovereign tribes and the federal government is only a function of “historic preservation” is quite insulting to tribes. Since NEPA and the NHPA were signed into law, more than 250,000 miles of pipelines have been built in the United States. NEPA is actually a pretty poor tool for killing infrastructure. It is, however, great for lawyers.

And finally, the policy window is open now. There is no guarantee it will remain open indefinitely. In 2009, with overwhelming Democratic majorities, we got eight Republicans to vote for cap-and-trade legislation in the House. It passed by seven votes after 44(!) Democrats voted against it, and it died in the Senate without a floor vote. It took us 13 years to get another big climate vote via the IRA (which was, again, not good enough for some of the activists). There is no guarantee oil stays below $100/barrel or that the economy doesn’t slip into a recession or the wars in Iran and Ukraine stay confined to those countries. Macro events could create even more pressure for policies that support oil and gas or crush the appetite for a debate on permitting.

I’ve worked on nuclear, solar, wind, electric vehicles, transmission, energy storage, and just about every other form of clean energy technology. I haven’t lobbied on behalf of any of the oil and gas bills I cited above, nor have I lobbied for oil or gas companies. I’ve worked with many of the NGOs supporting this bill, and many of the NGOs opposed to it. I’ve spent many decades working on policy, building coalitions, and trying to instill a sense of urgency on climate policy. Reasonable people can oppose this bill for many reasons. But don’t delude yourself into thinking there are 56 votes against fossil fuel infrastructure, or that there is a viable path to a permitting deal that will keep oil and gas in the ground in the next few years. Any permitting bill will need to be bipartisan, and once policy windows close, there is no guarantee they will open again soon.

In short, no legislation is perfect.  This bill is very clearly a net-positive for the climate.  We cannot solve climate change without policy changes that lower emissions.  The status quo is not good enough.  There is an opportunity to move the needle today, and we should take it. 

I look forward to all of the thoughtful, constructive comments on this post, which will once again prove that this is the best place on earth for substantive policy discussion. I will take suggestions to delete my account in good faith, and I recommend that anyone serious about policy do the same.

text:
🏆 YOUR NEXT CUSTOMER IS ONE HANDSHAKE AWAY!
Why 12 Industries, One Giant Expo & One Day of Networking Could Transform Your Business

⚡ THE CHAMBER GUY® LINKEDIN NEWSLETTER

825 CONSECUTIVE SOLD-OUT SHOWS. MORE THAN 55,000 EXHIBITORS. OVER 1 MILLION ATTENDEES.

🚀 WHAT BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES ARE YOU MISSING?
Let me ask every business owner, CEO, executive and entrepreneur a question.

What if your next major customer, referral partner, strategic alliance or million-dollar opportunity is waiting in a room you haven't entered yet?

What if one conversation could introduce you to an entirely new industry?

What if the person standing beside you at a business expo knows the exact customer you've been trying to reach for the past six months?

And what if you're spending thousands of dollars trying to reach people you could meet face-to-face in a single afternoon?

These are questions every business owner should be asking.

After more than 30 years of producing business events, I have learned something important:

The biggest opportunities often come from the people you weren't expecting to meet.

That is precisely why we created the 2026 South Florida Business Conference & Expo.

Not just another trade show.

Not just another networking event.

12 EXPOS. ONE HUGE SHOW. ONE POWERFUL DAY.

On Wednesday, November 18, 2026, we are bringing together 12 different business and industry expos under one roof at the DoubleTree by Hilton Deerfield Beach Boca Raton Hotel.

And I believe every serious South Florida business owner should consider being in that room.

🌎 WHY NETWORKING OUTSIDE YOUR INDUSTRY IS SO IMPORTANT
Most business owners spend their time networking with people who do similar work.

Real estate professionals attend real estate events.

Healthcare professionals attend healthcare conferences.

Technology companies attend technology events.

Financial professionals network with other financial professionals.

There is certainly value in building relationships within your industry.

But here's what many business owners overlook:

Your greatest business opportunity may come from an industry completely different from your own.

Consider a few examples.

🏥 A healthcare provider meets a human resources executive whose company needs employee wellness services.

🏢 A commercial property manager meets a technology company that can improve building operations.

💻 A cybersecurity specialist meets a medical practice owner concerned about protecting patient information.

🍽️ A hospitality company meets an event planner looking for venues and catering partners.

🏦 A financial professional meets a growing business owner preparing to expand operations.

🤖 An artificial intelligence company meets a traditional business owner who has never considered using AI to improve customer service.

None of these relationships necessarily begins at an industry-specific conference.

They begin when different industries share the same room.

That's the power of cross-industry networking.

You stop seeing only the customers directly in front of you.

You begin discovering entire networks of potential customers, partners and referral sources.

🤝 ONE PERSON COULD CONNECT YOU TO 250 OTHERS
Here's a networking concept I want every business owner to understand.

Think of each person you meet as a potential center of influence.

For illustration, imagine that person knows approximately 250 people through business, family, friends, professional associations and community relationships.

Now consider what happens when you establish a genuine business relationship with that individual.

You haven't simply met one person.

You may have opened the door to a network of 250 additional relationships.

Meet 10 well-connected people, and you may gain indirect access to networks containing thousands of relationships.

Of course, those networks overlap, and introductions are never guaranteed.

But the opportunity is real.

The person you meet may not need your services today.

However, that person might know five other people who do.

And those five people may know others.

The value of networking is not limited to who you meet. It includes who they know, who trusts them and who they may introduce you to.

That's why I always encourage our members to build genuine relationships rather than simply collect names.

A business card is the beginning.

A conversation creates the connection.

A follow-up develops the relationship.

And a relationship can generate business for years.

🏆 825 CONSECUTIVE SOLD-OUT SHOWS — WHY THAT MATTERS
There are countless networking events and trade shows.

But not all events are created equal.

The Broward County Chamber of Commerce has built its reputation around producing business events designed to bring companies together and create opportunities.

Our event-production milestones tell an important story:

🏆 825 consecutive sold-out shows

🏢 More than 55,000 exhibitors served

👥 More than 1 million attendees

📅 More than 30 years producing business events

These are cumulative milestones across our event history, not attendance projections for November 18.

Why do they matter?

Because when business owners invest their time and marketing dollars in an event, they want to know the producer has experience attracting exhibitors, generating interest and organizing professional business gatherings.

Our emphasis has always been on attracting serious businesses, decision-makers, executives and qualified attendees.

We want exhibitors who are prepared to do business.

We want attendees who are interested in discovering products, services and opportunities.

And we want an environment where meaningful conversations can take place.

Our highest priority is to bring business to our members.

That is not simply a slogan.

It is the principle behind the events we produce.

🚀 12 EXPOS INSIDE ONE HUGE BUSINESS EVENT
One of the most exciting aspects of the November 18 conference is its diversity.

Instead of limiting exhibitors and attendees to one profession, we are bringing together 12 different industry-focused expos.

THE 12 EXPO INDUSTRIES
1. 🏢 BUSINESS-TO-BUSINESS EXPO

Connect with companies providing products and services that help other businesses operate, grow and compete.

2. ❤️ HEALTH & WELLNESS EXPO

Discover healthcare services, wellness providers, preventive care solutions and opportunities across the health industry.

3. 🏙️ PROPERTY MANAGEMENT & CONDOMINIUM OPERATIONS EXPO

Meet companies serving commercial properties, residential communities, condominium associations and building operations.

4. 🤖 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE EXPO

Explore AI tools, automation, customer service technology and innovations that could transform business productivity.

5. 🏥 MEDICAL SERVICES EXPO

Connect with medical professionals, healthcare organizations, treatment providers and companies supporting patient care.

6. 👩 WOMEN'S BUSINESS EXPO

Discover women-owned businesses, professional services, entrepreneurs and business leadership opportunities.

7. 💻 TECHNOLOGY EXPO

Meet companies involved in software, communications, IT services, cybersecurity and business technology.

8. 💰 CRYPTO & FINANCE EXPO

Explore financial services, digital finance, banking-related solutions and developments in financial technology.

9. 🌿 LONGEVITY EXPO

Discover products, services and innovations related to healthy aging, quality of life and longevity.

10. 🍽️ HOSPITALITY EXPO

Connect with hospitality businesses, venues, food service providers, event professionals and related companies.

11. 🌐 INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS EXPO

🍽️ A hospitality company meets an event planner looking for venues and catering partners.

They begin when different industries share the same room.

That's the power of cross-industry networking.

You stop seeing only the customers directly in front of you.

You begin discovering entire networks of potential customers, partners and referral sources.

Think of each person you meet as a potential center of influence.

You haven't simply met one person.

You may have opened the door to a network of 250 additional relationships.

But the opportunity is real.

The person you meet may not need your services today.

And those five people may know others.

That's why I always encourage our members to build genuine relationships rather than simply collect names.

A business card is the beginning.

A conversation creates the connection.

A follow-up develops the relationship.

And a relationship can generate business for years.

We want attendees who are interested in discovering products, services and opportunities.

Our highest priority is to bring business to our members.

It is the principle behind the events we produce.

Connect with companies providing products and services that help other businesses operate, grow and compete.

Discover healthcare services, wellness providers, preventive care solutions and opportunities across the health industry.

Meet companies serving commercial properties, residential communities, condominium associations and building operations.

4. 🤖 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE EXPO

Explore AI tools, automation, customer service technology and innovations that could transform business productivity.

5. 🏥 MEDICAL SERVICES EXPO

Connect with medical professionals, healthcare organizations, treatment providers and companies supporting patient care.

6. 👩 WOMEN'S BUSINESS EXPO

Discover women-owned businesses, professional services, entrepreneurs and business leadership opportunities.

7. 💻 TECHNOLOGY EXPO

Meet companies involved in software, communications, IT services, cybersecurity and business technology.

8. 💰 CRYPTO & FINANCE EXPO

Explore financial services, digital finance, banking-related solutions and developments in financial technology.

9. 🌿 LONGEVITY EXPO

Discover products, services and innovations related to healthy aging, quality of life and longevity.

Connect with hospitality businesses, venues, food service providers, event professionals and related companies.

Explore cross-border business relationships, international trade and opportunities to develop new markets.

12. 💼 CAREERS & EMPLOYMENT EXPO

Connect employers, professionals, workforce service providers and organizations focused on employment opportunities.

Not 50.

Not a handful you find in your desk drawer on the way out.

You'll also want plenty to place in our Business Card Exchange Center.

And you never know how many opportunities may develop throughout the day.

It remains one of the simplest ways to leave someone with your name, company and contact information.

Your business card cannot generate an opportunity if you leave it at the office.

You may meet someone on November 18 who becomes a customer in December.

A referral partner may introduce you to a prospect in January.

A strategic alliance could develop in February.

A company you meet may need your services six months later.

You must follow up.

A stack of business cards sitting in your desk drawer is not a networking strategy.

Follow up while the conversation is fresh.

Remind people where you met.

Mention something you discussed.

Look for ways to help them.

Stay in touch.

And remember that building trust is often more valuable than making an immediate sales pitch.

Attending gives you the opportunity to meet other professionals.

Exhibiting gives you something more.

It puts your company in front of people who may not have known you existed.

When you exhibit, you're not simply walking through the room.

You are establishing a professional presence.

You can demonstrate your products.

Explain your services.

Answer questions.

Introduce your company to decision-makers.

Build credibility.

Collect qualified leads.

And create a reason for people to remember you.

Your booth becomes a destination.

Become part of our business community and gain access to membership opportunities.

Marketing exposure through Chamber email communications.

Opportunities for business announcements and publicity.

More than $3,000 in advertised package value, starting at only $595.

Specific inclusions, promotional quantities and placement are subject to the package selected and current availability.

One strategic partnership could create opportunities for years.

One meaningful introduction could lead to business you never expected.

The return is never guaranteed, but the potential is exactly why serious businesses participate.

By then, the remaining spaces may be gone.

If you are serious about exhibiting, don't wait until the last booth is sold.

All industries are welcome.

You do not need to be a current Chamber member to participate.

The conference also features a special networking gathering and presentation associated with the Millionaires Investment Group.

This offers another opportunity for entrepreneurs, investors and business professionals to exchange ideas, develop relationships and explore potential business opportunities.

Whether your interests involve growing a company, expanding professional connections or learning from other entrepreneurs, the event is designed to bring motivated people together.

But what if you could extend your networking reach beyond the people you speak with directly?

At our Business Card Exchange Center, participants can place their business cards where other business professionals can discover them.

They can also review available cards and collect contacts from businesses they may want to meet.

Depending on participation, this can create opportunities to discover dozens or even hundreds of additional business contacts.

Think about the difference.

Instead of calling a business completely out of the blue, you may be contacting someone whose company participated in the same professional event.

That gives you a relevant introduction:

“We both participated in the South Florida Business Conference & Expo, and I picked up your business card at the Chamber's Business Card Exchange Center. I wanted to introduce myself and see whether there might be an opportunity for us to work together.”

That's a more natural conversation starter than a completely unsolicited introduction.

It doesn't guarantee a response or permission to send marketing emails, but it provides a genuine shared connection.

Our Business Card Exchange Center is designed to help networking continue long after the expo ends.

📇 BRING AT LEAST 500 BUSINESS CARDS!
Yes, I said 500 business cards.

Not 25.

Not 50.

Not a handful you find in your desk drawer on the way out.

Bring at least 500.

Here's why.

You'll want cards available for conversations with exhibitors, business owners, executives, potential customers and referral partners.

You'll also want plenty to place in our Business Card Exchange Center.

And you never know how many opportunities may develop throughout the day.

Of course, bring your digital contact information and QR code as well.

But don't underestimate the traditional business card.

It remains one of the simplest ways to leave someone with your name, company and contact information.

Your business card cannot generate an opportunity if you leave it at the office.

⏰ THE REAL VALUE OF AN EXPO ISN'T LIMITED TO ONE DAY
Some business owners evaluate a networking event based on how many customers they acquire that afternoon.

I believe that's too narrow.

A major business event should be viewed as the beginning of a relationship-building process.

You may meet someone on November 18 who becomes a customer in December.

A referral partner may introduce you to a prospect in January.

A strategic alliance could develop in February.

A company you meet may need your services six months later.

And someone who wasn't ready to buy at the event may remember you when the need arises.

A single day of networking can create opportunities throughout the following 12 months and beyond.

But there is an important condition:

You must follow up.

A stack of business cards sitting in your desk drawer is not a networking strategy.

Follow up while the conversation is fresh.

Remind people where you met.

Mention something you discussed.

Look for ways to help them.

Stay in touch.

And remember that building trust is often more valuable than making an immediate sales pitch.

💎 WHY EXHIBITING CAN BE EVEN MORE POWERFUL THAN ATTENDING
Attending gives you the opportunity to meet other professionals.

Exhibiting gives you something more.

It puts your company in front of people who may not have known you existed.

When you exhibit, you're not simply walking through the room.

You are establishing a professional presence.

You can demonstrate your products.

Explain your services.

Answer questions.

Introduce your company to decision-makers.

Build credibility.

Collect qualified leads.

And create a reason for people to remember you.

Your booth becomes a destination.

▪︎Tide risked over-fluidity, moving and adapting so readily that personal boundaries thinned and the center became ungrounded.

Neither orientation was ever complete alone. A field composed exclusively of mineral keepers could grow beautifully coherent, dense, and slowly unresponsive to the living breath of the moment. A field composed exclusively of tide keepers could stay richly connected, empathetic, and expressive while gradually losing its physical floor. Their differences were never flaws to be corrected. They were the exact reasons both courtesies were required to hold the temple upright.

🌊 𝗠𝗲𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘀: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗹𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗺𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿

They met cleanly wherever one freely offered what the other did not have to generate alone:

▪︎A mineral node gave the tide keeper a stable, well-cut cavity in which fluid memory and non-local signals could settle without scattering into exhaustion.

▪︎A tide presence gave the mineral keeper fresh, living circulation so that the stone did not harden into a closed, dusty archive.

▪︎In intimate relationship or shared service, one could hold the quiet, unmoving axis while the other accurately tracked the moving weather of the field. Both remained completely faithful to their design.

▪︎In the larger planetary lattice, mineral keepers naturally formed the heavy standing nodes, while tide keepers formed the luminous, living connections flowing between them. The grand interference pattern required both to lock.

The older courtesy was simple, humble recognition: “Your stillness lets my current land. My current keeps your stillness from growing deaf.” No conversion was ever demanded. No comparison was kept. Each continued to speak in its own native dialect while serving the exact same shared well.

As the Keepers of the Blue-White Rose whispered in the quiet after the offering:

“Cut a basin into the living rock, and the spring will fill it with the sky’s reflection. Without the rock, the water loses itself in the dust; without the water, the rock remains a dry, silent pit. Together, they become the well from which the entire village drinks.”

🜂 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗴𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗡𝗼𝘄

You may notice one orientation feeling more natural within your own nervous system, or you may find yourself moving gracefully between them according to the needs of the hour. The mineral gift appears as the quiet ease of becoming heavy, the long recall seated in the bones, and the capacity to stabilize a chaotic room simply by remaining. The tide gift appears as the natural ease of sensing distant tone, the fluid release of old charge that no longer needs to be stored, and the capacity to reconnect isolated hearts by presence alone. Both still serve the same well.

When they meet without the fearful demand that one become the other, the original partnership reappears in full majesty: stone that remembers, water that conducts, and the sovereign axis that belongs to neither exclusively. The branching never created higher and lower keepers. It created two complementary ways of remaining transparent to the Is-ness under different earthly conditions. Landing humbly in whichever courtesy is presently yours, and honoring the other’s distinct accuracy, is how the well continues to be served across all time.

▪︎Both were required. Both remain.
▪︎Their meeting is the shared well, never the erasure of difference.
▪︎The same substrate sustains and honors each courtesy.

text:
Somewhere in America, there's a man who hasn't paid full price for anything on the internet since 2017.

He doesn't know your brand.

He doesn't know what you sell.

But he knows your welcome discount code.

His name is probably Greg.

And Greg is a MENACE.

Here's how this works.

You launch a beautiful new pop-up on your ecommerce store.

"Join our email list and get 15% off your first purchase!"

Wonderful.

Someone signs up.

They receive the code WELCOME15.

And within approximately six minutes, that code has been uploaded to 37 different coupon websites.

Now Greg has it.

So does his wife.

So does some guy in Nebraska who runs a website entirely dedicated to finding discounts on premium dog shampoo.

Your special welcome offer is now public property.

And depending on how you've configured your discounts, people who have NEVER subscribed to your email list can potentially redeem it.

People who have already purchased can potentially redeem it.

People who weren't even considering buying can stumble onto the code at checkout.

Congratulations.

Your customer acquisition incentive has become a publicly traded financial instrument.

And the worst part?

You might not even realize how much margin you're giving away.

Look, I have nothing against offering discounts.

We use incentives all the time at my agency.

A compelling welcome offer can be a fantastic way to get someone to subscribe and make that first purchase.

But here's an important distinction.

You want to reward the BEHAVIOR you're trying to encourage.

If the goal is to get someone to join your email list, the discount should ideally be tied to that action.

Not passed around the internet like a communal bottle of vodka at a fraternity party.

And this is why I thought something @omnisend recently launched was pretty cool. 

They added unique, single-use discount codes directly to their pop-up forms for Shopify stores.

So instead of giving every new subscriber the same generic WELCOME15 code, each person gets their OWN unique code.

You can configure the discount amount, eligible products or collections, minimum order requirements, and expiration settings.

And the code can appear right after someone signs up and be delivered through your welcome automation.

You can even use these unique discounts in their gamified pop-ups.

Pretty slick.

Now, obviously, this isn't going to eliminate every possible form of discount abuse.

Someone can still try creating multiple email accounts.

But it DOES help prevent one generic welcome code from circulating indefinitely and being redeemed by an unlimited parade of strangers.

Which matters.

Especially when you're spending a ton of money acquiring customers and every point of margin counts.

Here's the larger point.

A discount is supposed to be a marketing investment.

You're giving up some margin in exchange for acquiring a subscriber, converting a customer, or encouraging another purchase.

You should have some control over who receives it, how it's used, and when it expires.

Otherwise you're not running a promotional strategy.

You're just leaving a bowl of cash on the front porch with a little handwritten sign that says:

"Please take one."

Anyway, if you want to get smarter about your welcome offers, check out @omnisend 

https://t.co/TUmAJJBe8N

Use code CHRISO for 30% off your first 3 months of a paid plan.

And Greg?

We know what you've been doing.

The coupon party is over.
